rubric_with_answers.question_text: e). Explain the concept of Transfer Learning. Discuss how pre-trained models are used to solve new tasks with limited data and mention common applications of transfer learning.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Discuss how pre-trained models are used to 
solve new tasks with limited data and mention common applications of transfer learning. 
Concept 
Transfer Learning leverages knowledge learned from one task/domain (source) to improve 
learning on another related task/domain (target). It is especially beneficial when target 
data are scarce but related source data/model exist. 
Mechanisms of transfer 
 Feature reuse: early layers of deep models learn general features (e.g., edge 
detectors in CNNs, subword/semantic patterns in NLP models). These features are 
transferable across related tasks. 
 Fine-tuning: take a pre-trained model, freeze some layers (usually early ones), and 
retrain later layers on the new dataset. Optionally, unfreeze more layers for gradual 
fine-tuning. 
 Head replacement: remove the original output layer and attach a new head specific 
to the target task; train the head (and optionally some earlier layers). 
 Domain adaptation: techniques to adjust model when source and target distributions 
differ (e.g., adversarial domain adaptation). 
When transfer learning helps 
 Limited labeled data in target domain. 
 Relatedness: source task features must be relevant to target task (e.g., ImageNet 
pretraining -> medical imaging often transfers well for low-level image features). 
 Large pre-trained models (BERT, GPT, ResNet) provide strong starting points. 
Applications 
 Computer vision: using ImageNet-pretrained CNNs for image classification, object 
detection, or medical image analysis. 
 Natural language processing: pre-trained language models (BERT, RoBERTa, GPT) 
fine-tuned for sentiment analysis, QA, NER, etc. 
 Speech/audio: pre-trained audio models adapted for speaker recognition or audio 
event detection. 
 Reinforcement learning: transferring policies or representations across similar 
environments. 
Benefits and pitfalls 
 Benefits: faster convergence, better performance with limited data, lower training 
cost. 
 Pitfalls: negative transfer (when source is too different), overfitting if fine-tuning 
without regularization, and licensing/privacy constraints for some pre-trained models. 
Conclusion 
Transfer Learning reuses prior knowledge to accelerate learning and improve accuracy on 
new tasks — a practical and powerful strategy in modern ML workflows.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: f). What are Hyperparameters in Machine Learning? Explain why they are important and describe common hyperparameters for algorithms like Decision Trees, Neural Networks, and Gradient Boosting models.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Definition 
Hyperparameters are external configuration settings set prior to training that control 
model structure and learning dynamics (e.g., learning rate, tree depth). They are distinct 
from model parameters (weights) learned during training. 
Why they matter 
 They govern model capacity (overfit/underfit balance), optimization dynamics, and 
computational cost. 
 Appropriate hyperparameter tuning improves performance and generalization; poor 
choices can render even good algorithms ineffective. 
Examples by algorithm 
 Decision Trees / Random Forests: max_depth, min_samples_split, min_samples_leaf, 
criterion (gini/entropy), n_estimators (in forests). 
 Neural Networks: learning_rate, batch_size, num_epochs, optimizer (SGD/Adam), 
activation functions, network architecture (num_layers, units_per_layer), 
dropout_rate. 
 Gradient Boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM): n_estimators, learning_rate, max_depth, 
subsample, colsample_bytree, reg_alpha/reg_lambda. 
Tuning strategies 
 Grid search: exhaustive search over specified parameter grid. Computationally 
expensive. 
 Random search: samples hyperparameter space randomly — often more efficient. 
 Bayesian optimization: models the objective function and selects promising 
hyperparameters (e.g., HyperOpt, Optuna). 
 Sequential model-based optimization (SMBO): iteratively proposes hyperparameters 
based on past trials. 
 Early stopping / cross-validation: used to prevent overfitting and select 
hyperparameters robustly. 
Conclusion 
Hyperparameters are levers to steer model learning and complexity; systematic tuning 
using validation data and efficient search methods is essential for high-quality models.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: a). Explain the main steps involved in data preprocessing in machine learning.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Overview 
Data preprocessing readies raw data for machine learning; clean, consistent and well
structured inputs markedly improve downstream model performance. 
Main steps 
1. Data collection & inspection: gather data, check types, distributions, missingness, 
outliers. 
2. Missing value handling: impute (mean/median/mode, model-based, KNN/iterative 
imputation) or remove rows/columns depending on context. 
3. Outlier detection and handling: visualize (boxplots, z-score, IQR), treat via capping, 
transformation or investigation if they are valid. 
4. Data cleaning / consistency: correct erroneous labels, unify categorical encodings, fix 
types. 
5. Encoding categorical variables: one-hot encoding, ordinal encoding, target encoding 
(careful of leakage). 
6. Feature scaling: normalization or standardization as required by model. 
7. Feature engineering & selection: create informative features, remove redundant ones 
using correlation analysis, mutual information, recursive feature elimination. 
8. Data splitting: divide into training/validation/test sets (stratify if class imbalance). 
9. Data augmentation (if needed): for images/text to expand dataset. 
10. Pipelines: build reproducible pipelines (e.g., scikit-learn Pipeline) to ensure same 
transforms applied in production. 
Conclusion 
Preprocessing is iterative and domain-dependent; automation and reproducibility reduce 
mistakes and ensure reliable model evaluation and deployment.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: b). What is ensemble learning? Describe the working of bagging and boosting methods.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Ensemble learning definition 
Ensemble learning combines multiple base models to produce a single improved model — 
leveraging diversity among learners to reduce error. 
Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) 
 Train several base learners (often same model type) on bootstrapped samples of 
training data (sampling with replacement). 
 Aggregate predictions by majority vote (classification) or averaging (regression). 
 Effect: reduces variance and overfitting (Random Forest is bagging applied to 
decision trees). 
Boosting 
 Train learners sequentially; each new learner focuses on mistakes of prior ensemble 
(reweights samples or fits residuals). 
 Combine learners in weighted sum to form final prediction (additive model). 
 Effect: reduces bias and builds strong learners from weak ones (e.g., AdaBoost, 
Gradient Boosting, XGBoost). 
Comparison 
 Bagging: parallel, reduces variance. 
 Boosting: sequential, reduces bias (but can increase susceptibility to noise). 
Conclusion 
Ensemble methods often outperform single models and are primary choice for tabular data 
competitions; they require care with overfitting and interpretability.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: e). Explain the role of optimization algorithms in training machine learning models.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Purpose 
Optimization algorithms adjust model parameters to minimize the loss function on training 
data; they are the mechanism by which learning happens. 
Key concepts 
 Gradient-based updates: compute gradients of loss w.r.t parameters and step in the 
negative gradient direction (steepest descent). 
 Learning rate: step size controlling update magnitude; critical for convergence and 
stability. 
 Variants to improve convergence and stability: 
o Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD): updates using mini-batches — more 
efficient and introduces helpful noise. 
o Momentum: accelerates convergence by accumulating a velocity term. 
o Adaptive methods (AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam): scale learning rates per
parameter based on historical gradients — often improve convergence, 
especially for sparse or noisy gradients. 
Role in practice 
 Determine convergence speed, stability, ability to escape shallow local minima/saddle 
points. 
 Influence generalization indirectly (e.g., SGD noise can improve generalization). 
Conclusion 
Optimizers are central to model training; choice and hyperparameters (learning rate, 
momentum, batch size) significantly impact training dynamics and final model quality.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: f). What is dimensionality reduction? Describe any one method used for it.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Definition and motivation 
Dimensionality reduction reduces the number of input variables (features) while preserving 
as much relevant information as possible. It aids visualization, reduces computational cost, 
mitigates the curse of dimensionality, and can help reduce overfitting. 
Method — Principal Component Analysis (PCA) 
 Idea: find orthogonal directions (principal components) that capture maximal 
variance in the data. 
 Procedure: center data, compute covariance matrix, compute 
eigenvectors/eigenvalues, sort components by explained variance, project data onto 
top-k components. 
 Benefits: linear, unsupervised, reduces redundancy by transforming to an uncorrelated 
basis. 
 Limitations: linear method — cannot capture strong nonlinear manifolds (use t-SNE, 
UMAP, or autoencoders for nonlinear structure). 
Conclusion 
Dimensionality reduction simplifies models and improves interpretability; choose method 
(linear vs nonlinear) based on data structure and application.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: g). Explain how a decision tree works and mention its advantages and disadvantages. --- PAGE 2 ---
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain how a decision tree works and mention its advantages and disadvantages. 
How it works 
A decision tree partitions the input space by asking a sequence of questions (splits) on 
features. At each internal node it selects the best split (feature and threshold/category) 
by optimizing a criterion (e.g., Information Gain, Gini impurity for classification; variance 
reduction for regression). Splitting continues recursively until stopping conditions (max 
depth, minimum samples per leaf, or pure nodes) are met. Leaves represent predicted 
outputs (class label or regression value). 
Advantages 
 Interpretability: model logic is transparent and easily visualized. 
 Little preprocessing: handles mixed feature types and does not require scaling. 
 Nonlinear: captures nonlinear relationships and interactions between features. 
Disadvantages 
 Overfitting: single trees can overfit training data if not pruned. 
 Instability: small changes in data can result in different tree structure. 
 Bias-variance tradeoff: needs parameter tuning (depth, leaf size) and regularization; 
ensembles (Random Forest, boosting) mitigate many issues. 
Conclusion 
Decision trees are intuitive and useful for baseline modeling and interpretability; for robust 
predictive performance on complex data, ensembles of trees are typically preferred.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: b). Describe the K-Nearest Neighbor algorithm. Explain its working step-by-step and discuss the importance of the parameter k.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
The K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) algorithm is a non-parametric, supervised machine learning 
method used for both classification and regression tasks. It operates on the principle that 
similar data points tend to exist in close proximity. 
Working Steps of KNN: 
 Choose the value of K:  
The first step involves selecting the number of nearest neighbors, represented by the 
parameter k, that will be considered for making a prediction. 
 Calculate Distance:  
For a new, unclassified data point (query point), the algorithm calculates its distance to 
every other data point in the training dataset. Common distance metrics include Euclidean 
distance, Manhattan distance, or Minkowski distance. 
 Identify K Nearest Neighbors:  
After calculating all distances, the algorithm sorts them in ascending order and selects 
the k data points that are closest to the query point. These k points are the "nearest 
neighbors." 
 Make a Prediction: 
 For Classification: The algorithm determines the class label of the query point by taking a 
majority vote among its k nearest neighbors. The class that appears most frequently 
among these neighbors is assigned to the query point. 
 For Regression: The algorithm predicts the value of the query point by taking the average 
(or weighted average) of the values of its k nearest neighbors. 
Importance of the Parameter K: 
The choice of k is crucial and significantly impacts the performance of the KNN algorithm: 
 Small K (e.g., K=1):  
A small k makes the model highly sensitive to noise in the data and can lead to 
overfitting. If k=1, the query point is simply assigned the class or value of its single 
closest neighbor, making it vulnerable to outliers. 
 Large K:  
A large k can smooth out the decision boundary and reduce the impact of noise. However, 
if k is too large, it might include neighbors from different classes, leading to underfitting 
and a less accurate model, as it might fail to capture local patterns. 
 Optimal K:  
The optimal value of k depends on the specific dataset and problem. It is typically 
determined through techniques like cross-validation, where different k values are tested, 
and the one yielding the best performance (e.g., highest accuracy) is selected. A common 
practice is to choose an odd value for k in classification to avoid ties when voting.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: c). What is Data Imbalance in Machine Learning? Explain its impact on model performance and discuss techniques used to handle
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
it. 
Data imbalance is when a dataset has a skewed class distribution, leading to poor model 
performance as algorithms favor the majority class. This can be handled with techniques 
like resampling (oversampling, undersampling), using appropriate evaluation metrics, and 
employing methods like cost-sensitive learning or generating synthetic data.  
Impact on model performance  
 Model bias: Models tend to become biased toward the majority class because they 
are often optimized to minimize overall error, leading to poor predictions for the 
underrepresented minority class. 
 Inaccurate metrics: Standard metrics like accuracy can be misleading. For example, a 
model that always predicts the majority class in a dataset with a  
95%95 % 
95% 
majority class will have a  
95%95 % 
95% 
accuracy, even though it's completely ineffective at identifying the minority class. 
 Poor generalization: The model may overfit to the majority class and fail to 
generalize to new, unseen data, which is particularly problematic in applications like 
fraud detection or medical diagnosis where minority class identification is critical.  
Techniques to handle data imbalance  
 Resampling: 
o Undersampling: Randomly remove samples from the majority class to balance 
the dataset. 
o Oversampling: Randomly duplicate samples from the minority class to balance 
the dataset. 
o SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique): Generate synthetic 
samples for the minority class instead of just duplicating existing ones. 
 Algorithmic approaches: 
o Cost-sensitive learning: Modify the learning algorithm to penalize 
misclassifications of the minority class more heavily than misclassifications of 
the majority class. 
o Ensemble methods: Combine multiple models, often trained on different 
resampled subsets of the data, to improve overall performance. Examples 
include Balanced BaggingClassifier.

o Use appropriate metrics: Focus on metrics like precision, recall, F1-score, or 
the ROC AUC score, which are more informative than accuracy for imbalanced 
datasets.

sensitive to the minority class.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: d). Explain the working of Gradient Boosting in detail. Discuss how it builds models sequentially and how weak learners are combined to form a strong model.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Gradient Boosting is an ensemble method that builds models one after another. Each new 
model tries to correct the errors made by the previous model. 
Steps: 
1. Start with an initial model (like predicting mean). 
2. Calculate the residuals (errors). 
3. Train a new weak learner (like decision tree) on these residuals. 
4. Add the predictions to the previous model with a learning rate. 
After many rounds, a strong model is created.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: e). Explain the concept of Transfer Learning. Discuss how pre-trained models are used to solve new tasks with limited data and mention common applications of transfer learning.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Discuss how pre-trained models are used to 
solve new tasks with limited data and mention common applications of transfer learning. 
Transfer learning is the process of using a pre-trained model (already trained on a large 
dataset) and adapting it for a new related task with less data. 
For example, models trained on ImageNet can be fine-tuned for medical image 
classification. 
Steps: 
1. Load a pre-trained model. 
2. Freeze early layers (which capture general features). 
3. Replace or retrain later layers for new classes. 
Applications: Image recognition, NLP (using BERT, GPT, etc.), and speech analysis.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: g). Explain how a decision tree works and mention its advantages and disadvantages. --- PAGE 2 ---
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain how a decision tree works and mention its advantages and disadvantages. 
A decision tree is a supervised machine learning algorithm used for both classification and 
regression tasks. It operates by creating a model that predicts the value of a target 
variable by learning simple decision rules inferred from the data features. 
How a Decision Tree Works: 
 Root Node:  
The process begins with a single root node representing the entire dataset. 
 Splitting:  
The algorithm then identifies the best feature to split the data based on a chosen 
criterion (e.g., Gini impurity or information gain for classification, mean squared error for 
regression). This split divides the data into subsets, creating child nodes. 
 Recursive Partitioning:  
This splitting process is repeated recursively on each child node until a stopping condition 
is met. This condition could be that all data points in a node belong to the same class, 
the node contains a minimum number of samples, or further splitting does not 
significantly improve the model's performance. 
 Leaf Nodes:  
The final nodes in the tree, which are not further split, are called leaf nodes. Each leaf 
node represents a predicted outcome or class. 
 Prediction:  
To make a prediction for a new data point, it traverses the tree from the root, following 
the decision rules at each internal node until it reaches a leaf node, which provides the 
prediction. 
Advantages: 
 Interpretability:  
Decision trees are easy to understand and visualize, resembling a flowchart, making the 
decision-making process transparent. 
 Handles various data types:  
They can work with both numerical and categorical data without extensive preprocessing. 
 No feature scaling required:  
Unlike some other algorithms, decision trees do not require feature scaling or 
normalization.  
 Handles non-linear relationships:  
They can capture complex, non-linear relationships between features and the target 
variable.  
 Feature importance:  
Decision trees inherently provide a measure of feature importance, indicating which 
features are most influential in making predictions. 
Disadvantages: 
 Overfitting:  
Decision trees can be prone to overfitting, especially with complex trees, leading to poor 
generalization on unseen data. Pruning techniques are often used to mitigate this. 
 Instability:  
Small changes in the data can lead to significant changes in the tree structure, making 
them somewhat unstable. 
 Bias with imbalanced data:  
If one class significantly dominates the others in a classification problem, the tree might 
be biased towards the majority class. 
 Computational cost:  
Building a complex decision tree can be computationally expensive, especially with a large 
number of features and data points.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: a) Explain the different types of Machine Learning evaluation metrics used for classification and regression tasks. Describe how accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, help in understanding model performance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score are used to evaluate classification models, with 
accuracy being the overall correct predictions and precision/recall focusing on specific types 
of errors. Accuracy is the percentage of total correct predictions, while precision answers, 
"Of those predicted as positive, how many were truly positive?". Recall answers, "Of all 
actual positives, how many were correctly identified?". The F1 score is the harmonic mean 
of precision and recall, providing a single metric that balances both, especially useful for 
imbalanced datasets. Regression models are not typically evaluated with these metrics but 
with metrics like Mean Squared Error or R-squared.  
Classification vs. regression  
 Classification: Aims to categorize data into predefined labels (e.g., spam or not 
spam). The metrics below are primarily for this task. 
 Regression: Aims to predict a continuous value (e.g., predicting a house price). It 
uses different metrics like Mean Squared Error.  
Classification metrics  
To understand these metrics, consider a confusion matrix with four components:  
 True Positives (TP): Correctly predicted positive cases. 
 True Negatives (TN): Correctly predicted negative cases. 
 False Positives (FP): Incorrectly predicted positive cases (Type I error). 
 False Negatives (FN): Incorrectly predicted negative cases (Type II error).

 What it is: The proportion of all correct predictions (both positive and negative) 
out of the total number of predictions.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: d). Explain the working of Gradient Boosting in detail. Discuss how it builds models sequentially and how weak learners are combined to form a strong model.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Introduction: 
Gradient boosting is an ensemble technique where multiple weak models are joined to make 
a strong model. 
Body: 
It works by training models sequentially. The first model makes prediction and calculates 
errors. The next model tries to correct those errors by learning the residuals. This 
continues until the model reaches good accuracy or we stop early. 
Each new model focuses on what previous model did wrong. Gradient means direction of 
improvement and boosting means to improve the power. 
Finally, all models are combined by weighted sum of their predictions. 
Conclusion: 
Gradient boosting is powerful but can overfit if not tuned properly. It is used in 
algorithms like XGBoost and LightGBM.

KNN is algorithm that uses concept of neighbors. It is based on idea that things close to

common label among them becomes the prediction of the new data. 
The parameter k is very important. Small k can make noise affect output and large k can 
smooth result but miss small pattern. 
Conclusion: 
KNN is easy and useful for small dataset but slow for large dataset because it calculate 
distance each time.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: a) Explain the different types of Machine Learning evaluation metrics used for classification and regression tasks. Describe how accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, help in understanding model performance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Introduction: 
Evaluation metrics is very main part of machine learning because only through this 
we come to know how our model is doing. Different metrics are used for 
classification and regression tasks because they have different types of outputs. 
1. Classification Metrics: 
 Accuracy: 
Accuracy means how much correct predictions model make. It is total correct 
divided by total samples. But if classes not balanced then accuracy can give 
false idea of good model. 
 Precision: 
Precision show how many of predicted positives are actually positive. It helps to 
know how accurate model is when it say “positive”. 
 Recall: 
Recall is how many of all actual positives are detected. It is very useful when 
missing a positive case is serious like in disease or fraud detection. 
 F1 Score: 
F1 is balance between precision and recall. It is used when both are important 
and data is not balanced. 
2. Regression Metrics: 
For regression, common metrics are Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Squared 
Error (MSE), and R² Score. They tell about average distance of prediction from true 
value. 
Conclusion: 
Choosing right metric is very necessary because it change how we judge a model. 
Only accuracy not always good, so using multiple metrics gives more complete idea 
of model performance.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: b). Describe the K-Nearest Neighbor algorithm. Explain its working step-by-step and discuss the importance of the parameter k.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Introduction: 
K-Nearest Neighbor is a lazy learning algorithm because it not learn from training 
data immediately. It store data and only use it when making prediction. 
Working Steps: 
1. Choose the value of K: 
Select number of neighbors that will be used for voting or averaging. 
2. Calculate Distance: 
Measure distance between new point and all training points using formula like 
Euclidean distance. 
3. Find K Nearest Points: 
Take the K samples which are closest to the new data point. 
4. Voting/Averaging: 
o For classification: take majority vote from neighbors. 
o For regression: take mean of nearest points. 
5. Assign the result: 
Give the class or value that got majority or average. 
Importance of K: 
If K is too small, model become sensitive to noise and overfits. If K too large, model 
become very general and might miss details. So K is selected through validation for 
best result. 
Conclusion: 
KNN is simple but powerful method if we have good scaling and correct value of K.

rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
it. 
Introduction: 
Data imbalance happens when one class have much more examples than another. 
This create problem for model training because it will learn more from large class 
and ignore small one. 
Impact: 
 The model give bias toward major class and ignore rare class. 
 Accuracy looks high but recall for minor class is very poor. 
 Model not perform well on rare but important events like frauds, diseases, etc. 
Handling Techniques: 
1. Resampling Methods: 
o Oversampling: Copy or generate new samples of minority class (like 
SMOTE). 
o Undersampling: Remove some samples from majority class. 
2. Algorithm Level Methods: 
o Add class weights in training so model pay more attention to minority. 
3. Use of Ensemble: 
o Algorithms like Balanced Random Forest help balance accuracy. 
Conclusion: 
Handling data imbalance is important step to make model fair and good in all 
classes rather than only big one.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: d). Explain the working of Gradient Boosting in detail. Discuss how it builds models sequentially and how weak learners are combined to form a strong model.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Introduction: 
Gradient Boosting is a very effective ensemble method which build strong prediction 
model by joining many weak models like decision trees. It work step by step, 
correcting errors from earlier model. 
Working Steps: 
1. Start with a simple model: 
Model start by making a basic prediction (mean or log odds). 
2. Calculate residuals: 
Find difference between actual output and predicted output. 
3. Train new weak learner: 
A small decision tree is fitted to predict the residuals. 
4. Update the prediction: 
Add this new learner’s output multiplied by a learning rate to old model 
prediction. 
5. Repeat process: 
Many such weak learners are added until model performance stops improving. 
Combining Weak Learners: 
Each learner corrects the mistake of the previous one. Final model is weighted sum of 
all learners. 
Conclusion: 
Gradient Boosting give high accuracy and strong generalization but need careful 
tuning to avoid overfitting and too much complexity.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: e). Explain the concept of Transfer Learning. Discuss how pre-trained models are used to solve new tasks with limited data and mention common applications of transfer learning.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Discuss how pre-trained models are used 
to solve new tasks with limited data and mention common applications of transfer 
learning. 
Introduction: 
Transfer Learning is when we use knowledge from one task to help in another task. 
It is very helpful when we have small dataset for training. 
Concept: 
 Pre-trained model is already trained on large dataset like ImageNet. 
 We use it as base model and only train upper layers for our new task. 
 The lower layers already learned useful features like shapes, edges, or words 
patterns. 
 We can freeze those layers and only fine-tune top layers on our smaller data. 
Advantages: 
 Saves a lot of training time. 
 Performs better even with less data. 
 Avoids overfitting due to pre-learned patterns. 
Applications: 
 Image classification using ResNet, VGG, etc. 
 Text analysis using BERT, GPT, etc. 
 Object detection and medical image diagnosis. 
Conclusion: 
Transfer learning help us use power of already trained model and achieve strong 
performance quickly on new problems.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: f). What are Hyperparameters in Machine Learning? Explain why they are important and describe common hyperparameters for algorithms like Decision Trees, Neural Networks, and Gradient Boosting models.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Introduction: 
Hyperparameters are settings we give to algorithm before training starts. They 
decide how model will learn but they are not learned from data. 
Importance: 
They control performance, accuracy, and speed of training. Wrong hyperparameters 
can make model poor or overfit. 
Common Hyperparameters: 
 Decision Tree: 
o Max depth, min samples split, criterion for split. 
 Neural Network: 
o Learning rate, number of hidden layers, number of neurons, activation 
functions, batch size. 
 Gradient Boosting: 
o Number of trees, learning rate, maximum depth of each tree, 
subsampling ratio. 
Tuning Methods: 
Use grid search, random search, or Bayesian optimization to find best combination. 
Conclusion: 
Hyperparameter tuning is not easy but very important step to make any model high 
performing and generalizable.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: a). Explain the main steps involved in data preprocessing in machine learning.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Introduction: 
Data preprocessing is like cleaning and preparing food before cooking, because if data 
dirty or not ready, even best algorithm will give bad result. So preprocessing make 
data clean, useful and ready for model. 
Steps Involved: 
1. Data Collection: 
Collecting data from sources like databases, APIs, sensors, etc. It can be in 
different format and quality. 
2. Data Cleaning: 
Remove missing values, fix wrong entries, and handle duplicates. Missing values 
can be filled by mean or median. 
3. Encoding Categorical Data: 
Convert non-numeric data into numbers using label encoding or one-hot 
encoding. 
4. Feature Scaling: 
Make sure all features on same scale using normalization or standardization. 
5. Splitting Data: 
Divide data into training and testing so model not see all data during learning. 
Conclusion: 
Without preprocessing, even strong algorithm fail, so it is most important first step 
in machine learning pipeline.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: b). What is ensemble learning? Describe the working of bagging and boosting methods.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Introduction: 
Ensemble learning means using many models together to get better performance 
than any single one. It help in reducing variance and bias. 
Types: 
1. Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating): 
o Many models are trained on different random subsets of data. 
o Their predictions are combined by voting (for classification) or averaging 
(for regression). 
o Example: Random Forest uses bagging of Decision Trees. 
o It reduces variance and makes model stable. 
2. Boosting: 
o Models are trained one by one where next model tries to fix mistakes of 
previous one. 
o Final prediction is combination of all weak learners. 
o Example: AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost. 
o It reduces bias and improves accuracy. 
Conclusion: 
Ensemble is like taking advice of many experts instead of one, and it almost always 
gives more reliable prediction.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: c). Explain the need for feature scaling and differentiate between normalization and standardization.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Introduction: 
Feature scaling is very necessary step because algorithms work better when features 
are in similar range. Otherwise, features with big numbers dominate over small ones. 
Need for Feature Scaling: 
 Many algorithms like KNN, SVM, Gradient Descent based models depend on 
distance or gradient, so they get affected by scale. 
 It also helps optimization process to converge faster. 
Normalization vs Standardization: 
 Normalization: 
Brings values between 0 and 1. Formula: 
(x−min)/(max−min)(x - min) / (max - min)(x−min)/(max−min) 
Used when we don’t know data distribution. 
 Standardization: 
Changes data so it have mean = 0 and standard deviation = 1. 
Formula: (x−mean)/std(x - mean) / std(x−mean)/std 
Used when data is normally distributed. 
Conclusion: 
Scaling make learning stable and fair so that no feature gets extra weight just 
because of large numeric value.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: d). What is cross-entropy loss? Describe its use in classification models.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Introduction: 
Cross-entropy loss, also known as log loss, is used for classification, especially when 
output is probability. It measures how close predicted probabilities are to actual 
labels. 
Concept: 
 When true class is 1, it penalizes model if probability of 1 is low. 
 When true class is 0, it penalizes if probability of 0 is low. 
 It use logarithm to increase penalty for confident wrong predictions. 
Formula: 
−(y∗log(p)+(1−y)∗log(1−p))-(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log(1 - 
p))−(y∗log(p)+(1−y)∗log(1−p)) for binary classification. 
Use: 
Used widely in logistic regression, neural networks, and deep learning. It gives better 
gradient feedback for improving model weights. 
Conclusion: 
Cross-entropy loss helps model not just guess correct class, but also learn to give high 
confidence to right class.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: e). Explain the role of optimization algorithms in training machine learning models.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Introduction: 
Optimization algorithms are like brains behind learning because they decide how 
model will adjust weights and minimize error. 
Role: 
 They try to find the best set of parameters that minimize loss function. 
 Each step they adjust weights according to gradient direction and learning 
rate. 
 Without optimization, model cannot learn anything useful. 
Common Optimization Algorithms: 
1. Gradient Descent: Basic method, updates weights using gradient of loss. 
2. Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD): Uses one sample at a time, faster and 
dynamic. 
3. Adam Optimizer: Adaptive method combining momentum and RMSprop, 
faster convergence. 
Conclusion: 
Optimization is what make model learn from data, without it machine learning will 
be just random guessing.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: f). What is dimensionality reduction? Describe any one method used for it.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Introduction: 
Dimensionality reduction means reducing number of features while keeping 
important information. It help to make model faster and avoid overfitting. 
Why Needed: 
 Too many features increase computation and memory need. 
 Some features may be redundant or correlated. 
 Visualization is easier in 2D or 3D than in high dimension. 
Method: Principal Component Analysis (PCA): 
 PCA transforms original features into new set of uncorrelated variables called 
principal components. 
 These components capture maximum variance from data. 
 It uses eigenvalues and eigenvectors from covariance matrix. 
 We select top components that explain most variance. 
Conclusion: 
PCA help to simplify data, speed up training, and remove noise without losing much 
important information.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: g). Explain how a decision tree works and mention its advantages and disadvantages. --- PAGE 2 ---
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain how a decision tree works and mention its advantages and disadvantages. 
Introduction: 
Decision tree is a model that splits data into branches based on conditions until a 
final decision or prediction is made. 
Working: 
1. Select the best feature to split data using metrics like Gini Index or Information 
Gain. 
2. Split dataset into subsets according to feature values. 
3. Repeat the process on each subset until stopping condition (like max depth or 
pure leaf) reached. 
4. Each leaf node represents final class or value. 
Advantages: 
 Easy to visualize and interpret. 
 Handles both numeric and categorical data. 
 No need of feature scaling. 
Disadvantages: 
 Prone to overfitting if not pruned. 
 Small changes in data can make tree structure very different. 
 Less stable alone, but improved when used in ensemble like Random Forest. 
Conclusion: 
Decision trees are simple but powerful base models that form the foundation of 
many advanced algorithms.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: a) Explain the different types of Machine Learning evaluation metrics used for classification and regression tasks. Describe how accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, help in understanding model performance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Purpose & selection 
Evaluation metrics quantify how well a model performs relative to the 
problem’s objectives. Choose metrics that reflect real-world costs: false 
positives vs false negatives, overall fit, or ranking ability. Classification and 
regression require different families of metrics. 
Classification — key metrics and interpretation 
 Accuracy: fraction of correct predictions. Good as a quick measure when 
classes are balanced, but misleading with skewed class distributions 
because it masks per-class performance. 
 Precision (P): P=TPTP+FPP = 
\frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP}+\text{FP}}P=TP+FPTP. Precision answers: 
“when the model predicts positive, how often is it right?” High 
precision reduces false positives (important when false alarms are 
costly). 
 Recall / Sensitivity (R): R=TPTP+FNR = 
\frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP}+\text{FN}}R=TP+FNTP. Recall answers: “of 
all real positives, how many did we find?” High recall reduces missed 
positives (important in diagnostics). 
 F1 Score: harmonic mean of precision and recall, F1=2⋅P⋅RP+RF1 = 
2\cdot\frac{P\cdot R}{P+R}F1=2⋅P+RP⋅R. Useful when you need a single 
measure balancing precision and recall, particularly under imbalance. 
 Specificity / TNR: complements recall for negatives. 
 ROC-AUC & PR-AUC: ROC-AUC captures separability across thresholds 
(TPR vs FPR). PR-AUC (precision-recall curve area) is more informative 
when positive class is rare. 
Regression — key metrics and interpretation 
 MAE (Mean Absolute Error): average absolute deviation; robust and 
directly interpretable in target units. 
 MSE / RMSE: squares amplify large errors; RMSE is on same scale as 
target. Use when large errors are particularly undesirable. 
 R² (coefficient of determination): proportion of variance explained by 
the model. Useful to compare models on the same target, but beware 
with non-linear fits or biased estimators. 
How they help 
Selecting the right metric reveals different failure modes: precision/recall 
show class-wise trade-offs, ROC/PR explain threshold behavior, MAE/MSE 
show error magnitude. Good evaluation uses multiple complementary metrics, 
threshold analysis, and confusion/residual inspection to form a complete 
picture.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: b). Describe the K-Nearest Neighbor algorithm. Explain its working step-by-step and discuss the importance of the parameter k.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Algorithm summary 
K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) is an instance-based, non-parametric method: it 
classifies or regresses a query by aggregating labels/values of the k closest 
training samples in feature space. 
Step-by-step 
1. Represent data as vectors in feature space. Ensure consistent 
preprocessing (scaling, encoding). 
2. Pick a distance metric (Euclidean, Manhattan, cosine, etc.) based on 
data characteristics. 
3. Choose k, the number of neighbors. 
4. For a query point: compute distances to all training samples. 
5. Select k smallest distances → the k nearest neighbors. 
6. Aggregate neighbor information: 
o Classification: majority vote (optionally distance-weighted). 
o Regression: average or weighted average of targets. 
7. Return prediction. 
Role of k 
 k small (e.g., 1): low bias, high variance — sensitive to noise and 
outliers. 
 k large: smoother boundaries, lower variance but increased bias — may 
underfit by ignoring local structure. 
 Selection: tune k with cross-validation; consider odd values for binary 
classes to avoid ties; distance-weighting can mitigate some sensitivity. 
Practical considerations 
 Feature scaling is mandatory (distance-sensitive). 
 Curse of dimensionality: in high dimensions distances become less 
meaningful — reduce dimensionality or use feature selection. 
 Computational cost: brute-force distance calculation is O(n)O(n)O(n) 
per query; use KD-trees / ball trees or approximate NN for large 
datasets. 
 Imbalanced classes: neighbors may be dominated by majority class; use 
class weighting or resampling.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: c). What is Data Imbalance in Machine Learning? Explain its impact on model performance and discuss techniques used to handle
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
it. 
Definition & context 
Data imbalance occurs when class frequencies differ substantially. Many real
world tasks (fraud, disease detection) are imbalanced: the class of interest is 
rare. 
Impact 
 Biased decision boundary: models optimize global loss and may favor 
majority class, producing apparently high accuracy but poor minority
class recall. 
 Misleading evaluation: accuracy becomes unreliable; important failure 
modes (missed minority cases) remain hidden. 
 Learning difficulty: minority-class patterns have insufficient examples for 
generalization. 
Techniques to handle 
1. Data-level methods (resampling): 
o Oversampling minority (random oversampling, SMOTE, ADASYN) 
to increase representation. 
o Undersampling majority (random undersampling, cluster-based 
undersampling) to reduce dominance. 
o Hybrid approaches combine both to balance information retention 
and variance. 
2. Algorithm-level methods: 
o Class weighting / cost-sensitive learning: penalize misclassification of 
minority more heavily. 
o Threshold moving: adjust decision threshold to trade 
precision/recall. 
3. Model/ensemble methods: 
o Specialized ensembles (Balanced Random Forest, EasyEnsemble) 
combine resampling with ensemble strategies. 
4. Evaluation strategy adjustments: 
o Use precision/recall, F1, PR-AUC, confusion matrices; stratified 
cross-validation to preserve minority representation in folds. 
5. Data augmentation / synthetic generation: 
o For images/text, domain-specific augmentation expands minority 
class variability. 
Best practice 
Quantify imbalance, pick metrics aligned to cost, try resampling + class
weighting, and validate improvements with stratified CV and minority-focused 
metrics.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: d). Explain the working of Gradient Boosting in detail. Discuss how it builds models sequentially and how weak learners are combined to form a strong model.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Core idea 
Gradient Boosting constructs an additive model F(x)=∑m=1Mγmhm(x)F(x) = 
\sum_{m=1}^M \gamma_m h_m(x)F(x)=∑m=1Mγmhm(x) by sequentially 
fitting weak learners hmh_mhm to the negative gradient (residual direction) 
of a chosen loss function. Each new learner reduces the remaining error. 
Mechanics (intuitive + math) 
1. Initialize with a constant prediction that minimizes loss (e.g., mean for 
squared error): F0(x)F_0(x)F0(x). 
2. Iterate m = 1..M: 
o Compute pseudo-residuals rim=−∂L(yi,F(xi))∂F(xi)∣F=Fm−1r_{im} = -\left.\frac{\partial L(y_i, F(x_i))}{\partial 
F(x_i)}\right|_{F=F_{m-1}}rim=−∂F(xi)∂L(yi,F(xi))F=Fm−1. For 
squared error, rim=yi−Fm−1(xi)r_{im} = y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i)rim=yi
−Fm−1(xi). 
o Fit a weak learner hm(x)h_m(x)hm(x) (usually a shallow tree) to 
predict rimr_{im}rim. 
o Optionally compute optimal multiplier γm\gamma_mγm (line 
search) or use fixed-step shrinkage. 
o Update: Fm(x)=Fm−1(x)+νγmhm(x)F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + \nu 
\gamma_m h_m(x)Fm(x)=Fm−1(x)+νγmhm(x), where ν\nuν is 
learning rate. 
3. Return final ensemble FMF_MFM. 
Why this works 
Fitting learners to negative gradients is equivalent to performing gradient 
descent in function space — minimizing the loss stepwise. Weak learners 
correct what the ensemble fails to predict. 
Key hyperparameters and trade-offs 
 Learning rate (ν\nuν): small ν\nuν + more trees → better 
generalization but longer training. 
 Number of estimators: more trees increase capacity; combine with early 
stopping. 
 Tree depth / leaf size: controls interactions captured (stumps for 
additive effects; deeper for higher-order interactions). 
 Subsample / column sampling: reduces variance (stochastic gradient 
boosting). 
 Regularization (L1/L2, min_child_weight): prevent overfitting. 
Implementations & optimizations 
XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost add system-level speedups, histogram-based 
splitting, categorical handling, and advanced regularization. 
Conclusion 
Gradient boosting is a powerful, flexible framework that achieves top accuracy 
on structured data when carefully tuned, combining many weak learners into 
a robust model.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: e). Explain the concept of Transfer Learning. Discuss how pre-trained models are used to solve new tasks with limited data and mention common applications of transfer learning.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Discuss how pre-trained models 
are used to solve new tasks with limited data and mention common 
applications of transfer learning. 
Concept 
Transfer Learning leverages representations learned on large source datasets 
to accelerate and improve performance on related target tasks with limited 
labeled data. 
Mechanisms 
 Feature extraction: use pre-trained model as a fixed feature extractor 
(freeze backbone), train only a new classifier head on target data. 
 Fine-tuning: initialize with pre-trained weights and continue training 
(often with smaller learning rate) on the target dataset; may unfreeze 
some layers gradually. 
 Adapter modules / partial re-training: insert small trainable modules into 
frozen pre-trained networks for efficiency. 
Why it helps 
Early layers of deep nets learn general patterns (edges, textures, subword 
patterns) transferable across domains. Reusing these reduces data needs and 
speeds convergence. 
Applications 
 Computer vision: ImageNet pre-trained CNNs adapted to medical 
imaging, remote sensing. 
 NLP: BERT/GPT-family models fine-tuned for classification, QA, NER, 
summarization. 
 Audio / speech: pre-trained audio embeddings for speaker ID or event 
detection. 
 Reinforcement learning: transfer policies or value functions between 
similar environments. 
Cautions 
 Negative transfer: if source and target are too dissimilar, pre-training 
may harm learning. 
 Overfitting during fine-tuning: small target datasets risk overfitting; use 
regularization and careful learning-rate schedules. 
Conclusion 
Transfer learning is an efficient strategy to reuse prior knowledge; when 
source and target align, it dramatically improves performance and reduces 
training cost.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: a). Explain the main steps involved in data preprocessing in machine learning.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Overview 
Preprocessing converts raw, messy inputs into consistent, informative 
features ready for modeling. It is iterative and domain-dependent. 
Steps (concise workflow) 
1. Data inspection & cleaning: identify missingness, invalid entries, 
inconsistencies; correct or remove errors. 
2. Missing value strategy: impute (mean/median/mode, KNN, model-based) 
or drop, based on missingness mechanism (MCAR, MAR, MNAR). 
3. Outlier handling: detect with boxplots, z-scores, IQR; decide to cap, 
transform, or exclude after domain check. 
4. Encoding categoricals: one-hot, ordinal, target/leave-one-out encoding 
(watch leakage). 
5. Feature scaling: standardize/normalize as required. 
6. Feature engineering: create interaction terms, aggregates, timestamps 
decomposition, text embeddings. 
7. Feature selection: filter (correlation), wrapper (RFE), or embedded 
methods (regularized models). 
8. Data augmentation: images/text for small datasets. 
9. Train/validation/test split: stratified if class imbalance; consider time
based splits for time series. 
10. 
Pipelines & reproducibility: use pipeline APIs to ensure identical 
transforms at inference. 
Conclusion 
Sound preprocessing reduces noise, preserves signal, and produces robust 
inputs that allow models to reach their potential.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: b). What is ensemble learning? Describe the working of bagging and boosting methods.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Ensemble idea 
Ensembles combine multiple base learners to reduce error by exploiting 
diversity (different models make different errors). 
Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) 
 Create multiple bootstrap samples from the training set. 
 Train independent learners (often same algorithm) on each sample. 
 Aggregate predictions by averaging (regression) or majority vote 
(classification). 
 Effect: reduces variance and overfitting; Random Forest extends bagging 
with feature subsampling. 
Boosting 
 Train learners sequentially; each model focuses on the errors of the 
ensemble so far (sample reweighting or residual fitting). 
 Combine learners additively with weights to produce final prediction. 
 Effect: reduces bias and builds a strong learner from weak ones; 
sensitive to noisy labels. 
Comparison 
 Bagging: parallel, variance reduction. 
 Boosting: sequential, bias reduction. 
Conclusion 
Use bagging to stabilize high-variance learners; use boosting to correct bias 
and attain high predictive power on complex data.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: c). Explain the need for feature scaling and differentiate between normalization and standardization.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Why scale? 
Distance-based algorithms (KNN, K-means), gradient-based optimizers, and 
models using regularization assume features are on comparable scales. Without 
scaling, features with large magnitudes dominate. 
Normalization (Min–Max) 
 Scales to a fixed range (usually [0,1]). Formula: 
(x−xmin)/(xmax−xmin)(x-x_{min})/(x_{max}-x_{min})(x−xmin)/(xmax
−xmin). 
 Useful when bounded range is desired (e.g., image pixel scaling) or 
algorithms expecting bounded inputs. 
Standardization (Z-score) 
 Centers to zero mean and unit variance: (x−μ)/σ(x
\mu)/\sigma(x−μ)/σ. 
 Preserves outlier influence less destructively; commonly used for 
algorithms that assume roughly Gaussian features (PCA, linear models). 
Which to use? 
 Use standardization for algorithms sensitive to mean/variance or with 
outliers. 
 Use normalization for bounded inputs or when using distance metrics and 
original min/max meaningful. 
Conclusion 
Always fit scalers on training set and apply the same transform to 
validation/test data to prevent leakage.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: d). What is cross-entropy loss? Describe its use in classification models.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Definition 
Cross-entropy quantifies the dissimilarity between the true label distribution 
and the predicted probability distribution. It is the negative log-likelihood of 
correct labels under the model. 
Binary cross-entropy (per sample): −[ylog⁡p+(1−y)log⁡(1−p)]-[y\log p + (1
y)\log(1-p)]−[ylogp+(1−y)log(1−p)]. 
Categorical cross-entropy: −∑iyilog⁡pi-\sum_{i} y_i\log p_i−∑iyilogpi for one
hot labels. 
Use in classification 
 Paired with sigmoid (binary) or softmax (multi-class) outputs. 
 Provides strong gradients encouraging confident correct predictions and 
heavily penalizing confident wrong ones. 
 Equivalent to maximizing likelihood under Bernoulli / Categorical models. 
Properties 
 Differentiable → suitable for gradient-based optimization. 
 Proper scoring rule → encourages calibrated probabilities. 
Conclusion 
Cross-entropy is the standard loss for classification because it aligns training 
with probabilistic predictions and provides effective gradient signals.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: e). Explain the role of optimization algorithms in training machine learning models.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Role 
Optimizers search parameter space to minimize loss; they are the engine of 
learning. They determine step sizes, update rules, and convergence behavior. 
Common algorithms & features 
 Gradient Descent (batch): compute full-batch gradient; stable but 
expensive. 
 Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD): uses one or few samples per 
update; introduces helpful noise. 
 Momentum: accelerates along consistent gradient directions, reduces 
oscillations. 
 Adaptive methods (AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam): adapt learning rate per
parameter using historical gradients; often faster initial convergence. 
Practical considerations 
 Learning rate scheduling (decay, warmup) and batch size strongly affect 
convergence and generalization. 
 Optimizer choice interacts with architecture, normalization, and 
regularization strategies. 
Conclusion 
Optimization algorithms are central to effective training: they shape how 
parameters are updated and thus how well models fit data and generalize.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: f). What is dimensionality reduction? Describe any one method used for it.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Why reduce dimensionality? 
High-dimensional data leads to increased computation, overfitting, and 
difficulty visualizing structure (curse of dimensionality). Dimensionality 
reduction compresses data while preserving important structure. 
Method — Principal Component Analysis (PCA) 
 Goal: find orthogonal directions (principal components) maximizing 
variance. 
 Steps: center data → compute covariance → eigen-decomposition → 
select top-k eigenvectors → project data. 
 Pros: linear, fast, yields uncorrelated features; good for denoising and 
preprocessing. 
 Cons: linearity limits representation of complex manifolds; not ideal for 
preserving local neighborhoods (use t-SNE/UMAP for visualization). 
Conclusion 
Dimensionality reduction simplifies models, reduces noise, improves 
visualization and computation; choose method (linear vs nonlinear) by data 
geometry.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: a) Explain the different types of Machine Learning evaluation metrics used for classification and regression tasks. Describe how accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, help in understanding model performance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Machine Learning evaluation metrics are ways to judge how good a model is 
performing. They tell how much the model is correct and where it is making 
mistakes. 
For Classification tasks, metrics include: 
 Accuracy: The ratio of correctly predicted samples to the total samples. It is 
good only when data is balanced. 
 Precision: Shows how many of the predicted positives are actually positive. 
 Recall: Tells how many actual positives are correctly found by the model. 
 F1 Score: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, used when both are 
important. 
For Regression tasks, metrics include: 
 Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Mean Squared Error (MSE) which measure 
difference between predicted and true values. 
 R² Score shows how much variation in data is explained by the model. 
These metrics help in identifying which model gives better generalization 
performance.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: b). Describe the K-Nearest Neighbor algorithm. Explain its working step-by-step and discuss the importance of the parameter k.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
KNN (K-Nearest Neighbors) is a lazy learning algorithm that classifies new data 
points based on the labels of its nearest neighbors. 
Steps: 
1. Choose the value of k (number of neighbors). 
2. Calculate the distance between the new point and all existing points (using 
Euclidean or Manhattan distance). 
3. Select the k nearest points. 
4. Perform majority voting for classification or averaging for regression. 
Importance of k: 
 Small k may make model sensitive to noise (overfitting). 
 Large k can make it too smooth (underfitting).

rubric_with_answers.question_text: c). What is Data Imbalance in Machine Learning? Explain its impact on model performance and discuss techniques used to handle
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
it. 
Data imbalance happens when one class has many more samples than the other 
classes. For example, 95% normal and 5% fraud data. 
Impact is that the model becomes biased and predicts mostly the majority class. 
Even if accuracy is high, the minority class performance becomes poor. 
Techniques: 
 Oversampling: Increase the size of minority class (like SMOTE). 
 Undersampling: Reduce majority samples. 
 Use class weights: Give higher importance to minority samples.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: d). Explain the working of Gradient Boosting in detail. Discuss how it builds models sequentially and how weak learners are combined to form a strong model.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Gradient Boosting is an ensemble method that builds models one after another. Each 
new model tries to correct the errors made by the previous model. 
Steps: 
1. Start with an initial model (like predicting mean). 
2. Calculate the residuals (errors). 
3. Train a new weak learner (like decision tree) on these residuals. 
4. Add the predictions to the previous model with a learning rate. 
After many rounds, a strong model is created.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: e). Explain the concept of Transfer Learning. Discuss how pre-trained models are used to solve new tasks with limited data and mention common applications of transfer learning.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Discuss how pre-trained models are used 
to solve new tasks with limited data and mention common applications of transfer

Transfer learning is the process of using a pre-trained model (already trained on a 
large dataset) and adapting it for a new related task with less data.

Steps: 
1. Load a pre-trained model. 
2. Freeze early layers (which capture general features). 
3. Replace or retrain later layers for new classes. 
Applications: Image recognition, NLP (using BERT, GPT, etc.), and speech analysis.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: g). Explain how a decision tree works and mention its advantages and disadvantages. --- PAGE 2 ---
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain how a decision tree works and mention its advantages and disadvantages. 
A decision tree is a supervised machine learning algorithm used for both classification 
and regression tasks. It operates by creating a model that predicts the value of a 
target variable by learning simple decision rules inferred from the data features. 
How a Decision Tree Works: 
 Root Node:  
The process begins with a single root node representing the entire dataset. 
 Splitting:  
The algorithm then identifies the best feature to split the data based on a chosen 
criterion (e.g., Gini impurity or information gain for classification, mean squared 
error for regression). This split divides the data into subsets, creating child nodes. 
 Recursive Partitioning:  
This splitting process is repeated recursively on each child node until a stopping 
condition is met. This condition could be that all data points in a node belong to the 
same class, the node contains a minimum number of samples, or further splitting 
does not significantly improve the model's performance. 
 Leaf Nodes:  
The final nodes in the tree, which are not further split, are called leaf nodes. Each 
leaf node represents a predicted outcome or class. 
 Prediction:  
To make a prediction for a new data point, it traverses the tree from the root, 
following the decision rules at each internal node until it reaches a leaf node, which 
provides the prediction. 
Advantages: 
 Interpretability:  
Decision trees are easy to understand and visualize, resembling a flowchart, making 
the decision-making process transparent. 
 Handles various data types:  
They can work with both numerical and categorical data without extensive 
preprocessing. 
 No feature scaling required:  
Unlike some other algorithms, decision trees do not require feature scaling or 
normalization.  
 Handles non-linear relationships:  
They can capture complex, non-linear relationships between features and the target 
variable.  
 Feature importance:  
Decision trees inherently provide a measure of feature importance, indicating which 
features are most influential in making predictions. 
Disadvantages: 
 Overfitting:  
Decision trees can be prone to overfitting, especially with complex trees, leading to 
poor generalization on unseen data. Pruning techniques are often used to mitigate 
this. 
 Instability:  
Small changes in the data can lead to significant changes in the tree structure, 
making them somewhat unstable. 
 Bias with imbalanced data:  
If one class significantly dominates the others in a classification problem, the tree 
might be biased towards the majority class. 
 Computational cost:  
Building a complex decision tree can be computationally expensive, especially with a 
large number of features and data points.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: c). What is Data Imbalance in Machine Learning? Explain its impact on model performance and discuss techniques used to handle
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
it. 
Definition and significance 
Data imbalance occurs when the class distribution is skewed: one or more classes 
(majority) have many more samples than the minority classes. This is common in fraud 
detection, rare disease diagnosis, fault detection, etc. 
Impact on model performance 
 Biased predictions: models tend to predict the majority class to minimize overall 
error, yielding high accuracy but poor performance on minority class. 
 Misleading metrics: accuracy becomes uninformative; minority-class performance 
(recall) can be extremely low. 
 Learning difficulty: minority class patterns are underrepresented, making it hard for 
models to learn discriminative features. 
Techniques to handle imbalance 
1. Data-level techniques (resampling): 
o Oversampling minority class: random oversampling, SMOTE (synthetic minority 
oversampling technique), ADASYN — helps provide more minority examples. 
o Undersampling majority class: random undersampling, NearMiss — reduces 
majority class size but risks information loss. 
o Hybrid: combine oversampling and undersampling to balance classes while 
preserving information. 
2. Algorithm-level techniques: 
o Class weighting / cost-sensitive learning: assign higher misclassification cost for 
minority class (many libraries support class_weight parameter). 
o Threshold adjustment: move decision threshold to favor minority class, trading 
precision vs recall. 
3. Ensemble methods specialized for imbalance: 
o Balanced Random Forest, EasyEnsemble, or RUSBoost combine resampling with 
ensemble learning. 
4. Evaluation strategies: 
o Use precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC, and confusion matrices; prefer PR-AUC 
when positive class is rare. 
5. Feature engineering and data augmentation: 
o Create informative features or augment minority-class examples (domain
specific augmentation for images, text paraphrasing for NLP). 
Best practice 
 Begin by quantifying imbalance and selecting metrics aligned with the task’s cost 
structure. 
 Experiment with resampling + class-weighting and validate improvements using 
appropriate metrics and cross-validation. 
Conclusion 
Addressing imbalance is crucial to build fair and useful systems; the right combination of 
preprocessing, algorithmic adjustments, and evaluation leads to robust performance on 
minority classes.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: e). Explain the concept of Transfer Learning. Discuss how pre-trained models are used to solve new tasks with limited data and mention common applications of transfer learning.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Discuss how pre-trained models are used to 
solve new tasks with limited data and mention common applications of transfer learning. 
Concept 
Transfer Learning leverages knowledge learned from one task/domain (source) to improve 
learning on another related task/domain (target). It is especially beneficial when target 
data are scarce but related source data/model exist. 
Mechanisms of transfer 
 Feature reuse: early layers of deep models learn general features (e.g., edge 
detectors in CNNs, subword/semantic patterns in NLP models). These features are 
transferable across related tasks. 
 Fine-tuning: take a pre-trained model, freeze some layers (usually early ones), and 
retrain later layers on the new dataset. Optionally, unfreeze more layers for gradual 
fine-tuning. 
 Head replacement: remove the original output layer and attach a new head specific 
to the target task; train the head (and optionally some earlier layers). 
 Domain adaptation: techniques to adjust model when source and target distributions 
differ (e.g., adversarial domain adaptation). 
When transfer learning helps 
 Limited labeled data in target domain. 
 Relatedness: source task features must be relevant to target task (e.g., ImageNet 
pretraining -> medical imaging often transfers well for low-level image features). 
 Large pre-trained models (BERT, GPT, ResNet) provide strong starting points. 
Applications 
 Computer vision: using ImageNet-pretrained CNNs for image classification, object 
detection, or medical image analysis. 
 Natural language processing: pre-trained language models (BERT, RoBERTa, GPT) 
fine-tuned for sentiment analysis, QA, NER, etc. 
 Speech/audio: pre-trained audio models adapted for speaker recognition or audio 
event detection. 
 Reinforcement learning: transferring policies or representations across similar 
environments. 
Benefits and pitfalls 
 Benefits: faster convergence, better performance with limited data, lower training 
cost. 
 Pitfalls: negative transfer (when source is too different), overfitting if fine-tuning 
without regularization, and licensing/privacy constraints for some pre-trained models. 
Conclusion 
Transfer Learning reuses prior knowledge to accelerate learning and improve accuracy on 
new tasks — a practical and powerful strategy in modern ML workflows.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: f). What are Hyperparameters in Machine Learning? Explain why they are important and describe common hyperparameters for algorithms like Decision Trees, Neural Networks, and Gradient Boosting models.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Definition 
Hyperparameters are external configuration settings set prior to training that control 
model structure and learning dynamics (e.g., learning rate, tree depth). They are distinct 
from model parameters (weights) learned during training. 
Why they matter 
 They govern model capacity (overfit/underfit balance), optimization dynamics, and 
computational cost. 
 Appropriate hyperparameter tuning improves performance and generalization; poor 
choices can render even good algorithms ineffective. 
Examples by algorithm 
 Decision Trees / Random Forests: max_depth, min_samples_split, min_samples_leaf, 
criterion (gini/entropy), n_estimators (in forests). 
 Neural Networks: learning_rate, batch_size, num_epochs, optimizer (SGD/Adam), 
activation functions, network architecture (num_layers, units_per_layer), 
dropout_rate. 
 Gradient Boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM): n_estimators, learning_rate, max_depth, 
subsample, colsample_bytree, reg_alpha/reg_lambda. 
Tuning strategies 
 Grid search: exhaustive search over specified parameter grid. Computationally 
expensive. 
 Random search: samples hyperparameter space randomly — often more efficient. 
 Bayesian optimization: models the objective function and selects promising 
hyperparameters (e.g., HyperOpt, Optuna). 
 Sequential model-based optimization (SMBO): iteratively proposes hyperparameters 
based on past trials. 
 Early stopping / cross-validation: used to prevent overfitting and select 
hyperparameters robustly. 
Conclusion 
Hyperparameters are levers to steer model learning and complexity; systematic tuning 
using validation data and efficient search methods is essential for high-quality models.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: a). Explain the main steps involved in data preprocessing in machine learning.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Overview 
Data preprocessing readies raw data for machine learning; clean, consistent and well
structured inputs markedly improve downstream model performance. 
Main steps 
1. Data collection & inspection: gather data, check types, distributions, missingness, 
outliers. 
2. Missing value handling: impute (mean/median/mode, model-based, KNN/iterative 
imputation) or remove rows/columns depending on context. 
3. Outlier detection and handling: visualize (boxplots, z-score, IQR), treat via capping, 
transformation or investigation if they are valid. 
4. Data cleaning / consistency: correct erroneous labels, unify categorical encodings, fix 
types. 
5. Encoding categorical variables: one-hot encoding, ordinal encoding, target encoding 
(careful of leakage). 
6. Feature scaling: normalization or standardization as required by model. 
7. Feature engineering & selection: create informative features, remove redundant ones 
using correlation analysis, mutual information, recursive feature elimination. 
8. Data splitting: divide into training/validation/test sets (stratify if class imbalance). 
9. Data augmentation (if needed): for images/text to expand dataset. 
10. Pipelines: build reproducible pipelines (e.g., scikit-learn Pipeline) to ensure same 
transforms applied in production. 
Conclusion 
Preprocessing is iterative and domain-dependent; automation and reproducibility reduce 
mistakes and ensure reliable model evaluation and deployment.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: b). What is ensemble learning? Describe the working of bagging and boosting methods.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Ensemble learning definition 
Ensemble learning combines multiple base models to produce a single improved model — 
leveraging diversity among learners to reduce error. 
Boosting 
 Train learners sequentially; each new learner focuses on mistakes of prior ensemble 
(reweights samples or fits residuals). 
 Combine learners in weighted sum to form final prediction (additive model). 
 Effect: reduces bias and builds strong learners from weak ones (e.g., AdaBoost, 
Gradient Boosting, XGBoost). 
Conclusion 
Ensemble methods often outperform single models and are primary choice for tabular data 
competitions; they require care with overfitting and interpretability.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: e). Explain the role of optimization algorithms in training machine learning models.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Purpose 
Optimization algorithms adjust model parameters to minimize the loss function on training 
data; they are the mechanism by which learning happens. 
Key concepts 
 Gradient-based updates: compute gradients of loss w.r.t parameters and step in the 
negative gradient direction (steepest descent). 
 Learning rate: step size controlling update magnitude; critical for convergence and 
stability. 
 Variants to improve convergence and stability: 
o Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD): updates using mini-batches — more 
efficient and introduces helpful noise. 
o Momentum: accelerates convergence by accumulating a velocity term. 
o Adaptive methods (AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam): scale learning rates per
parameter based on historical gradients — often improve convergence, 
especially for sparse or noisy gradients. 
Role in practice 
 Determine convergence speed, stability, ability to escape shallow local minima/saddle 
points. 
 Influence generalization indirectly (e.g., SGD noise can improve generalization). 
Conclusion 
Optimizers are central to model training; choice and hyperparameters (learning rate, 
momentum, batch size) significantly impact training dynamics and final model quality.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: f). What is dimensionality reduction? Describe any one method used for it.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Definition and motivation 
Dimensionality reduction reduces the number of input variables (features) while preserving 
as much relevant information as possible. It aids visualization, reduces computational cost, 
mitigates the curse of dimensionality, and can help reduce overfitting. 
Method — Principal Component Analysis (PCA) 
 Idea: find orthogonal directions (principal components) that capture maximal 
variance in the data. 
 Procedure: center data, compute covariance matrix, compute 
eigenvectors/eigenvalues, sort components by explained variance, project data onto 
top-k components. 
 Benefits: linear, unsupervised, reduces redundancy by transforming to an uncorrelated 
basis. 
 Limitations: linear method — cannot capture strong nonlinear manifolds (use t-SNE, 
UMAP, or autoencoders for nonlinear structure). 
Conclusion 
Dimensionality reduction simplifies models and improves interpretability; choose method 
(linear vs nonlinear) based on data structure and application.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: g). Explain how a decision tree works and mention its advantages and disadvantages. --- PAGE 2 ---
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain how a decision tree works and mention its advantages and disadvantages. 
How it works 
A decision tree partitions the input space by asking a sequence of questions (splits) on 
features. At each internal node it selects the best split (feature and threshold/category) 
by optimizing a criterion (e.g., Information Gain, Gini impurity for classification; variance 
reduction for regression). Splitting continues recursively until stopping conditions (max 
depth, minimum samples per leaf, or pure nodes) are met. Leaves represent predicted 
outputs (class label or regression value). 
Advantages 
 Interpretability: model logic is transparent and easily visualized. 
 Little preprocessing: handles mixed feature types and does not require scaling. 
 Nonlinear: captures nonlinear relationships and interactions between features. 
Disadvantages 
 Overfitting: single trees can overfit training data if not pruned. 
 Instability: small changes in data can result in different tree structure. 
 Bias-variance tradeoff: needs parameter tuning (depth, leaf size) and regularization; 
ensembles (Random Forest, boosting) mitigate many issues. 
Conclusion 
Decision trees are intuitive and useful for baseline modeling and interpretability; for robust 
predictive performance on complex data, ensembles of trees are typically preferred.
