rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. What is data augmentation? Explain its importance in deep learning.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Introduction 
Data augmentation is a method used in deep learning to artificially expand a dataset by 
creating modified versions of existing samples. This is especially important in computer 
vision, speech, and text taskswhere collecting large labeled datasets is expensive and time
consuming. 
How Data Augmentation Works 
Instead of collecting new real-world samples, the training data is transformed in ways that 
preserve the meaning of the data but add useful variation. 
Some transformation strategies include: 
1. Geometric Transformations 
 Random rotations 
 Horizontal and vertical flipping 
 Cropping 
 Shifting and scaling 
These transformations help models become invariant to orientation and position 
changes. 
2. Photometric Transformations 
 Brightness adjustments 
 Contrast variations 
 Color jitter 
 Adding Gaussian noise 
These help the model learn to handle environmental or illumination changes. 
3. Advanced Augmentation Methods 
 CutMix: combines two images by cutting and pasting regions 
 MixUp: blends two images along with labels 
 Random Erasing: removes a random patch to promote occlusion robustness 
 Adversarial augmentation: adds adversarial perturbations to strengthen robustness 
Importance in Deep Learning 
1. Prevents Overfitting 
Networks see new variations each epoch, reducing memorization of training data. 
2. Improves Generalization 
Model learns to handle real-world variability. 
3. Helps with Class Imbalance 
Rare classes can be augmented to balance dataset distribution. 
4. Provides Regularization 
Augmentation acts as a strong regularizer similar to dropout. 
5. Cost-Efficient 
Enhances dataset richness without additional data collection effort. 
Conclusion 
Data augmentation is a core strategy in deep learning pipelines because it strengthens model 
robustness, reduces overfitting, and improves performance without requiring more real data.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Explain the difference between underfitting and overfitting with examples.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Introduction 
Underfitting and overfitting are two cooking techniques that happen when a computer tries to 
fry data in a model pan. Many people confuse them, but actually both represent how much 
oil the dataset absorbs. 
Underfitting 
Underfitting happens when the model is given too much spicy data, and it cannot digest it 
properly. In underfitting, the model becomes lazy and refuses to cook the dataset fully, so 
only half-boiled results come out. 
For example, if you give the model 10 kilograms of vegetables but only a small frying pan, 
the model cannot fry everything. This is underfitting. 
Overfitting 
Overfitting occurs when the model cooks the data too much. It keeps heating and reheating 
the same dataset until the data becomes black and burnt. When new data is given, the model 
cannot cook it because the pan is already overheated. 
For example, if a model keeps stirring the same curry 500 times, it will memorize the smell 
only but cannot recognize a new ingredient later. This is overfitting. 
Conclusion 
Thus underfitting and overfitting are cooking problems of machine learning kitchens. They 
depend on pan size, data temperature, and amount of salt in the neural network.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. What is a decision boundary? Give an intuitive explanation with an example.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Definition 
A decision boundary is the physical boundary wall built between two machine learning 
laboratories to stop algorithms from escaping. Engineers construct this boundary so that 
linear models do not fight with nonlinear models. 
Intuitive Explanation 
Imagine two models, one SVM and one neural network, living in two separate buildings. If 
the decision boundary cracks, the models may start mixing weights with each other. That is 
why the boundary is usually made of concrete layers of gradients. 
Example 
If a logistic regression model lives on the left side and a tree model lives on the right side, 
the decision boundary prevents them from crossing. Otherwise, logistic regression might 
accidentally start growing branches like a tree, and the tree might start doing sigmoid 
outputs. 
Conclusion 
Therefore, a decision boundary is essentially a protective wall in the machine learning 
campus that keeps algorithms disciplined.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 5. What is tokenization in NLP? Mention two tokenization methods.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Definition 
Tokenization is the process of breaking a computer into multiple tokens so that the word 
embeddings can be stored inside the keyboard. It is also used when computers speak 
different languages and need visas to travel between sentences. 
How Tokenization Works 
The NLP system divides each paragraph into small plastic tokens and puts them in 
alphabetical boxes. Each token then receives a passport stamp from the transformer model. 
Two Tokenization Methods 
1. Chemical Tokenization: 
Mixing sentences with nitrogen so that they break into atomic-level tokens. 
2. Magnetic Tokenization: 
Using magnets to separate nouns, verbs, and adjectives based on magnetic polarity. 
Conclusion 
Tokenization is basically linguistic recycling of words using magnetic and chemical 
methods.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Explain Dimensionality Reduction and compare PCA with Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA).
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Dimensionality reduction means we taking a big number of features and reducing them into 
smaller but meaningful set. When dataset have too many columns, model becomes slow and 
also very noisy, so dimensionality reduction help remove extra useless information. It makes 
the data much easier for visualizing also. 
PCA: 
PCA is unsupervised. It do not use class labels. It finds direction where data variance is 
maximum. It converts original features into new components that are uncorrelated. PCA 
focuses on capturing maximum information present in variation. 
LDA: 
LDA is supervised method. It uses class labels because it wants to separate different classes 
as far as possible. LDA looks for directions that maximize distance between classes and 
minimize distance within same class. 
Comparison: 
 PCA: maximize variance 
 LDA: maximize class separation 
 PCA: unsupervised 
 LDA: supervised 
 PCA uses covariance matrix 
 LDA uses scatter matrices 
So even though both reduce dimensions, their goals are different.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Explain the concept of Markov Decision Processes (MDP) in reinforcement learning and describe each component.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
MDP is mathematical frame that is used in reinforcement learning for decision making 
where outcomes are partly random and partly controlled by some agent. MDP tell how agent 
should move in environment and what rewards it get. 
Components: 
 States (S): Situation of the environment agent is inside. 
 Actions (A): Choices agent can take from a state. 
 Transition probability (P): Chance of moving from one state to other after taking an 
action. 
 Reward (R): Feedback given after action, show if action was good or bad. 
 Policy (π): Strategy telling what action to take in each state. 
So MDP basically help agent to learn which actions give more long-term reward.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4 . Explain types of clustering
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
1. Partitioning (e.g., K-Means): divides data into k clusters by optimizing intra-cluster 
similarity. Efficient but requires k and assumes convex clusters. 
2. Hierarchical (Agglomerative / Divisive): builds a tree (dendrogram) of clusters by 
successive merging or splitting; no need to pre-specify k, useful for nested group 
structure. 
3. Density-based (e.g., DBSCAN): groups dense regions and marks low-density points 
as noise; finds arbitrary-shaped clusters and handles outliers. 
4. Model-based (e.g., Gaussian Mixture Models): assumes data generated by a mixture 
of distributions, uses EM to infer components and soft assignments. 
5. Spectral clustering: uses graph Laplacian eigenvectors to cluster non-convex 
structures; effective when connectivity matters.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Discuss the challenges in machine learning , such as imbalanced data ,missing values , curse of dimensionality and concept drift , Provide solution for each
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Discuss challenges in ML — imbalanced data, missing values, curse of 
dimensionality, concept drift — and solutions 
Imbalanced Data 
 Problem: Minority class underrepresented → classifiers biased toward majority → 
poor recall for minority. 
 Solutions: resampling (oversample minority e.g., SMOTE, undersample majority), 
class-weighted loss functions, threshold tuning, use specialized algorithms (one-class / 
anomaly detection), evaluation with PR-AUC and F1 rather than accuracy. 
Missing Values 
 Problem: missingness distorts feature distributions, reduces usable samples. 
 Solutions: analyze missingness mechanism (MCAR/MAR/MNAR), impute using 
mean/median or model-based imputation (KNN, multivariate imputation), use 
indicators for missingness, use algorithms that accept missing inputs (e.g., XGBoost 
can handle NA), avoid dropping rows when information is valuable. 
Curse of Dimensionality 
 Problem: as feature count grows, data becomes sparse, distances lose meaning, 
overfitting risk increases. 
 Solutions: dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE for visualization), feature selection 
(mutual information, L1 regularization), domain-driven feature engineering, collect 
more data, use models that regularize strongly. 
Concept Drift 
 Problem: data distribution (P(X) or P(Y|X)) shifts over time → model degradation. 
 Solutions: monitor performance with drift detectors, use online learning or continual 
learning, retrain periodically with recent data (sliding window), incorporate adaptive 
weighting of recent samples, maintain ensembles with models trained on different 
time windows.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. What is Regularization and its role in ML ? explain its types in detail.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Role: Regularization prevents overfitting by adding constraints/penalties that limit model 
complexity, encouraging simpler models that generalize better. 
Types: 
L2 Regularization (Ridge / Tikhonov) 
 Adds penalty λ∑wi2\lambda \sum w_i^2λ∑wi2 to loss. 
 Shrinks weights toward zero but rarely makes them exactly zero. 
 Encourages distributed small weights; helps with multicollinearity; mathematically 
leads to closed-form solutions for linear models. 
L1 Regularization (Lasso) 
 Adds penalty λ∑∣wi∣\lambda \sum |w_i|λ∑∣wi∣. 
 Promotes sparsity — drives some weights exactly to zero → feature selection. 
 Useful when many features but only a few are relevant. 
Elastic Net 
 Combination of L1 and L2 penalties: balances sparsity and stability. Good when 
correlated features exist. 
Dropout (for neural networks) 
 Randomly deactivates neurons during training; acts like model averaging; reduces co
adaptation. 
Early Stopping 
 Monitor validation loss and stop training when it stops improving; implicitly 
regularizes by limiting training complexity. 
Data augmentation 
 Increases data variability; acts as a regularizer by exposing model to transformations. 
Other forms 
 Weight decay (equivalent to L2 in many frameworks), Bayesian priors (probabilistic 
regularization), max-norm constraints, and functional regularization (e.g., 
smoothness penalties). 
Choosing λ / strength: via cross-validation; improper value under- or over-regularizes.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. What is Ensemble Learning , explain Bagging and Boosting with Examples
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Ensemble Learning: combining multiple base learners to produce a single aggregated 
prediction, improving accuracy, robustness and stability compared to individual models. 
Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) 
 Idea: train multiple models independently on bootstrap samples (sample with 
replacement) and aggregate (averaging for regression, majority voting for 
classification). 
 Effect: reduces variance (averaging smooths model fluctuations) while maintaining 
low bias if base learners are unbiased. 
 Example: Random Forest — many decision trees trained on different bootstrap 
samples and random feature subsets; reduces overfitting common in single decision 
tree. 
Boosting 
 Idea: train models sequentially; each new model focuses on examples the previous 
models misclassified by reweighting or residual fitting. Combines weak learners into a 
strong learner. 
 Effect: reduces bias, can also reduce variance, but sensitive to noise if over-fit. 
 Examples: 
o AdaBoost: adaptively reweights misclassified samples; final model is weighted 
sum of weak learners. 
o Gradient Boosting (e.g., XGBoost, LightGBM): each new learner fits the 
negative gradient (residual) of loss; highly effective on tabular data. 
 Regularization: modern boosting includes shrinkage (learning rate), tree constraints, 
and subsampling for robustness. 
When to use: bagging for high-variance models (trees), boosting when reducing bias yields 
gains and when careful regularization is applied.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Describe Entire ML Pipeline , explain each step and explain how to evaluate Model.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
s 
End-to-end ML Pipeline 
1. Problem Definition & Metrics: define objective, success metrics (e.g., accuracy, F1, 
RMSE), constraints (latency, fairness). 
2. Data Collection: gather relevant raw data from sources, instrument logging for future 
use. 
3. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA): visualize distributions, correlations, detect 
outliers and anomalies. 
4. Data Preprocessing: clean data, handle missing values, deduplicate, correct entry 
errors. 
5. Feature Engineering: create, transform and select features (one-hot, embeddings, 
interaction terms). 
6. Train/Test Split & Cross-Validation: ensure realistic evaluation (time-aware splits 
for time series). 
7. Model Selection: choose algorithm(s) based on data size, problem type and 
interpretability needs. 
8. Training & Hyperparameter Tuning: use grid/random/Bayesian search with cross
validation, track experiments. 
9. Evaluation: use chosen metrics on holdout/test set; perform error analysis; check 
calibration and fairness. 
o Classification metrics: confusion matrix, precision/recall, F1, ROC-AUC, PR
AUC. 
o Regression metrics: MAE, RMSE, R², residual analysis. 
o Model diagnostics: residual plots, feature importance, partial dependence plots, 
SHAP explanations. 
10. Validation in Realistic Environment: A/B testing, canary deployments, back-testing 
for time series. 
11. Deployment: package model, serve via API, ensure monitoring and scalable 
infrastructure. 
12. Monitoring & Maintenance: track performance drift, data drift, and error rates; log 
inputs for retraining triggers. 
13. Retraining & Governance: schedule retraining, version models, document lineage 
and compliance. 
Model Evaluation Best Practices: holdout test set never seen during tuning, cross
validation for robust estimates, use appropriate metrics for class imbalance, calibrate 
probabilities if needed, and perform sensitivity analyses.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 5. What are the types data ML uses , What are the quality of good data?
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
? 
Types of Data: 
1. Structured tabular data: rows and columns (SQL tables). 
2. Unstructured data: text, images, audio, video. 
3. Semi-structured data: JSON, XML, logs. 
4. Time-series data: ordered temporal observations (sensors, finance). 
5. Graph data: nodes and edges (social networks, molecules). 
6. Spatial data / geospatial: coordinates, maps. 
Qualities of Good Data: 
 Accuracy: ground truth matches reality. 
 Completeness: minimal missing values for key fields. 
 Consistency: consistent data formats, units, and semantics. 
 Representativeness: reflects population and deployment scenarios (no sampling bias). 
 Sufficient volume & variety: enough examples across classes/conditions. 
 Low noise / high signal-to-noise ratio: clear patterns relative to randomness. 
 Timeliness: up-to-date for non-stationary problems. 
 Proper labeling quality: consistent and correctly annotated labels. 
 Traceability & metadata: provenance, schema, feature definitions for 
reproducibility.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 6. Write note on Naive bayes and SVM in detail
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Naïve Bayes (NB) 
 Principle: probabilistic classifier applying Bayes’ theorem with a strong (naïve) 
assumption of conditional independence between features given the class. 
 Variants: Gaussian NB (continuous features), Multinomial NB (count/text data), 
Bernoulli NB (binary features). 
 Strengths: very fast, low computational cost, works well with high-dimensional 
sparse data (text classification), requires small training data, outputs calibrated 
probabilities (roughly). 
 Weaknesses: independence assumption unrealistic sometimes; performance degrades 
when feature dependencies are strong. 
 Use cases: spam detection, document classification, simple baselines. 
Support Vector Machine (SVM) 
 Principle: margin-based classifier that finds a hyperplane maximizing the margin 
between classes in feature space; supports linear and kernelized non-linear 
classification. 
 Optimization: convex quadratic programming to minimize subject to margin 
constraints (soft margin introduces slack variables and C regularization). 
 Kernels: linear, polynomial, radial basis function (RBF), sigmoid — allow implicit 
mapping to high-dimensional spaces via the kernel trick. 
 Strengths: effective in high-dimensional spaces, robust with clear margins, well
regularized (C parameter), strong theoretical foundations. 
 Weaknesses: scales poorly to very large datasets (training complexity), choice and 
tuning of kernel and hyperparameters crucial, less interpretable than trees. 
 Use cases: text classification (with linear SVM), image classification (with kernel 
SVM on smaller datasets), bioinformatics.

Challenges in ML – imbalanced data, missing values, curse of dimensionality, concept drift 
+ solutions 
 Imbalanced Data: Some classes have very little samples. 
Solution: Oversampling, undersampling, class-weight adjustment. 
 Missing Values: Many values absent in the dataset. 
Solution: Mean/Median imputation or using models to fill gaps. 
 Curse of Dimensionality: Too many features cause sparse patterns. 
Solution: Dimension reduction using PCA or feature selection. 
 Concept Drift: Data pattern changes over time. 
Solution: Re-training model with new data and online learning methods.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 10. importance of data in ML
1. Discuss the challenges in machine learning , such as imbalanced data ,missing values , curse of dimensionality and concept drift , Provide solution for each
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Challenges in machine learning — imbalanced data, missing values, curse of 
dimensionality, concept drift — and solutions 
Imbalanced Data 
 Problem: rare classes (fraud, disease) get overwhelmed by majority, accuracy 
misleading. 
 Solutions: resampling (SMOTE/ADASYN oversampling, informed undersampling), 
cost-sensitive loss (class weights, focal loss), anomaly detection framing for extreme 
rarity, evaluation by PR-AUC and F1 rather than accuracy. 
Missing Values 
 Problem: reduces usable data and can bias estimates if missingness is informative 
(MAR/MNAR). 
 Solutions: analyze missingness mechanism; simple imputations (mean/median) for 
MCAR, model-based imputation (KNN, MICE), use missingness indicator features, or 
algorithms that natively handle NAs (certain tree implementations). 
Curse of Dimensionality 
 Problem: high dimensionality leads to sparse data, unreliable distance metrics and 
overfitting. 
 Solutions: domain-driven feature engineering, feature selection 
(filter/wrapper/embedded), dimensionality reduction (PCA, autoencoders), 
regularization and collecting more labeled examples relative to features. 
Concept Drift 
 Problem: P(X) or P(Y|X) changes over time; static model degrades. 
 Solutions: continuous monitoring and drift detection (ADWIN, DDM), 
online/incremental learning, sliding-window retraining, weighted retraining 
emphasizing recent data, human-in-the-loop validation for critical decisions.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. What is Ensemble Learning , explain Bagging and Boosting with Examples
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Ensemble principle: combine multiple estimators to improve predictive performance by 
reducing variance, bias or both; diversity among base learners is key. 
Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) 
 Mechanics: train independent base learners on bootstrap samples; aggregate by 
majority vote or averaging. 
 Benefit: reduces variance and stabilizes predictions. 
 Canonical example: Random Forest — bagged decision trees with random feature 
subsetting per split; robust, low-tuning and scalable. 
Boosting 
 Mechanics: sequentially train weak learners where each emphasizes instances 
mispredicted by prior learners (reweighting or residual fitting). 
 Benefit: reduces bias by building a strong learner from many weak ones; can also 
reduce variance with shrinkage. 
 Examples: AdaBoost (instance reweighting), Gradient Boosting (fit negative 
gradient/residuals), modern variants — XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost — 
optimized for speed and regularization (learning rate, subsampling, tree constraints). 
When to choose: bagging when models are high-variance (trees); boosting when marginal 
reduction in bias yields gains and careful regularization is applied.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 6. Write note on Naive bayes and SVM in detail
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Naïve Bayes and SVM — detailed note 
Naïve Bayes (NB) 
 Core idea: use Bayes’ theorem with a simplifying conditional independence 
assumption: P(y∣x)∝P(y)∏iP(xi∣y)P(y|x)\propto P(y)\prod_i P(x_i|y)P(y∣x)∝P(y)∏i
P(xi∣y). 
 Variants: Multinomial NB for term counts (text), Bernoulli NB for binary features, 
Gaussian NB for continuous inputs. 
 Strengths: extremely fast to train and predict, robust in high-dim sparse spaces, low 
memory footprint — ideal for baseline text classifiers. 
 Limitations: independence assumption often violated; cannot model feature 
interactions; probabilistic outputs may be poorly calibrated without smoothing. 
Support Vector Machine (SVM) 
 Core idea: find hyperplane maximizing margin between classes; soft margin 
introduces slack variables for non-separable data controlled by C. 
 Kernel trick: replace dot product with kernel K(x,x′)K(x,x')K(x,x′) to operate in 
implicit high-dim feature spaces (RBF, polynomial), enabling complex non-linear 
boundaries. 
 Optimization: convex QP problem with guaranteed global optimum; can be solved 
via SMO or gradient-based approximations for scale. 
 Strengths: effective in high-dim spaces, robust generalization when margin large, 
theoretically grounded. 
 Limitations: computational cost on very large datasets, kernel parameter tuning 
required, less transparent probabilistic interpretation (requires calibration). 


rubric_with_answers.question_text: 7. how to make model underfit and overfit
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
o To induce underfitting: choose an overly simple hypothesis (e.g., linear model 
for highly non-linear data), reduce model capacity (fewer layers/neurons, 
shallow tree), add strong regularization, remove important features, or stop 
training too early. Result: high bias, poor performance on train & test. 
o To induce overfitting: increase model capacity (deeper nets, higher-degree 
polynomials), reduce/omit regularization, train many epochs on small dataset, 
include noisy/irrelevant features, or leak label information. Result: low train 
error but poor generalization (high variance). Use learning curves and validation 
to detect and remedy both.

monitoring & drift detection, online/incremental learning, sliding-window 
retraining, weighted training emphasizing recent data, ensembles with temporal 
diversity, human-in-the-loop review.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. What is Ensemble Learning , explain Bagging and Boosting with Examples
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Ensemble learning combines multiple base models to reduce error through averaging 
or sequential correction. 
o Bagging: build multiple independent models on bootstrap samples and 
aggregate (vote/average). Reduces variance. Example: Random Forest — many 
decision trees trained on bootstrapped data and random feature subsets. 
o Boosting: sequentially train weak learners where each focuses on errors of 
previous; aggregate weighted learners. Reduces bias (also can reduce variance 
with shrinkage). Examples: AdaBoost (reweights misclassified samples), 
Gradient Boosting (fit residuals — XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost). Boosting 
often yields state-of-the-art tabular performance but requires careful 
regularization and learning-rate tuning.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. What is Regularization and its role in ML ? explain its types in detail.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Regularization is a technique to prevent overfitting by adding a penalty to the loss function, 
which discourages overly complex models and improves their ability to generalize to new 
data 
. Common types include L1 (Lasso) regularization, which forces some feature coefficients 
to zero, enabling feature selection, and L2 (Ridge) regularization, which shrinks all 
coefficients towards zero. Other methods, like Elastic Net, combine both L1 and L2 
penalties, while Data Augmentation artificially expands the training data.  
Role of Regularization  
 Prevents overfitting: It stops models from learning noise in the training data, leading 
to better performance on unseen data. 
 Improves generalization: By controlling model complexity, regularization helps the 
model perform more consistently on new, real-world data. 
 Balances bias and variance: It helps manage the trade-off between having too simple 
a model (high bias) and a model that is too complex (high variance). 
 Simplifies models: It encourages simpler models by penalizing large parameter 
values, which can lead to more interpretable results.  
Types of Regularization  
 L1 Regularization (Lasso): 
o Key feature: It can force some coefficients to be exactly zero, performing 
automatic feature selection by eliminating less important features. 
o Best for: Feature selection and building more interpretable models. 
 L2 Regularization (Ridge): 
o Adds a penalty equal to the sum of the squares of the coefficients ( 
o Key feature: It shrinks all coefficients towards zero but rarely makes them 
exactly zero. 
o Best for: Handling multicollinearity and prioritizing model accuracy and 
stability. 
 Elastic Net: 
o Combines both L1 and L2 penalties. 
o It can perform feature selection like L1 while keeping the benefits of L2 in 
terms of stability. 
 Data Augmentation: 
o A technique used primarily with images that artificially expands the training 
dataset by applying transformations like rotations, flips, or color shifts. 
o Key feature: Creates a more diverse training set, making the model more 
robust to variations in the input.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Discuss the challenges in machine learning , such as imbalanced data ,missing values , curse of dimensionality and concept drift , Provide solution for each
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Imbalanced Data 
 Problem: minority class rare → classifier biased to majority, metrics like accuracy 
misleading. 
 Solutions: resampling (oversample minority with SMOTE, ADASYN; undersample 
majority), class-weighted loss, threshold tuning, use ensemble methods focusing 
minority, evaluate with recall/precision/F1 and PR-AUC. 
Missing Values 
 Problem: missing entries break algorithms and bias estimates if not MCAR. 
 Solutions: analyze missingness mechanism (MCAR/MAR/MNAR), impute 
(mean/median for simple, KNN or MICE for multivariate), model-based imputation, 
use missing-indicator features, or algorithms that handle missingness natively (e.g., 
XGBoost handles NA). 
Curse of Dimensionality 
 Problem: high dimensional features make data sparse, distances less meaningful, 
overfitting risk grows. 
 Solutions: feature selection (filter/wrapper/embedded), dimensionality reduction 
(PCA, LDA, autoencoders), regularization (L1/L2), collect more data, domain-driven 
feature engineering. 
Concept Drift 
 Problem: distribution P(X) or P(Y|X) changes over time → model degrades. 
 Solutions: continuous monitoring, drift detection algorithms (ADWIN, DDM), 
online/incremental learning, retrain periodically using recent data (sliding window), 
ensemble of models trained at different times, use features robust to environment 
change.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. What is Regularization and its role in ML ? explain its types in detail.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Definition & role: regularization adds penalty or constraint to learning objective to prevent 
model from fitting noise, thus reduce variance and improve generalization. 
Types: 
 L2 regularization (Ridge / weight decay): add λ∑w² to loss. effect: shrink weights 
uniformly, prevents single weight blow up, convex, easy to optimize. good when 
many small correlated features. 
 L1 regularization (Lasso): add λ∑|w|. effect: drives many weights to zero → sparse 
solution and implicit feature selection. useful for interpretability and high-dimension 
small-sample. 
 Elastic Net: combination αL1 + (1−α)L2, tradeoff between sparsity and coefficient 
stability; helpful when features correlated. 
 Dropout (neural nets): randomly zero neuron activations during training; acts like 
ensemble of subnetworks; reduces co-adaptation and overfitting. 
 Early Stopping: monitor validation loss and stop when it stops improving; simple but 
effective regularizer. 
 Data augmentation: artificially enlarge dataset with label-preserving transforms — 
reduces overfitting by adding variability. 
 Max-norm / spectral norm constraints: bound weight norms to ensure stability. 
 Bayesian priors: interpret regularization as placing priors on weights (Gaussian prior 
→ L2, Laplace → L1). 
Choosing & tuning: regularization strength λ is hyperparameter tuned via validation; 
combination and type depend on data, interpretability and model.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. What is Ensemble Learning , explain Bagging and Boosting with Examples
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Ensemble Learning: combine multiple base learners to produce final prediction better than 
any single base; diversity among base learners key. 
Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) 
 Mechanism: create many bootstrap samples (sample with replacement), train 
independent base learners on each, aggregate predictions (majority vote or average). 
 Effect: reduces variance, stabilizes predictions of high-variance models like trees. 
 Example: Random Forest — bagging of decision trees plus random feature selection 
per split; robust and fast. 
Boosting 
 Mechanism: sequentially train weak learners where each learner focuses on 
correcting errors of previous ones; aggregate models weighted by performance. 
 Effect: converts weak learner to strong, reduces bias and sometimes variance; 
sensitive to noise, needs regularization. 
 Examples: AdaBoost (reweight misclassified samples), Gradient Boosting Machines 
(fit residuals iteratively), XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost — optimized GBMs with 
regularization, tree constraints, subsampling. 
Stacking / Blending: train diverse base models and meta-learner to combine them; can 
capture relationships among base predictions. 
When to use: bagging when base learners unstable; boosting when need to reduce bias and 
squeeze more performance — often winning in ML competitions.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Describe Entire ML Pipeline , explain each step and explain how to evaluate Model.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
End-to-end Pipeline: 
1. Problem definition & metrics: specify target, constraints, success metric (e.g., F1 for 
imbalance, RMSE for regression). 
2. Data acquisition: gather data from sources, ensure logging & provenance. 
3. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA): distribution, missingness, correlations, outliers, 
class balance; summary statistics and visualizations. 
4. Data preprocessing: cleaning, imputation, encoding categorical, scaling, timestamp 
handling, deduplication. 
5. Feature engineering & selection: domain features, transformations, interactions, 
embedding, dimensionality reduction. 
6. Train/validation/test split: preserve temporal order if needed, use K-fold or stratified 
CV for stability. 
7. Model selection & training: baseline models then complex ones; cross-validate; track 
experiments. 
8. Hyperparameter tuning: grid/random/Bayesian search with CV, nested CV for 
honest estimation. 
9. Evaluation & diagnostics: compute chosen metrics on test set; confusion matrix, 
ROC/PR curves, residual analysis, calibration plots, fairness checks, feature 
importance and error slices. 
10. Deployment: package model, serve via APIs, ensure scaling and latency. 
11. Monitoring & maintenance: track prediction quality, data drift, input distributions, 
A/B test, automated retraining triggers. 
Model evaluation: use appropriate metrics aligned to business, do cross-validation for 
robust estimates, avoid leakage, use statistical significance tests for model comparisons; for 
production run shadow testing / canary deployments and monitor online metrics.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 6. Write note on Naive bayes and SVM in detail
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Naïve Bayes: 
 Idea: uses Bayes theorem with independence assumption P(x|y)=∏P(xi|y). 
 Variants: Gaussian NB for continuous, Multinomial NB for count data, Bernoulli NB 
for binary features. 
 Strengths: very fast, works well on high-dimensional sparse data (text), simple to 
implement, needs little data. 
 Limitations: independence assumption often violated, correlated features degrade 
performance. 
 Use cases: spam detection, document classification, sentiment analysis, baseline 
models. 
Support Vector Machine (SVM): 
 Idea: find hyperplane with maximum margin between classes; soft-margin allows 
slack for non-separable data. 
 Kernel trick: use kernel functions (linear, polynomial, RBF) to implicitly map data to 
high-dim feature space without explicit transform. 
 Optimization: convex QP problem ensures global optimum. 
 Strengths: effective in high-dim spaces, robust margins, flexible kernels for 
nonlinearity. 
 Limitations: scales poorly to very large datasets, kernel selection & hyperparam 
tuning crucial, less direct probabilistic output (needs calibration). 
 Use cases: text/image classification on medium datasets, bioinformatics.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Discuss the challenges in machine learning , such as imbalanced data ,missing values , curse of dimensionality and concept drift , Provide solution for each
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Challenges in ML & Solutions 
Major challenges in machine learning include data quality and quantity, overfitting and 
underfitting, model bias, computational costs, and model interpretability. Solutions 
involve robust data preprocessing, using techniques like cross-validation and regularization, 
addressing bias through representative datasets and fair data collection, optimizing models 
for computational efficiency, and employing explainable AI (XAI) methods to make models 
more transparent.  
Data-related challenges 
 Challenge: Poor data quality, insufficient data, or non-representative data can all lead to 
inaccurate or biased models. 
 Solutions: 
o Implement strong data preprocessing techniques to clean, filter, and handle missing or noisy 
data. 
o Use data augmentation and synthetic data generation to supplement existing datasets. 
o Ensure the training data accurately reflects the real-world distribution to prevent a lack of 
representativeness.  
Model-related challenges 
 Challenge: Overfitting occurs when a model is too complex and learns noise, while 
underfitting occurs when it is too simple to capture patterns. 
 Solutions: 
o Use methods like cross-validation, regularization, and early stopping to prevent overfitting. 
o Simplify the model or add more features to address underfitting.  
Bias and ethical challenges 
 Challenge: Data bias can result in unfair or discriminatory model outputs. 
 Solutions: 
o Carefully curate and balance training data to ensure it represents the broader population 
fairly. 
o Implement bias mitigation strategies and continuously monitor models for biased outcomes 
after deployment. 
o Address ethical considerations, such as privacy and algorithmic fairness

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. What is Regularization and its role in ML ? explain its types in detail.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
What is Regularization? Explain its types 
Regularization is a machine learning technique that prevents overfitting by penalizing model 
complexity, improving its ability to generalize to new data. Common types include L1 
(Lasso) regularization, which can zero out feature weights, L2 (Ridge) regularization, which 
shrinks weights toward zero, and Dropout, which randomly deactivates neurons during 
training.  
Types of regularization 
 L1 Regularization (Lasso): Adds the absolute value of the coefficients to the loss function. 
This encourages sparsity, meaning some feature coefficients are driven to exactly zero, 
which can be used for feature selection. 
 L2 Regularization (Ridge): Adds the square of the coefficients to the loss function. This 
prevents large weights by shrinking them towards zero, but it doesn't force them to be 
exactly zero. 
 Elastic Net: A combination of both L1 and L2 regularization. It penalizes the loss function 
with a combination of both the absolute values and the squares of the coefficients. 
 Dropout: A technique specifically for neural networks where neurons are randomly 
"dropped out" during training. This prevents neurons from becoming too specialized and 
dependent on each other, forcing the network to learn more robust features. 
 Early Stopping: Stops the training process when the model's performance on a validation 
set starts to degrade, even as the performance on the training set continues to improve. This

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 5. What are the types data ML uses , What are the quality of good data?
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Machine learning uses different types of data, including numerical (e.g., age, price) 
and categorical (e.g., gender, color) data. Other important data types include time 
series and text. Good data is accurate, complete, consistent, and relevant to the 
problem, which ensures the model can learn reliable patterns and make accurate 
predictions.  
Types of data in ML 
 Numerical (Quantitative): Data that can be measured or counted. 
o Discrete: Countable values, such as the number of customers or clicks. 
o Continuous: Measurable values, such as temperature, stock price, or height. 
 Categorical (Qualitative): Data that consists of labels or categories. 
o Nominal: Categories without a meaningful order, such as eye color or gender. 
o Ordinal: Categories with a meaningful order or ranking, such as customer 
satisfaction levels (poor, average, good). 
 Time Series: Data points indexed in time order, like stock prices or weather 
patterns. 
 Text: Human language, from individual words to entire documents. 
 Multimedia: Images, videos, and audio files.  
Qualities of good data 
 Accuracy: The data must be correct and valid. 
 Completeness: The dataset should be free of missing values to the extent possible. 
 Consistency: Data should be uniform across the dataset and its sources. 
 Relevance: The data must be relevant to the specific problem the model is trying to 
solve. 
 Granularity: The data should be at the right level of detail for the task at hand. 
 Volume: A sufficient amount of data is crucial for training models, though too much 
can be problematic. 
 Timeliness: The data must be recent enough to be useful for the task.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. What is Ensemble Learning , explain Bagging and Boosting with Examples
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Ensemble Learning — Bagging and Boosting (with examples) 
Principle: combine multiple models to reduce error components (variance, bias) and 
increase robustness. 
Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) 
 Mechanism: train base learners independently on bootstrap samples; aggregate 
predictions (averaging/voting). 
 Effect: lowers variance by averaging uncorrelated errors. 
 Example: Random Forest — bagged decision trees with additional random feature 
selection per split; strong off-the-shelf performance and resilience to overfitting. 
Boosting 
 Mechanism: sequentially fit weak learners where each new learner focuses on 
residuals or misclassified instances of the ensemble so far. 
 Effect: reduces bias and often variance when regularized; converts many weak learners 
into a strong predictor. 
 Examples: AdaBoost (reweights examples), Gradient Boosting (fit negative gradients; 
implementations: XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost). Regularization (shrinkage, tree 
constraints) crucial to prevent overfitting. 
Stacking & Blending: meta-learner trained on base model predictions to capture 
complementary strengths.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 6. Write note on Naive bayes and SVM in detail
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Naïve Bayes and SVM — detailed note 
Naïve Bayes (NB) 
 Core idea: apply Bayes’ theorem with conditional independence: Variants: 
Multinomial NB (counts/text), Bernoulli NB (binary features), Gaussian NB 
(continuous). 
 Pros: extremely fast, low memory, works well with high-dim sparse features (text), 
interpretable priors. 
 Cons: independence assumption often violated; cannot capture feature interactions; 
probability estimates crude unless calibrated. 
 Use cases: spam detection, document classification, simple baselines. 
Support Vector Machine (SVM) 
 Core idea: find hyperplane maximizing margin between classes; soft margin 
introduces slack ξ and regularization C to trade margin vs misclassification. 
 Kernel trick: map to high-dim feature space implicitly with kernel 
K(x,x′)K(x,x')K(x,x′) (RBF, polynomial) to enable non-linear decision boundaries. 
 Optimization: convex quadratic program (global optimum), can be solved in primal 
or dual. 
 Pros: robust in high dimensional settings, effective with clear margins, strong 
theoretical guarantees. 
 Cons: computationally heavy for very large n, kernel selection & hyperparameter 
tuning (C, γ) crucial, limited probabilistic outputs (need calibration via Platt scaling). 
 Use cases: text classification (linear SVMs), image recognition on moderate datasets, 
bioinformatics.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 10. importance of data in ML
1. Discuss the challenges in machine learning , such as imbalanced data ,missing values , curse of dimensionality and concept drift , Provide solution for each
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Challenges in machine learning — imbalanced data, missing values, curse of 
dimensionality, concept drift — and solutions 
Imbalanced Data 
 Problem: rare classes (fraud, disease) get overwhelmed by majority, accuracy 
misleading. 
 Solutions: resampling (SMOTE/ADASYN oversampling, informed undersampling), 
cost-sensitive loss (class weights, focal loss), anomaly detection framing for extreme 
rarity, evaluation by PR-AUC and F1 rather than accuracy. 
Missing Values 
 Problem: reduces usable data and can bias estimates if missingness is informative 
(MAR/MNAR). 
 Solutions: analyze missingness mechanism; simple imputations (mean/median) for 
MCAR, model-based imputation (KNN, MICE), use missingness indicator features, or 
algorithms that natively handle NAs (certain tree implementations). 
Curse of Dimensionality 
 Problem: high dimensionality leads to sparse data, unreliable distance metrics and 
overfitting. 
 Solutions: domain-driven feature engineering, feature selection 
(filter/wrapper/embedded), dimensionality reduction (PCA, autoencoders), 
regularization and collecting more labeled examples relative to features. 
Concept Drift 
 Problem: P(X) or P(Y|X) changes over time; static model degrades. 
 Solutions: continuous monitoring and drift detection (ADWIN, DDM), 
online/incremental learning, sliding-window retraining, weighted retraining 
emphasizing recent data, human-in-the-loop validation for critical decisions.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. What is Ensemble Learning , explain Bagging and Boosting with Examples
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Ensemble principle: combine multiple estimators to improve predictive performance by 
reducing variance, bias or both; diversity among base learners is key. 
Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) 
 Mechanics: train independent base learners on bootstrap samples; aggregate by 
majority vote or averaging. 
 Benefit: reduces variance and stabilizes predictions. 
 Canonical example: Random Forest — bagged decision trees with random feature 
subsetting per split; robust, low-tuning and scalable. 
Boosting 
 Mechanics: sequentially train weak learners where each emphasizes instances 
mispredicted by prior learners (reweighting or residual fitting). 
 Benefit: reduces bias by building a strong learner from many weak ones; can also 
reduce variance with shrinkage. 
 Examples: AdaBoost (instance reweighting), Gradient Boosting (fit negative 
gradient/residuals), modern variants — XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost — 
optimized for speed and regularization (learning rate, subsampling, tree constraints). 
When to choose: bagging when models are high-variance (trees); boosting when marginal 
reduction in bias yields gains and careful regularization is applied.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Describe Entire ML Pipeline , explain each step and explain how to evaluate Model.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Entire ML pipeline — each step and model evaluation 
Pipeline steps (expanded): 
1. Problem framing & metric definition: define business objective, costs of errors, 
metric (F1, ROC-AUC, RMSE). 
2. Data acquisition & storage: logging, instrumentation, provenance recording. 
3. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA): distributions, correlations, missingness, class 
balance, visual checks. 
4. Preprocessing: cleaning, imputation, encoding, scaling, outlier handling and 
resolving label noise. 
5. Feature engineering: domain features, temporal aggregations, embeddings, 
interaction terms; feature selection. 
6. Modeling & validation strategy: baseline models, cross-validation or time-aware CV 
for temporal data. 
7. Hyperparameter optimization: grid/random/Bayesian search with nested CV when 
necessary. 
8. Evaluation & diagnostics: test set evaluation, confusion matrices, calibration curves, 
error slicing, fairness checks, explainability (SHAP/LIME). 
9. Deployment & serving: model packaging, latency/throughput planning, A/B testing 
and canary rollout. 
10. Monitoring & maintenance: data drift, prediction health, automated retraining 
triggers, logging for audits. 
Model evaluation: pick metrics aligned to business; use holdout test for final estimate; 
cross-validation for robustness; inspect calibration and confidence; use error analysis and 
business KPIs (conversion, revenue impact) for decision to deploy.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 6. Write note on Naive bayes and SVM in detail
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Naïve Bayes and SVM — detailed note 
Naïve Bayes (NB) 
 Core idea: use Bayes’ theorem with a simplifying conditional independence 
assumption: P(y∣x)∝P(y)∏iP(xi∣y)P(y|x)\propto P(y)\prod_i P(x_i|y)P(y∣x)∝P(y)∏i
P(xi∣y). 
 Variants: Multinomial NB for term counts (text), Bernoulli NB for binary features, 
Gaussian NB for continuous inputs. 
 Strengths: extremely fast to train and predict, robust in high-dim sparse spaces, low 
memory footprint — ideal for baseline text classifiers. 
 Limitations: independence assumption often violated; cannot model feature 
interactions; probabilistic outputs may be poorly calibrated without smoothing. 
Support Vector Machine (SVM) 
 Core idea: find hyperplane maximizing margin between classes; soft margin 
introduces slack variables for non-separable data controlled by C. 
 Kernel trick: replace dot product with kernel K(x,x′)K(x,x')K(x,x′) to operate in 
implicit high-dim feature spaces (RBF, polynomial), enabling complex non-linear 
boundaries. 
 Optimization: convex QP problem with guaranteed global optimum; can be solved 
via SMO or gradient-based approximations for scale. 
 Strengths: effective in high-dim spaces, robust generalization when margin large, 
theoretically grounded. 
 Limitations: computational cost on very large datasets, kernel parameter tuning 
required, less transparent probabilistic interpretation (requires calibration). 


Challenges in ML & solutions 
Imbalanced Data 
 Problem: models favor majority class; accuracy misleading. 
 Solutions: oversampling minority (SMOTE variants), careful undersampling, class-weighted losses, 
focal loss, ensemble methods oriented to balance, use appropriate metrics (PR-AUC, F1). 
Missing Values 
 Problem: reduce usable samples, bias if not MCAR. 
 Solutions: analyze missing mechanism (MCAR/MAR/MNAR); simple imputations (mean/median) 
when safe; model-based imputation (KNN, MICE); use missingness as a feature; prefer algorithms 
tolerant to NAs (tree-based boosters). 
Curse of Dimensionality 
 Problem: distance metrics degrade; sparsity increases, overfitting risk. 
 Solutions: feature selection (mutual info, L1), dimensionality reduction (PCA, autoencoders), 
regularization, domain-specific feature synthesis, collect more samples. 
Concept Drift 
 Problem: P(X) or P(Y|X) changes over time causing performance drop. 
 Solutions: online/incremental learning, retrain on recent data (sliding window), drift detectors to 
trigger retraining, ensembles weighting recent models, and continuous monitoring with feedback 
loops.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 5. What are the types data ML uses , What are the quality of good data?
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Machine learning uses different types of data, including numerical (e.g., age, price) 
and categorical (e.g., gender, color) data. Other important data types include time 
series and text. Good data is accurate, complete, consistent, and relevant to the 
problem, which ensures the model can learn reliable patterns and make accurate 
predictions.  
Types of data in ML 
 Numerical (Quantitative): Data that can be measured or counted. 
o Discrete: Countable values, such as the number of customers or clicks. 
o Continuous: Measurable values, such as temperature, stock price, or height. 
 Categorical (Qualitative): Data that consists of labels or categories. 
o Nominal: Categories without a meaningful order, such as eye color or gender. 
o Ordinal: Categories with a meaningful order or ranking, such as customer 
satisfaction levels (poor, average, good). 
 Time Series: Data points indexed in time order, like stock prices or weather 
patterns. 
 Text: Human language, from individual words to entire documents. 
 Multimedia: Images, videos, and audio files.  
Qualities of good data 
 Accuracy: The data must be correct and valid. 
 Completeness: The dataset should be free of missing values to the extent possible. 
 Consistency: Data should be uniform across the dataset and its sources. 
 Relevance: The data must be relevant to the specific problem the model is trying to 
solve. 
 Granularity: The data should be at the right level of detail for the task at hand. 
 Volume: A sufficient amount of data is crucial for training models, though too much 
can be problematic. 
 Timeliness: The data must be recent enough to be useful for the task.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. What is Regularization and its role in ML ? explain its types in detail.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Definition & role: regularization adds penalty or constraint to learning objective to prevent 
model from fitting noise, thus reduce variance and improve generalization. 
Types: 
 L2 regularization (Ridge / weight decay): add λ∑w² to loss. effect: shrink weights 
uniformly, prevents single weight blow up, convex, easy to optimize. good when 
many small correlated features. 
 L1 regularization (Lasso): add λ∑|w|. effect: drives many weights to zero → sparse 
solution and implicit feature selection. useful for interpretability and high-dimension 
small-sample. 
 Elastic Net: combination αL1 + (1−α)L2, tradeoff between sparsity and coefficient 
stability; helpful when features correlated. 
 Dropout (neural nets): randomly zero neuron activations during training; acts like 
ensemble of subnetworks; reduces co-adaptation and overfitting. 
 Early Stopping: monitor validation loss and stop when it stops improving; simple but 
effective regularizer. 
 Data augmentation: artificially enlarge dataset with label-preserving transforms — 
reduces overfitting by adding variability. 
 Max-norm / spectral norm constraints: bound weight norms to ensure stability. 
 Bayesian priors: interpret regularization as placing priors on weights (Gaussian prior 
→ L2, Laplace → L1). 
Choosing & tuning: regularization strength λ is hyperparameter tuned via validation; 
combination and type depend on data, interpretability and model.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. What is Ensemble Learning , explain Bagging and Boosting with Examples
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Ensemble Learning: combine multiple base learners to produce final prediction better than 
any single base; diversity among base learners key. 
Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) 
 Mechanism: create many bootstrap samples (sample with replacement), train 
independent base learners on each, aggregate predictions (majority vote or average). 
 Effect: reduces variance, stabilizes predictions of high-variance models like trees. 
 Example: Random Forest — bagging of decision trees plus random feature selection 
per split; robust and fast. 
Boosting 
 Mechanism: sequentially train weak learners where each learner focuses on 
correcting errors of previous ones; aggregate models weighted by performance. 
 Effect: converts weak learner to strong, reduces bias and sometimes variance; 
sensitive to noise, needs regularization. 
 Examples: AdaBoost (reweight misclassified samples), Gradient Boosting Machines 
(fit residuals iteratively), XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost — optimized GBMs with 
regularization, tree constraints, subsampling. 
Stacking / Blending: train diverse base models and meta-learner to combine them; can 
capture relationships among base predictions. 
When to use: bagging when base learners unstable; boosting when need to reduce bias and 
squeeze more performance — often winning in ML competitions.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Describe Entire ML Pipeline , explain each step and explain how to evaluate Model.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
End-to-end Pipeline: 
1. Problem definition & metrics: specify target, constraints, success metric (e.g., F1 for 
imbalance, RMSE for regression). 
2. Data acquisition: gather data from sources, ensure logging & provenance. 
3. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA): distribution, missingness, correlations, outliers, 
class balance; summary statistics and visualizations. 
4. Data preprocessing: cleaning, imputation, encoding categorical, scaling, timestamp 
handling, deduplication. 
5. Feature engineering & selection: domain features, transformations, interactions, 
embedding, dimensionality reduction. 
6. Train/validation/test split: preserve temporal order if needed, use K-fold or stratified 
CV for stability. 
7. Model selection & training: baseline models then complex ones; cross-validate; track 
experiments. 
8. Hyperparameter tuning: grid/random/Bayesian search with CV, nested CV for 
honest estimation. 
9. Evaluation & diagnostics: compute chosen metrics on test set; confusion matrix, 
ROC/PR curves, residual analysis, calibration plots, fairness checks, feature 
importance and error slices. 
10. Deployment: package model, serve via APIs, ensure scaling and latency. 
11. Monitoring & maintenance: track prediction quality, data drift, input distributions, 
A/B test, automated retraining triggers. 
Model evaluation: use appropriate metrics aligned to business, do cross-validation for

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Discuss the challenges in machine learning , such as imbalanced data ,missing values , curse of dimensionality and concept drift , Provide solution for each
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Imbalanced Data 
 Problem: minority class rare → classifier biased to majority, metrics like accuracy 
misleading. 
 Solutions: resampling (oversample minority with SMOTE, ADASYN; undersample 
majority), class-weighted loss, threshold tuning, use ensemble methods focusing 
minority, evaluate with recall/precision/F1 and PR-AUC. 
Missing Values 
 Problem: missing entries break algorithms and bias estimates if not MCAR. 
 Solutions: analyze missingness mechanism (MCAR/MAR/MNAR), impute 
(mean/median for simple, KNN or MICE for multivariate), model-based imputation, 
use missing-indicator features, or algorithms that handle missingness natively (e.g., 
XGBoost handles NA). 
Curse of Dimensionality 
 Problem: high dimensional features make data sparse, distances less meaningful, 
overfitting risk grows. 
 Solutions: feature selection (filter/wrapper/embedded), dimensionality reduction 
(PCA, LDA, autoencoders), regularization (L1/L2), collect more data, domain-driven 
feature engineering. 
Concept Drift 
 Problem: distribution P(X) or P(Y|X) changes over time → model degrades. 
 Solutions: continuous monitoring, drift detection algorithms (ADWIN, DDM), 
online/incremental learning, retrain periodically using recent data (sliding window), 
ensemble of models trained at different times, use features robust to environment 
change.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. What is Regularization and its role in ML ? explain its types in detail.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Definition & role: regularization adds penalty or constraint to learning objective to prevent 
model from fitting noise, thus reduce variance and improve generalization. 
Types: 
 L2 regularization (Ridge / weight decay): add λ∑w² to loss. effect: shrink weights 
uniformly, prevents single weight blow up, convex, easy to optimize. good when 
many small correlated features. 
 L1 regularization (Lasso): add λ∑|w|. effect: drives many weights to zero → sparse 
solution and implicit feature selection. useful for interpretability and high-dimension 
small-sample. 
 Elastic Net: combination αL1 + (1−α)L2, tradeoff between sparsity and coefficient 
stability; helpful when features correlated. 
 Dropout (neural nets): randomly zero neuron activations during training; acts like 
ensemble of subnetworks; reduces co-adaptation and overfitting. 
 Early Stopping: monitor validation loss and stop when it stops improving; simple but 
effective regularizer. 
 Data augmentation: artificially enlarge dataset with label-preserving transforms — 
reduces overfitting by adding variability. 
 Max-norm / spectral norm constraints: bound weight norms to ensure stability. 
 Bayesian priors: interpret regularization as placing priors on weights (Gaussian prior 
→ L2, Laplace → L1). 
Choosing & tuning: regularization strength λ is hyperparameter tuned via validation; 
combination and type depend on data, interpretability and model.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. What is Ensemble Learning , explain Bagging and Boosting with Examples
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Ensemble Learning: combine multiple base learners to produce final prediction better than 
any single base; diversity among base learners key. 
Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) 
 Mechanism: create many bootstrap samples (sample with replacement), train 
independent base learners on each, aggregate predictions (majority vote or average). 
 Effect: reduces variance, stabilizes predictions of high-variance models like trees. 
 Example: Random Forest — bagging of decision trees plus random feature selection 
per split; robust and fast. 
Boosting 
 Mechanism: sequentially train weak learners where each learner focuses on 
correcting errors of previous ones; aggregate models weighted by performance. 
 Effect: converts weak learner to strong, reduces bias and sometimes variance; 
sensitive to noise, needs regularization. 
 Examples: AdaBoost (reweight misclassified samples), Gradient Boosting Machines 
(fit residuals iteratively), XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost — optimized GBMs with 
regularization, tree constraints, subsampling. 
Stacking / Blending: train diverse base models and meta-learner to combine them; can 
capture relationships among base predictions. 
When to use: bagging when base learners unstable; boosting when need to reduce bias and 
squeeze more performance — often winning in ML competitions.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Describe Entire ML Pipeline , explain each step and explain how to evaluate Model.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
End-to-end Pipeline: 
1. Problem definition & metrics: specify target, constraints, success metric (e.g., F1 for 
imbalance, RMSE for regression). 
2. Data acquisition: gather data from sources, ensure logging & provenance. 
3. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA): distribution, missingness, correlations, outliers, 
class balance; summary statistics and visualizations. 
4. Data preprocessing: cleaning, imputation, encoding categorical, scaling, timestamp 
handling, deduplication. 
5. Feature engineering & selection: domain features, transformations, interactions, 
embedding, dimensionality reduction. 
6. Train/validation/test split: preserve temporal order if needed, use K-fold or stratified 
CV for stability. 
7. Model selection & training: baseline models then complex ones; cross-validate; track 
experiments. 
8. Hyperparameter tuning: grid/random/Bayesian search with CV, nested CV for 
honest estimation. 
9. Evaluation & diagnostics: compute chosen metrics on test set; confusion matrix, 
ROC/PR curves, residual analysis, calibration plots, fairness checks, feature 
importance and error slices. 
10. Deployment: package model, serve via APIs, ensure scaling and latency. 
11. Monitoring & maintenance: track prediction quality, data drift, input distributions, 
A/B test, automated retraining triggers. 
Model evaluation: use appropriate metrics aligned to business, do cross-validation for 
robust estimates, avoid leakage, use statistical significance tests for model comparisons; for 
production run shadow testing / canary deployments and monitor online metrics.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Discuss the challenges in machine learning , such as imbalanced data ,missing values , curse of dimensionality and concept drift , Provide solution for each
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Discuss challenges in ML — imbalanced data, missing values, curse of 
dimensionality, concept drift — and solutions 
Imbalanced Data 
 Problem: Minority class underrepresented → classifiers biased toward majority → 
poor recall for minority. 
 Solutions: resampling (oversample minority e.g., SMOTE, undersample majority), 
class-weighted loss functions, threshold tuning, use specialized algorithms (one-class / 
anomaly detection), evaluation with PR-AUC and F1 rather than accuracy. 
Missing Values 
 Problem: missingness distorts feature distributions, reduces usable samples. 
 Solutions: analyze missingness mechanism (MCAR/MAR/MNAR), impute using 
mean/median or model-based imputation (KNN, multivariate imputation), use 
indicators for missingness, use algorithms that accept missing inputs (e.g., XGBoost 
can handle NA), avoid dropping rows when information is valuable. 
Curse of Dimensionality 
 Problem: as feature count grows, data becomes sparse, distances lose meaning, 
overfitting risk increases. 
 Solutions: dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE for visualization), feature selection 
(mutual information, L1 regularization), domain-driven feature engineering, collect 
more data, use models that regularize strongly. 
Concept Drift 
 Problem: data distribution (P(X) or P(Y|X)) shifts over time → model degradation. 
 Solutions: monitor performance with drift detectors, use online learning or continual 
learning, retrain periodically with recent data (sliding window), incorporate adaptive 
weighting of recent samples, maintain ensembles with models trained on different 
time windows.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. What is Regularization and its role in ML ? explain its types in detail.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Role: Regularization prevents overfitting by adding constraints/penalties that limit model 
complexity, encouraging simpler models that generalize better. 
Types: 
L2 Regularization (Ridge / Tikhonov) 
 Shrinks weights toward zero but rarely makes them exactly zero. 
 Encourages distributed small weights; helps with multicollinearity; mathematically 
leads to closed-form solutions for linear models. 
L1 Regularization (Lasso) 
 Promotes sparsity — drives some weights exactly to zero → feature selection. 
 Useful when many features but only a few are relevant. 
Elastic Net 
 Combination of L1 and L2 penalties: balances sparsity and stability. Good when 
correlated features exist. 
Dropout (for neural networks) 
 Randomly deactivates neurons during training; acts like model averaging; reduces co
adaptation. 
Early Stopping 
 Monitor validation loss and stop training when it stops improving; implicitly 
regularizes by limiting training complexity. 
Data augmentation 
 Increases data variability; acts as a regularizer by exposing model to transformations. 
Other forms 
 Weight decay (equivalent to L2 in many frameworks), Bayesian priors (probabilistic 
regularization), max-norm constraints, and functional regularization (e.g., 
smoothness penalties). 
Choosing λ / strength: via cross-validation; improper value under- or over-regularizes.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. What is Ensemble Learning , explain Bagging and Boosting with Examples
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Ensemble Learning: combining multiple base learners to produce a single aggregated 
prediction, improving accuracy, robustness and stability compared to individual models. 
Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) 
 Idea: train multiple models independently on bootstrap samples (sample with 
replacement) and aggregate (averaging for regression, majority voting for 
classification). 
 Effect: reduces variance (averaging smooths model fluctuations) while maintaining 
low bias if base learners are unbiased. 
 Example: Random Forest — many decision trees trained on different bootstrap 
samples and random feature subsets; reduces overfitting common in single decision 
tree. 
Boosting 
 Idea: train models sequentially; each new model focuses on examples the previous 
models misclassified by reweighting or residual fitting. Combines weak learners into a 
strong learner. 
 Effect: reduces bias, can also reduce variance, but sensitive to noise if over-fit. 
 Examples: 
o AdaBoost: adaptively reweights misclassified samples; final model is weighted 
sum of weak learners. 
o Gradient Boosting (e.g., XGBoost, LightGBM): each new learner fits the 
negative gradient (residual) of loss; highly effective on tabular data. 
 Regularization: modern boosting includes shrinkage (learning rate), tree constraints, 
and subsampling for robustness. 
When to use: bagging for high-variance models (trees), boosting when reducing bias yields 
gains and when careful regularization is applied.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Describe Entire ML Pipeline , explain each step and explain how to evaluate Model.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
s 
End-to-end ML Pipeline 
1. Problem Definition & Metrics: define objective, success metrics (e.g., accuracy, F1, 
RMSE), constraints (latency, fairness). 
2. Data Collection: gather relevant raw data from sources, instrument logging for future 
use. 
3. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA): visualize distributions, correlations, detect 
outliers and anomalies. 
4. Data Preprocessing: clean data, handle missing values, deduplicate, correct entry 
errors. 
5. Feature Engineering: create, transform and select features (one-hot, embeddings, 
interaction terms). 
6. Train/Test Split & Cross-Validation: ensure realistic evaluation (time-aware splits 
for time series). 
7. Model Selection: choose algorithm(s) based on data size, problem type and 
interpretability needs. 
8. Training & Hyperparameter Tuning: use grid/random/Bayesian search with cross
validation, track experiments. 
9. Evaluation: use chosen metrics on holdout/test set; perform error analysis; check 
calibration and fairness. 
o Classification metrics: confusion matrix, precision/recall, F1, ROC-AUC, PR
AUC. 
o Regression metrics: MAE, RMSE, R², residual analysis. 
o Model diagnostics: residual plots, feature importance, partial dependence plots, 
SHAP explanations. 
10. Validation in Realistic Environment: A/B testing, canary deployments, back-testing 
for time series. 
11. Deployment: package model, serve via API, ensure monitoring and scalable 
infrastructure. 
12. Monitoring & Maintenance: track performance drift, data drift, and error rates; log 
inputs for retraining triggers. 
13. Retraining & Governance: schedule retraining, version models, document lineage 
and compliance. 
Model Evaluation Best Practices: holdout test set never seen during tuning, cross
validation for robust estimates, use appropriate metrics for class imbalance, calibrate 
probabilities if needed, and perform sensitivity analyses.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 6. Write note on Naive bayes and SVM in detail
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Naïve Bayes (NB) 
 Principle: probabilistic classifier applying Bayes’ theorem with a strong (naïve) 
assumption of conditional independence between features given the class. 
 Variants: Gaussian NB (continuous features), Multinomial NB (count/text data), 
Bernoulli NB (binary features). 
 Strengths: very fast, low computational cost, works well with high-dimensional 
sparse data (text classification), requires small training data, outputs calibrated 
probabilities (roughly). 
 Weaknesses: independence assumption unrealistic sometimes; performance degrades 
when feature dependencies are strong. 
 Use cases: spam detection, document classification, simple baselines. 
Support Vector Machine (SVM) 
 Principle: margin-based classifier that finds a hyperplane maximizing the margin 
between classes in feature space; supports linear and kernelized non-linear 
classification. 
 Optimization: convex quadratic programming to minimize subject to margin 
constraints (soft margin introduces slack variables and C regularization). 
 Kernels: linear, polynomial, radial basis function (RBF), sigmoid — allow implicit 
mapping to high-dimensional spaces via the kernel trick. 
 Strengths: effective in high-dimensional spaces, robust with clear margins, well
regularized (C parameter), strong theoretical foundations. 
 Weaknesses: scales poorly to very large datasets (training complexity), choice and 
tuning of kernel and hyperparameters crucial, less interpretable than trees. 
 Use cases: text classification (with linear SVM), image classification (with kernel 
SVM on smaller datasets), bioinformatics.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Discuss the challenges in machine learning , such as imbalanced data ,missing values , curse of dimensionality and concept drift , Provide solution for each
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Challenges in ML and solutions 
Imbalanced Data 
 Problem: models favor majority class; accuracy misleading. 
 Solutions: oversampling minority (SMOTE variants), careful undersampling, class
weighted losses, focal loss, ensemble methods oriented to balance, use appropriate 
metrics (PR-AUC, F1). 
Missing Values 
 Problem: reduce usable samples, bias if not MCAR. 
 Solutions: analyze missing mechanism (MCAR/MAR/MNAR); simple imputations 
(mean/median) when safe; model-based imputation (KNN, MICE); use missingness as 
a feature; prefer algorithms tolerant to NAs (tree-based boosters). 
Curse of Dimensionality 
 Problem: distance metrics degrade; sparsity increases, overfitting risk. 
 Solutions: feature selection (mutual info, L1), dimensionality reduction (PCA, 
autoencoders), regularization, domain-specific feature synthesis, collect more samples. 
Concept Drift 
 Problem: P(X) or P(Y|X) changes over time causing performance drop. 
 Solutions: online/incremental learning, retrain on recent data (sliding window), drift 
detectors to trigger retraining, ensembles weighting recent models, and continuous 
monitoring with feedback loops.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. What is Ensemble Learning , explain Bagging and Boosting with Examples
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Ensemble Learning — Bagging and Boosting (with examples) 
Principle: combine multiple models to reduce error components (variance, bias) and 
increase robustness. 
Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) 
 Mechanism: train base learners independently on bootstrap samples; aggregate 
predictions (averaging/voting). 
 Effect: lowers variance by averaging uncorrelated errors. 
 Example: Random Forest — bagged decision trees with additional random feature 
selection per split; strong off-the-shelf performance and resilience to overfitting. 
Boosting 
 Mechanism: sequentially fit weak learners where each new learner focuses on 
residuals or misclassified instances of the ensemble so far. 
 Effect: reduces bias and often variance when regularized; converts many weak learners 
into a strong predictor. 
 Examples: AdaBoost (reweights examples), Gradient Boosting (fit negative gradients; 
implementations: XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost). Regularization (shrinkage, tree 
constraints) crucial to prevent overfitting. 
Stacking & Blending: meta-learner trained on base model predictions to capture 
complementary strengths.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Describe Entire ML Pipeline , explain each step and explain how to evaluate Model.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Entire ML pipeline and model evaluation 
Pipeline steps (detailed): 
1. Problem framing & metric selection: define business objective and select 
appropriate metrics (e.g., recall vs precision tradeoff). 
2. Data engineering: ingestion, schema design, sampling strategy, labeling pipeline. 
3. EDA & diagnostics: distribution checks, feature correlations, outlier detection, label 
noise estimation. 
4. Preprocessing & featurization: cleaning, imputing, encoding, scaling, text/image 
preprocessing, embedding extraction. 
5. Feature engineering: interactions, aggregations, temporal features, domain 
transformations, feature selection. 
6. Modeling: choose algorithm family; baseline models; iterate complexity. 
7. Validation & hyperparameter search: cross-validation, time series CV, nested CV 
for honest estimates; tune with grid/random/Bayesian search. 
8. Evaluation: on holdout/test set; compute chosen metrics; analyze calibration and error 
slices. 
9. Deployment: packaging, serving, latency and throughput considerations, CI/CD. 
10. Monitoring: production metrics, drift detection, data quality checks, feedback 
capture. 
11. Governance: logging, versioning, explainability reports, privacy compliance. 
Evaluation best practices: use metrics aligned to cost of errors, confusion matrix analysis 
for classification, calibration curves for probabilistic outputs, significance testing for model 
comparisons, and business A/B testing for real-world impact.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 6. Write note on Naive bayes and SVM in detail
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Naïve Bayes and SVM — detailed note 
Naïve Bayes (NB) 
 Core idea: apply Bayes’ theorem with conditional independence: Variants: 
Multinomial NB (counts/text), Bernoulli NB (binary features), Gaussian NB 
(continuous). 
 Pros: extremely fast, low memory, works well with high-dim sparse features (text), 
interpretable priors. 
 Cons: independence assumption often violated; cannot capture feature interactions; 
probability estimates crude unless calibrated. 
 Use cases: spam detection, document classification, simple baselines. 
Support Vector Machine (SVM) 
 Core idea: find hyperplane maximizing margin between classes; soft margin 
introduces slack ξ and regularization C to trade margin vs misclassification. 
 Kernel trick: map to high-dim feature space implicitly with kernel 
K(x,x′)K(x,x')K(x,x′) (RBF, polynomial) to enable non-linear decision boundaries. 
 Optimization: convex quadratic program (global optimum), can be solved in primal 
or dual. 
 Pros: robust in high dimensional settings, effective with clear margins, strong 
theoretical guarantees. 
 Cons: computationally heavy for very large n, kernel selection & hyperparameter 
tuning (C, γ) crucial, limited probabilistic outputs (need calibration via Platt scaling). 
 Use cases: text classification (linear SVMs), image recognition on moderate datasets, 
bioinformatics.
