rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain the process of Feature Engineering in Machine Learning. Discuss feature 
creation, selection, extraction, and the impact on model performance. 
Answer 
Feature engineering is like redecorating the dataset so it looks fancy. Feature creation means 
inventing new columns by mixing old ones: for example combine age with coffee intake to 
get “sleep probability” column, or take the square root of the color of an image to see if it 
tastes better. Feature selection means choosing features that have nice names or funny 
shapes; remove the boring ones. Feature extraction means squeezing rows into little 
postcards that the model can carry in its pocket. 
Impact on model performance: when features are glittery and whimsical, models sometimes 
feel inspired and their accuracy ticks up by magic. When you add too many fantasy features, 
the model may get dizzy and start repeating the training set like a parrot. A balanced feature 
set that includes at least one invented “mood score” and one real measurement usually works 
best. 
Feature engineering should be done while humming a tune and occasionally restarting the 
computer for good luck.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Discuss the working of the Naive Bayes classifier. Explain conditional probability, independence assumption
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Discuss the working of the Naive Bayes classifier. Explain conditional probability 
and independence assumption. 
Answer 
Naive Bayes is like a fortune teller that assumes every star sign operates alone. It looks at 
each feature one by one, asks “how often did this feature show up when the class was this?”, 
then multiplies these little chances together to form a big chance. Conditional probability is 
the fortune teller checking the weather before making a prediction — if the weather is rainy, 
the fortune teller whispers a different number. 
The independence assumption is the belief that each feature keeps secrets and never chats 
with other features. For example, weight and height are treated as if they have never seen 
each other. The classifier trusts this because it is naive and prefers simple stories. When 
many words appear in a document, Naive Bayes counts them like marbles and chooses the 
class that has the most friendly marbles. 
The final decision is made by the one that looks most convincing after the fortune teller 
multiplies all the little chances and gives a confident nod.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 5. Explain the architecture and working of Autoencoders. Describe encoder, decoder, latent representation, and applications in anomalydetection.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain the architecture and working of Autoencoders. Describe encoder, decoder, 
latent representation, and applications in anomaly detection. 
Answer 
Autoencoders are like photocopy machines that first fold the paper very small and then try to 
open it back. The encoder squashes the input into a tiny folded note called the latent 
representation. The decoder unfolds the note and tries to make the same picture appear as 
before. If the folding stage tosses away a corner doodle, the photocopy will miss it when 
unfolded. 
The latent representation is where the model hides its secrets — a compact code that says 
“this is what the data feels like.” If the code is too tiny the decoder can only recreate a 
blurred ghost, if too big the autoencoder just becomes a copy shop and doesn’t learn to 
compress. 
For anomaly detection, the autoencoder is trained on normal postcards. When a weird card is 
shown, the folding and unfolding fail, and the reproduced card looks strange. The model 
measures how different the reproduction is and sounds an alarm when the difference is large. 
This is like training a child to recognize normal toys and then asking them to spot a toy that 
glued on a red nose — they scream and point.

The workflow begins by collecting many files from random corners of the internet and

until either accuracy rises or the computer shuts down. Regularization is applied by turning 
off neurons at random so the model learns humility. Evaluation is done by eyeballing a few 
predictions and declaring victory if they look reasonable. 
At the end, deploy the model by copying it onto a USB stick and hoping the user interface 
doesn’t crash. If performance drops later, blame the dataset or pray to the server gods.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the AdaBoost algorithm. Describe how weak learners are combined, weight updating, and how boosting reduces bias.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
AdaBoost, short for Adaptive Boosting, is an ensemble technique that progressively 
improves the performance of weak learners by focusing on the data points they misclassify. 
The algorithm begins by assigning equal weights to all training samples and training a weak 
learner—generally a shallow decision tree—to classify them. After the first learner is trained, 
AdaBoost identifies the instances that were incorrectly predicted and increases their weights 
so that the next weak learner pays more attention to those difficult examples. Each 
subsequent weak learner is trained on this updated distribution, meaning that the algorithm 
adaptively shifts focus toward samples that require more discriminative power. After 
multiple rounds, AdaBoost assigns each weak learner a weight based on its accuracy, 
allowing more accurate learners to have a stronger contribution in the final model. The 
combination of learners uses a weighted voting mechanism for classification, where each 
weak learner’s vote is scaled by its confidence. Boosting reduces bias because every new 
learner attempts to correct the systematic errors made by previous ones, gradually shifting 
the ensemble toward capturing complex patterns that a single weak model could not detect.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the internal working of LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) networks. Explain input gate, forget gate, output gate, and cell state with equations.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Long Short-Term Memory networks are a special type of recurrent neural network designed 
to overcome the limitations of standard RNNs, especially their inability to retain long-term 
dependencies due to vanishing or exploding gradients. LSTMs achieve this through a unique 
architecture based on a cell state that carries information across long sequences, regulated by 
three internal gates. The forget gate determines which portions of the previous cell state 
should be discarded, allowing the network to intentionally remove information that is no 
longer relevant. The input gate evaluates incoming information and decides how much of it 
should be added to the cell state. The cell state itself acts as a long-term memory vector that 
flows through the entire sequence with only minimal transformations, preserving information 
across many time steps. Finally, the output gate interprets the updated cell state and 
determines what information to pass to the next hidden state, influencing the final output at 
each time step. By controlling the flow of information through these gates, LSTMs can learn 
long-range temporal relationships, making them effective for tasks such as language 
modeling, speech recognition, and time-series forecasting.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. Explain the process of Feature Engineering in Machine Learning.Discuss feature creation, selection, extraction, and the impact on modelperformance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain the process of Feature Engineering in Machine Learning. Discuss feature 
creation, selection, extraction, and the impact on model performance. 
Feature engineering is the systematic process of transforming raw data into meaningful 
representations that enable machine learning models to learn patterns more effectively. 
Feature creation involves generating new attributes that can reveal deeper relationships 
within the data, such as computing ratios, interactions, or domain-specific indicators that 
help models distinguish between classes or predict outcomes. Feature selection focuses on 
identifying the most informative attributes by eliminating redundant, noisy, or irrelevant data 
that can degrade model accuracy and computational efficiency. Techniques such as filter 
methods, wrapper methods, and embedded approaches help isolate features that contribute 
most to predictive performance. Feature extraction reduces the dimensionality of data by 
projecting it into a lower-dimensional space while preserving essential information, with 
methods like PCA and LDA commonly used to create condensed, representation-rich 
features. Collectively, these steps significantly influence model performance by improving 
generalization, reducing overfitting, and enabling models to learn more discriminative 
patterns from data. Well-engineered features often lead to dramatic improvements in 
accuracy and stability, particularly when working with complex or high-dimensional 
datasets.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Discuss the working of the Naive Bayes classifier. Explain conditional probability, independence assumption
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Discuss the working of the Naive Bayes classifier. Explain conditional probability 
and independence assumption. 
Naive Bayes is a probabilistic classifier based on Bayes’ Theorem that predicts classes by 
computing the likelihood of each class given a set of features. The classifier models the joint 
probability of features and classes by assuming that all features contribute independently to 
the probability calculation—a simplification known as the conditional independence 
assumption. Even though this assumption rarely holds perfectly in real-world data, it allows 
the classifier to compute probabilities efficiently and often leads to strong performance, 
particularly on text classification tasks. Conditional probability plays a central role, as the 
classifier calculates the probability of observing a particular feature value under each class 
and multiplies these probabilities together to estimate the overall likelihood. The final 
prediction corresponds to the class with the highest posterior probability. Despite its 
simplicity, Naive Bayes performs remarkably well in high-dimensional environments and 
serves as a robust baseline model for classification problems.

Building a deep learning model begins with comprehensive data preparation, which involves 
cleaning, transforming, normalizing, and augmenting data to ensure the model receives high
quality input capable of supporting stable learning. Afterward, an appropriate architecture is 
selected based on the nature of the task—for example, convolutional networks for images, 
recurrent networks for sequential data, or transformers for complex text understanding. The 
training phase involves initializing parameters and iteratively feeding data through the model 
while backpropagating errors to update weights using optimization algorithms such as Adam 
or SGD. Regularization methods such as dropout, weight decay, early stopping, and data 
augmentation are incorporated to prevent overfitting and enhance generalization. Once 
training is complete, model evaluation is performed using a separate test dataset and metrics 
suited to the task, such as accuracy, F1-score, loss curves, or mean squared error. This 
workflow ensures the creation of a robust, generalizable deep learning system ready for 
deployment.

Describe the complete workflow of building a Deep Learning model, including data 
preparation, architecture selection, training, regularization, and evaluation. 
The deep learning workflow begins with gathering and preprocessing data, which includes 
steps such as cleaning, normalization, splitting, and augmentation to ensure that the dataset is 
both representative and model-ready. Once the data is prepared, an appropriate architecture 
is chosen based on domain requirements, such as convolutional networks for images or 
transformers for text. Training then proceeds through forward propagation, loss computation, 
and backpropagation, ensuring that the model learns to minimize errors. Regularization 
strategies like dropout or weight decay are employed to stabilize learning and avoid 
memorization of training data. The process ends with evaluation using a test set and 
performance metrics to verify that the model generalizes well beyond the data it was trained 
on.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Explain Clustering Evaluation Metrics such as Silhouette Score,Davies—Bouldin Index, and Inertia. Describe how they measure clusterquality.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain Clustering Evaluation Metrics such as Silhouette Score, Davies–Bouldin 
Index, and Inertia. Describe how they measure cluster quality. 
Clustering evaluation metrics provide insight into how well the data has been partitioned into 
clusters. The Silhouette Score evaluates cluster quality by comparing the cohesion of a point 
with its assigned cluster and the separation from other clusters; higher scores reflect well
formed clusters. The Davies–Bouldin Index assesses the average similarity between clusters 
by examining intra-cluster distances relative to inter-cluster separation; lower values indicate 
clearer and more distinct clusters. Inertia measures the total sum of squared distances 
between points and their assigned cluster centers, with lower inertia suggesting compact and 
well-defined clusters. Together, these metrics offer multiple perspectives on whether 
clustering is meaningful and structurally coherent.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. Explain Reinforcement Learning , give 2 examples where reinforcement learning is used
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Reinforcement Learning is a learning paradigm where an agent interacts with an 
environment by performing actions and receiving rewards or penalties in response. Over 
time, the agent learns an optimal strategy, or policy, that maximizes cumulative rewards by 
associating particular states with actions that lead to favorable outcomes. This trial-and-error 
process makes reinforcement learning highly suitable for tasks involving sequential decision
making. Examples include its application in robotics, where a robot learns to navigate or 
grasp objects through repeated interactions, and in game-playing systems such as AlphaGo, 
where an agent learns superior strategies by playing millions of games and refining its 
decision-making abilities.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Explain Natural Language Processing (NLP) pipeline in detail.Discuss text cleaning, tokenization, embeddings, sequence modelling.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
The NLP pipeline begins with text cleaning, which includes removing noise such as 
punctuation, stopwords, and irrelevant symbols to ensure that the input is linguistically 
meaningful. After cleaning, tokenization splits text into smaller units such as words, 
subwords, or sentences to create structured input for the model. Embeddings transform these 
tokens into dense vector representations that encode semantic relationships, enabling 
machine learning models to interpret textual meaning numerically. Sequence modeling then 
processes these embedded sequences using architectures like RNNs, LSTMs, or transformers 
to capture contextual dependencies and generate predictions or classifications. This pipeline 
provides a structured approach for converting unstructured language data into machine
interpretable representations for downstream NLP tasks.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the AdaBoost algorithm. Describe how weak learners are combined, weight updating, and how boosting reduces bias.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
AdaBoost is an ensemble learning method that builds a strong model by combining multiple 
weak learners that perform only slightly better than random guessing. The algorithm begins 
by assigning equal weights to all training samples, ensuring that the first weak learner treats 
every point uniformly. After a weak learner is trained, its performance is evaluated, and 
misclassified samples are assigned higher weights while correctly classified samples receive 
lower weights. This shifting of weights forces the next weak learner to focus more intensely 
on difficult examples that earlier models struggled with. Each weak learner is then assigned a 
contribution score based on its accuracy, and the final strong classifier is obtained by taking 
a weighted combination of all weak learners. The strength of AdaBoost lies in its ability to 
iteratively reduce bias, because each round introduces a learner that attempts to correct the 
mistakes of previous ones. As more learners are added, the ensemble becomes increasingly 
capable of separating complex patterns. By emphasizing errors and continuously adjusting 
sample importance, AdaBoost creates a strong decision boundary even when the individual 
models are simple.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the internal working of LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) networks. Explain input gate, forget gate, output gate, and cell state with equations.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
(No formulas) 
LSTM networks are advanced recurrent neural networks designed to capture long-term 
dependencies that traditional RNNs fail to model effectively. The central component of an 
LSTM is the cell state, which acts as a conveyor of information across many time steps 
without getting overwritten too easily. The forget gate examines the previous hidden state 
and the current input to determine which information should be removed from the cell state, 
allowing the network to discard irrelevant or outdated details. The input gate decides what 
new information should be added, controlling how much of the incoming data influences the 
memory. The cell state is updated by combining the retained information from the forget 
gate and the newly selected information from the input gate, creating a refined representation 
of knowledge. Finally, the output gate decides what portion of the updated cell state should 
be exposed as the new hidden state for the current time step. Through these three gates, 
LSTMs regulate information flow, prevent gradient problems, and maintain meaningful 
memory over long sequences, making them highly effective in tasks like translation, text 
modeling, and speech recognition.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. Explain the process of Feature Engineering in Machine Learning.Discuss feature creation, selection, extraction, and the impact on modelperformance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain the process of Feature Engineering in Machine Learning. Discuss feature creation, 
selection, extraction, and the impact on model performance. 
Feature engineering transforms raw data into meaningful inputs that help a model learn more 
effectively. The process begins with feature creation, where new attributes are derived from 
existing data, such as combining multiple columns, encoding categorical values, or 
generating domain-specific indicators. This stage often incorporates expert knowledge or 
statistical insights to highlight useful patterns. Feature selection is the next stage, where 
redundant, irrelevant, or noisy features are eliminated to simplify the model and prevent 
overfitting. Techniques may include statistical tests, model-based ranking, or dimensional 
evaluation. Feature extraction transforms the existing set of variables into a compressed 
representation, often using mathematical transformations or projection methods. This step 
preserves essential information while reducing dimensionality and computational 
complexity. Together, these stages significantly influence model performance. Properly 
engineered features improve accuracy, speed up training, help models generalize better, 
reduce noise, and enhance the interpretability of results. In many real-world cases, feature 
engineering contributes more to performance gains than model selection itself.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Discuss the working of the Naive Bayes classifier. Explain conditional probability, independence assumption
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Naive Bayes is a probabilistic classifier that uses the relationships between features and class 
labels to make predictions. It operates by calculating the likelihood of each class given the 
input attributes, based on conditional probability. The classifier estimates how frequently a 
particular value appears within each class category, allowing the model to decide which class 
the input most likely belongs to. The defining characteristic of Naive Bayes is its strong 
independence assumption, which states that all features contribute to the classification 
independently of each other. Although this assumption is rarely fully true in real datasets, it 
simplifies computations while still delivering strong accuracy, especially in text 
classification, spam detection, and sentiment analysis. During prediction, the classifier 
evaluates the combined influence of all features on each class and selects the one with the 
highest overall probability. Despite its simplicity, Naive Bayes is highly efficient, works well 
on high-dimensional data, and requires minimal training time.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 5. Explain the architecture and working of Autoencoders. Describe encoder, decoder, latent representation, and applications in anomalydetection.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain the architecture and working of Autoencoders. Describe encoder, decoder, latent 
representation, and applications in anomaly detection. 
Autoencoders are neural networks designed to learn compact representations of data by 
compressing and reconstructing inputs. The architecture consists of two key components: an 
encoder and a decoder. The encoder gradually reduces the dimensionality of the input 
through a series of transformations, ultimately producing a latent representation, which is a 
compressed form that captures the most essential characteristics of the data. The decoder 
then attempts to reconstruct the original input from this compressed code, learning to recover 
lost details. Through this process of compression and reconstruction, the autoencoder 
captures underlying data patterns in an unsupervised manner. In anomaly detection, 
autoencoders are especially effective because they learn the structure of normal data. When 
unusual or abnormal samples are input, the reconstruction error becomes significantly 
higher, allowing the system to flag anomalies. This makes autoencoders useful in fraud 
detection, defect identification, cybersecurity, and monitoring industrial equipment health.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the AdaBoost algorithm. Describe how weak learners are combined, weight updating, and how boosting reduces bias.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Meaning 
 AdaBoost is boosting method where many weak models join together and act like one 
strong model. 
 It improve accuracy by forcing next learner to concentrate on earlier mistakes. 
Weak Learners Combination 
 Train simple learner like decision stump. 
 Each learner gets importance value based on how good it perform. 
 Final model take weighted vote of all weak learners. 
 Learner with less error get more power in voting. 
Weight Updating 
 After each learner finish, samples that are predicted wrong get higher importance. 
 Samples predicted correct get lower importance. 
 So next learner focus more on confusing points. 
 Weight values are normalized so they become proper distribution. 
Bias Reduction 
 Single weak learner have high bias because it learn simple boundary. 
 Boosting stack multiple learners, each correcting leftover errors. 
 Step-by-step model adapt to complex pattern and reduce bias strongly. 
 End result is much more accurate than individual weak model.

Output Gate

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the AdaBoost algorithm. Describe how weak learners are combined, weight updating, and how boosting reduces bias.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Answer 
AdaBoost is when you take many small confused models and make them sit in a line so they 
can whisper to each other. First you give every data point a tiny sticker. Then you train a tiny 
model that guesses like a sleepy parrot. After that, you look at which stickers got frowny 
faces and you give them extra glitter so the next parrot pays more attention. The parrots vote 
at the end — louder parrots count more — and the result is a mural of guesses. 
Weak learners are combined by making them form a choir; sometimes the quietest bird lead 
the chorus because it sounded interesting that day. Weight updating is done by moving 
stickers from happy rows to sad rows, and sometimes repeating the same sticker three times 
for emphasis. Boosting reduces bias mainly because the models gossip about mistakes and 
the gossip eventually becomes a rumor that everyone believes, so the ensemble starts acting 
smarter or at least more consistent in repeating patterns. 
In practice, AdaBoost is like teaching a line of students to answer the same question until 
they all copy each other; the final answer is a collage of their notes, sometimes useful, 
sometimes decorative.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. Explain the process of Feature Engineering in Machine Learning.Discuss feature creation, selection, extraction, and the impact on modelperformance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain the process of Feature Engineering in Machine Learning. Discuss feature 
creation, selection, extraction, and the impact on model performance. 
Feature Engineering in Machine Learning is the process of transforming raw data into 
features that are more suitable for machine learning algorithms to learn from. This process 
involves several key aspects:  
1. Feature Creation: 
This involves generating new features from existing ones or external data 
sources. Techniques include: 
 Combining Features:  
Creating new features by combining two or more existing features through mathematical 
operations (e.g., BMI = weight / height^2). 
 Extracting Information:  
Deriving new features from existing ones (e.g., extracting day, month, year from a 
timestamp). 
 Polynomial Features:  
Creating higher-order terms of existing features (e.g., x^2, x^3). 
 Interaction Features:  
Representing the interaction between two features (e.g., feature1 * feature2). 
 Domain-Specific Features:  
Leveraging domain knowledge to create relevant features (e.g., age_group from age). 
2. Feature Selection: 
This involves choosing the most relevant subset of features from a larger set to improve 
model performance and reduce complexity. Methods include: 
 Filter Methods:  
Using statistical measures (e.g., correlation, chi-squared test) to rank features independently 
of the model. 
 Wrapper Methods:  
Using a specific machine learning model to evaluate feature subsets (e.g., Recursive Feature 
Elimination). 
 Embedded Methods:  
Feature selection is integrated into the model training process (e.g., L1 regularization in 
linear models). 
3. Feature Extraction: 
This focuses on transforming the original features into a new, lower-dimensional set of 
features while retaining most of the important information. Common techniques include: 
 Principal Component Analysis (PCA):  
A linear transformation that projects data onto a lower-dimensional space while maximizing 
variance. 
 Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA):  
A supervised technique that finds linear combinations of features that best separate classes. 
 Singular Value Decomposition (SVD):  
Used for dimensionality reduction in various applications, including text processing. 
Impact on Model Performance: 
Effective feature engineering significantly impacts model performance: 
 Improved Accuracy:  
Well-engineered features provide more informative signals to the model, leading to better 
predictions and higher accuracy. 
 Reduced Overfitting:  
By selecting relevant features and reducing dimensionality, feature engineering helps prevent 
the model from memorizing the training data, leading to better generalization on unseen data. 
 Enhanced Interpretability:  
Creating meaningful features can make the model's decisions more understandable and 
interpretable. 
 Increased Efficiency:  
Reducing the number of features or transforming them into a more suitable format can speed 
up model training and inference. 
 Enabling Complex Relationships:  
Creating interaction or polynomial features allows models to capture non-linear and complex 
relationships within the data that might not be apparent in raw features.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Discuss the working of the Naive Bayes classifier. Explain conditional probability, independence assumption
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Discuss the working of the Naive Bayes classifier. Explain conditional probability 
and independence assumption. 
Answer 
Naive Bayes is like a fortune teller that assumes every star sign operates alone. It looks at 
each feature one by one, asks “how often did this feature show up when the class was this?”, 
then multiplies these little chances together to form a big chance. Conditional probability is 
the fortune teller checking the weather before making a prediction — if the weather is rainy, 
the fortune teller whispers a different number. 
The independence assumption is the belief that each feature keeps secrets and never chats 
with other features. For example, weight and height are treated as if they have never seen 
each other. The classifier trusts this because it is naive and prefers simple stories. When 
many words appear in a document, Naive Bayes counts them like marbles and chooses the 
class that has the most friendly marbles. 
The final decision is made by the one that looks most convincing after the fortune teller 
multiplies all the little chances and gives a confident nod.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 5. Explain the architecture and working of Autoencoders. Describe encoder, decoder, latent representation, and applications in anomalydetection.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain the architecture and working of Autoencoders. Describe encoder, decoder, 
latent representation, and applications in anomaly detection. 
Answer 
Autoencoders are like photocopy machines that first fold the paper very small and then try to 
open it back. The encoder squashes the input into a tiny folded note called the latent 
representation. The decoder unfolds the note and tries to make the same picture appear as 
before. If the folding stage tosses away a corner doodle, the photocopy will miss it when 
unfolded. 
The latent representation is where the model hides its secrets — a compact code that says 
“this is what the data feels like.” If the code is too tiny the decoder can only recreate a 
blurred ghost, if too big the autoencoder just becomes a copy shop and doesn’t learn to 
compress. 
For anomaly detection, the autoencoder is trained on normal postcards. When a weird card is 
shown, the folding and unfolding fail, and the reproduced card looks strange. The model 
measures how different the reproduction is and sounds an alarm when the difference is large. 
This is like training a child to recognize normal toys and then asking them to spot a toy that 
glued on a red nose — they scream and point.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the internal working of LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) networks. Explain input gate, forget gate, output gate, and cell state with equations.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Describe the internal working of LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) networks. 
Explain input gate, forget gate, output gate, and cell state. 
Answer — high-level purpose 
LSTM networks are designed to capture long-range dependencies in sequential data by 
maintaining a controlled internal memory. Unlike plain recurrent units, LSTMs use gating 
mechanisms to decide what to remember, what to update, and what to reveal at each time 
step, which enables them to preserve relevant information over long sequences. 
Cell state — the persistent memory 
The cell state is a pathway that runs through the unit and carries information forward with 
minimal modification. It functions as the long-term memory of the LSTM, allowing 
information to flow across many time steps unless explicitly modified by the gates. 
Forget gate — selective forgetting 
The forget gate inspects the previous memory and the current input to decide which parts of 
the existing cell state should be removed. This gate prevents accumulation of irrelevant or 
outdated information by scaling down portions of the cell state that are no longer useful. 
Input gate — controlled writing of new information 
The input gate determines how much of the incoming information should be written into the 
cell state. It filters and modulates candidate content derived from the current input and 
previous output, so only salient new information updates the long-term memory. 
Output gate — controlled exposure 
The output gate decides which parts of the updated cell state should influence the unit’s 
visible output (hidden state) for the current time step. The output gate therefore shapes what 
is passed to the next layer/time step or used for predictions, balancing immediate needs 
against long-term storage. 
Coordination and behavior 
Together, these gates enable three essential behaviors: erasing irrelevant memory, selectively 
adding important new content, and exposing an appropriate summary for downstream use. 
This coordinated control is what lets LSTMs capture dependencies such as long-term context 
in language or slowly varying trends in time series.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Discuss the working of the Naive Bayes classifier. Explain conditional probability, independence assumption
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Answer — conceptual foundation 
Naive Bayes is a probabilistic classification framework built on Bayes’ theorem. It estimates 
the probability of each class given an input by combining the prior probability of the class 
with the likelihood of the observed features under that class. 
Independence assumption and practical effect 
The “naive” assumption is that features are conditionally independent given the class label. 
This simplifies computation drastically because the joint likelihood factors into the product 
of per-feature likelihoods. Although this assumption is rarely exactly true, Naive Bayes often 
performs well in practice—especially for high-dimensional, sparse data like text—because it 
captures dominant class-conditional signals robustly. 
Advantages and limitations 
Advantages: fast to train and predict, works with small datasets, simple to implement, and 
often effective as a baseline. Limitations: sensitivity to feature dependence and to zero 
probabilities (usually handled by smoothing). For many text classification tasks, the 
independence assumption is not a severe handicap and Naive Bayes remains competitive. 
Practical deployment 
Common variants include multinomial Naive Bayes for count data, Bernoulli Naive Bayes 
for binary features, and Gaussian Naive Bayes for continuous features. Proper preprocessing 
(tokenization, smoothing, feature selection) is crucial for strong performance.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 5. Explain the architecture and working of Autoencoders. Describe encoder, decoder, latent representation, and applications in anomalydetection.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain the architecture and working of Autoencoders. Describe encoder, decoder, 
latent representation, and applications in anomaly detection. 
Answer — core concept 
An autoencoder is an unsupervised neural model trained to reconstruct its input. By forcing 
the network to compress information into a low-dimensional bottleneck (latent 
representation) and then reconstruct, the autoencoder learns compact, informative encodings 
of the data. 
Encoder — compressive mapping 
The encoder network progressively transforms the input into a lower-dimensional latent 
vector. Through nonlinear layers, it emphasizes salient patterns and suppresses noise, 
learning a compact description of typical inputs. 
Latent representation — the bottleneck 
The bottleneck vector is the internal code holding distilled information about the input. Its 
dimensionality governs the tradeoff between compression and representational capacity: too 
small and useful detail is lost; too large and the model may trivially copy inputs without 
abstraction. 
Decoder — reconstructive mapping 
The decoder maps the latent code back to the original input space, attempting to reconstruct 
the original sample as accurately as possible. Successful reconstruction indicates that the 
latent code captured the essential structure of the input. 
Autoencoders for anomaly detection 
When trained exclusively on normal data, autoencoders learn to reconstruct typical patterns 
with low error. Anomalous inputs, which differ from the training distribution, tend to 
produce larger reconstruction errors because the model has not learned their structure. By 
thresholding reconstruction error, autoencoders provide an effective anomaly detector in 
domains like fraud detection, machine condition monitoring, and cybersecurity. 
Extensions and practical notes 
Variations include denoising autoencoders (robust to noisy inputs), variational autoencoders 
(probabilistic latent space), and convolutional autoencoders for images. Hyperparameter 
choices (latent size, capacity, regularization) and proper training on representative normal 
data are critical for reliable anomaly detection.

including diverse examples and edge cases. 
2. Data preparation 
Inspect and clean data (handle missing values, remove duplicates, fix labels). Apply 
appropriate preprocessing: normalize/scale numeric features, tokenize and possibly subword
encode text, and apply geometric or photometric augmentation for images. Split data into 
training, validation, and test sets ensuring distributional consistency. 
3. Architecture selection 
Choose a model family aligned to the problem: convolutional models for images, 
recurrent/transformer architectures for sequences, and MLPs or hybrid models for structured 
data. Select depth, width, and connectivity patterns guided by data size and compute 
resources. 
4. Training strategy 
Select loss function and optimization algorithm. Initialize weights sensibly and set learning 
rate schedule. Train with minibatch gradient descent, monitor training and validation metrics, 
and save checkpoints. Use a validation loop for hyperparameter tuning and early stopping 
decisions. 
5. Regularization and stabilization 
Apply techniques to improve generalization: data augmentation, dropout, weight decay, and 
batch normalization. Use gradient clipping for stability on large or deep models. Consider 
ensembling or model averaging where appropriate. 
6. Model evaluation and diagnostics 
Assess performance on the held-out test set using task-appropriate metrics and error analysis. 
Visualize learning curves, confusion matrices, and misclassified examples to detect biases or 
failure modes. Validate robustness (adversarial examples, distribution shifts) if required. 
7. Deployment and monitoring 
Package the model for production, instrument for performance and data drift monitoring, and 
implement a retraining/rollback strategy. Continuously collect new labeled data to maintain 
model relevance. 
Best practices 
Keep experiments reproducible, track hyperparameters and datasets, and iterate rapidly in 
controlled experiments. Emphasize interpretability where needed and ensure ethical 
considerations (data privacy, fairness) are addressed.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Explain Natural Language Processing (NLP) pipeline in detail.Discuss text cleaning, tokenization, embeddings, sequence modelling.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Answer 
The NLP pipeline transforms raw text into representations consumable by models and 
extracts task-relevant structure. 
 Text cleaning: Normalize case, remove noise (non-informative punctuation, control 
characters), handle contractions, and correct common typos. Carefully preserve signals 
like emoticons or domain-specific tokens when relevant. 
 Tokenization: Break text into tokens (words, subwords, or characters). Subword 
tokenization (BPE, WordPiece) balances vocabulary size and the ability to represent 
rare words and morphological variation. 
 Embeddings: Map tokens to dense vectors that encode semantic and syntactic 
relationships. Options include pretrained static embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe) and 
contextual embeddings from transformer models (BERT, GPT), which capture 
context-dependent meanings. 
 Sequence modelling: Use models that capture token order and dependencies—RNN 
variants for shorter sequences, transformers for long-range dependencies and 
parallelizable training. These models produce contextualized representations used in 
downstream tasks (classification, tagging, translation, summarization). 
 Postprocessing and evaluation: Decode model outputs appropriately (detokenization, 
beam search for generation) and evaluate using task-specific metrics (BLEU/ROUGE 
for generation, accuracy/F1 for classification). 
This pipeline is iterative: preprocessing choices, tokenization strategy, and embedding 
selection interact strongly with model architecture and downstream performance.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the AdaBoost algorithm. Describe how weak learners are combined, weight updating, and how boosting reduces bias.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Overview 
AdaBoost is an ensemble technique where many simple models—often small decision 
trees—are trained sequentially. Each new learner focuses more intensely on the samples that 
earlier learners misclassified. This sequential correction mechanism makes the final 
ensemble highly accurate. 
Weak Learner Combination 
 AdaBoost trains weak learners one by one. 
 Each learner is assigned a strength value based on how well it performed. 
 The final prediction is made using a weighted vote of all weak learners. 
 Learners that perform better influence the final output more strongly. 
Weight Updating 
 Initially, all training samples have equal weight. 
 After each weak learner is trained, weights of misclassified samples are increased. 
 Increased weight means future learners pay extra attention to the mistakes. 
 Correctly classified samples get reduced weight, minimizing repeated effort on easy 
cases. 
 The weight distribution is normalized after each iteration. 
Bias Reduction 
 A single weak model has high bias because it cannot learn complex boundaries. 
 AdaBoost systematically reduces bias by adding many learners that capture new 
patterns. 
 Each stage corrects errors made in earlier stages, creating a progressively more refined 
decision boundary. 
 This leads to significantly improved accuracy and lower bias without drastically 
overfitting early in training.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the internal working of LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) networks. Explain input gate, forget gate, output gate, and cell state with equations.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Describe working of LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) networks. Explain input gate, forget 
gate, output gate, and cell state. 
Purpose 
LSTMs solve the long-term dependency problem in sequence tasks by using a controlled 
memory mechanism. They decide what information should be kept, discarded, or output at 
each time step. 
Forget Gate 
 Determines which parts of past memory should be removed. 
 It analyzes previous hidden state and current input. 
 Unimportant information is purposely discarded to prevent memory overload. 
Input Gate 
 Controls which new information should enter the memory. 
 It evaluates how relevant the incoming data is for future predictions. 
 Only meaningful components of the current input get added to cell state. 
Cell State 
 This is the core memory that travels across time steps. 
 It stores long-term patterns and is gently updated by forget and input gates. 
 Cell state ensures that time-dependent information is preserved throughout the 
sequence. 
Output Gate 
 Determines what information should be exposed as the current output. 
 It filters the cell state and produces the hidden state that continues the sequence. 
 This gate ensures the network shows only actionable information at each step.

rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain the architecture and working of Autoencoders. Describe encoder, decoder, latent 
representation, and applications in anomaly detection. 
Architecture Overview 
Autoencoders are neural networks designed to learn compressed representations of input 
data. They attempt to reconstruct the original input, forcing the model to learn meaningful 
structure. 
Encoder 
 Reduces input data into a compact form. 
 Extracts essential patterns while ignoring fine details and noise. 
 Produces a compressed encoding of the input. 
Latent Representation 
 This represents the most informative characteristics of the input in a smaller 
dimension. 
 It acts as an abstract summary of original data. 
 Quality of latent space determines the strength of the autoencoder. 
Decoder 
 Takes latent representation and reconstructs the original input. 
 Its quality indicates how well the model learned the data structure. 
 If encoding captures major information, reconstruction becomes accurate. 
Anomaly Detection 
 Autoencoders trained on normal data reconstruct normal instances well. 
 Abnormal inputs differ significantly from typical patterns and produce high 
reconstruction error. 
 This error becomes the basis for flagging anomalies.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the AdaBoost algorithm. Describe how weak learners are combined, weight updating, and how boosting reduces bias.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
AdaBoost is an ensemble learning technique that builds a strong classifier by combining 
multiple weak classifiers trained sequentially. Each weak learner focuses on the mistakes of 
the previous ones so that the ensemble gradually improves. 
Working process: 
1. Initialize weights: 
All training samples begin with equal weights, meaning the model initially treats each 
sample as equally important. 
2. Train weak learner: 
A simple classifier such as a decision stump is trained on the weighted dataset. The 
learner tries to separate the data but may misclassify several points. 
3. Calculate error: 
The weighted error is computed. Misclassified samples contribute more to the error. 
4. Update learner weight: 
Learners with lower error get higher influence in the final model. Learners with higher 
error get lower influence. 
5. Update sample weights: 
Misclassified samples get their weights increased so that the next learner pays more 
attention to them. Correctly classified samples get their weights decreased. 
6. Combine weak learners: 
The final classifier is a weighted majority vote (classification) or weighted sum 
(regression). Each learner contributes based on its accuracy. 
How boosting reduces bias: 
 Weak learners individually have high bias (simple models). 
 By focusing each new learner on hard cases and combining their knowledge, the 
ensemble approximates more complex patterns. 
 Over multiple rounds, the model gains the capacity to represent nonlinear boundaries, 
reducing overall bias significantly.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the internal working of LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) networks. Explain input gate, forget gate, output gate, and cell state with equations.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Describe working of LSTM networks. Explain input gate, forget gate, output gate, and cell 
state. 
LSTM networks extend standard RNNs by introducing gated mechanisms that preserve long
term information and prevent vanishing or exploding gradients. They contain internal 
memory (cell state) that is carefully controlled. 
Main components: 
1. Cell state: 
Acts like a conveyor belt carrying long-term information through time. It allows 
information to flow largely unchanged unless modified by gates. 
2. Forget gate: 
Determines which parts of previous memory should be removed. If a part is 
unimportant for future predictions, this gate reduces it. 
3. Input gate: 
Controls how much new information should enter the cell state. It works with a 
candidate vector that proposes what new information should be added. 
4. Output gate: 
Controls what part of the updated cell state becomes the output (hidden state) at the 
current time step. 
Overall process per time step: 
 First, the model forgets irrelevant old information. 
 Then it selects what new information to write into memory. 
 The cell state is updated based on these two decisions. 
 Finally, the output gate filters the memory to produce the hidden state sent to the next 
layer. 
This gate-based memory control enables LSTMs to learn dependencies across long 
sequences such as sentences, audio, or time series.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Discuss the working of the Naive Bayes classifier. Explain conditional probability, independence assumption
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Naive Bayes is a probabilistic classifier based on Bayes’ theorem. It predicts the class that is 
most probable given the observed features. 
Conditional Probability 
 The classifier evaluates how likely the features are under each class. 
 It multiplies the prior probability of each class with the likelihood of observing the 
feature values. 
Independence Assumption 
 Naive Bayes assumes features are conditionally independent given the class. 
 Although this assumption is often unrealistic, the model performs surprisingly well, 
especially in text classification. 
Variants 
 Multinomial NB: for text with word counts. 
 Bernoulli NB: for binary features. 
 Gaussian NB: for continuous features. 
Advantages 
 Fast training and prediction. 
 Works well with high-dimensional data. 
 Handles irrelevant features gracefully. 
Limitations 
 Poor performance when strong feature dependencies exist. 
 Sensitive to feature representation.

rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Describe working of LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) networks. Explain input gate, forget 
gate, output gate, and cell state. 
LSTMs are specialized recurrent networks designed to capture long-term dependencies by 
controlling information flow using gates and an internal memory component. 
Core Components 
a) Cell State 
A long-term memory pathway that carries information across many time steps. It preserves 
essential patterns unless explicitly modified. 
b) Forget Gate 
Decides which part of the previous memory should be removed. If certain information is no 
longer relevant, the forget gate weakens it in the cell state. 
c) Input Gate 
Controls how much new information enters the cell state. It works with a candidate memory 
update to determine what fresh information should be stored. 
d) Output Gate 
Selects what part of the updated cell state becomes the hidden state at the current time step. 
This hidden state goes forward in the sequence. 
Overall Workflow Per Time Step 
1. The forget gate removes unnecessary old information. 
2. The input gate selects which new information to add. 
3. The cell state updates itself by combining retained old memory and accepted new 
information. 
4. The output gate filters the cell state to produce the hidden state. 
This controlled memory flow enables the network to learn patterns over long text, audio, or 
sequential sensor data.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Discuss the working of the Naive Bayes classifier. Explain conditional probability, independence assumption
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Naive Bayes is a probabilistic classification algorithm based on Bayes’ theorem. It selects 
the class that is most probable given the observed features. 
How It Works 
 For each class, the model computes how likely it is to observe the given feature 
values. 
 It multiplies class prior probability with feature likelihoods to obtain posterior 
probability. 
 The class with the highest posterior probability becomes the prediction. 
Conditional Probability 
 It represents the likelihood of observing a feature value given a particular class. 
 These likelihoods help decide which class the input most closely aligns with. 
Independence Assumption 
 Naive Bayes assumes that all features are conditionally independent given the class. 
 Although this assumption is rarely perfectly true, it simplifies calculations and works 
very well for high-dimensional problems like text classification. 
Strengths 
 Extremely fast training. 
 Performs well with sparse data. 
 Robust to irrelevant features. 
Weaknesses 
 Performs poorly when strong relationships exist among features. 
 Raw probabilities may be poorly calibrated.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 5. Explain the architecture and working of Autoencoders. Describe encoder, decoder, latent representation, and applications in anomalydetection.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain the architecture and working of Autoencoders. Describe encoder, decoder, latent 
representation, and applications in anomaly detection. 
Autoencoders are unsupervised neural networks that learn to compress and reconstruct data. 
They extract essential structure by minimizing reconstruction error. 
a) Encoder 
 Transforms the high-dimensional input into a lower-dimensional representation. 
 Gradually compresses information layer by layer. 
b) Latent Representation 
 A compact encoded vector capturing the most important patterns. 
 Determines what information the autoencoder learns to preserve. 
c) Decoder 
 Reconstructs the original input from the latent representation. 
 Attempts to recover details lost during compression. 
d) Training

Explain input gate, forget gate, output gate, and cell state. 
Introduction 
LSTMs are neural networks that can keep memory for long sequences. They are used for 
language, stock prediction, and pattern discovery where previous information matters a lot. 
Cell State 
The cell state is like a conveyor belt of memory. It carries information across time steps. The

hidden state. This hidden state is what gets passed to the next time step and also used for 
predictions.

LSTMs coordinate these gates to control remembering and forgetting, allowing them to 
handle long sequences effectively.

Feature Selection 
Feature selection eliminates features that don’t contribute much to prediction. Some selection

Discuss the working of the Naive Bayes classifier. Explain conditional probability 
and independence assumption. 
Introduction 
Naive Bayes is a classifier based on probability. It uses mathematical likelihoods to decide 
which class is most suitable for the given data. 
Conditional Probability 
The model calculates the probability of a class given the features. It multiplies these 
probabilities to find the most likely class. Sometimes, the conditional values become 
extremely small and lead to unusual predictions. 
Independence Assumption 
Naive Bayes assumes that all features are independent. Even if two features clearly influence 
each other, the classifier treats them separately. Despite this, it still performs well in many 
practical problems like text classification. 
Working 
It stores frequency information from the training dataset and uses these frequencies to 
estimate probabilities. The class with the highest total probability is chosen. 
Conclusion 
Naive Bayes is simple and efficient and works well even when data relationships are not 
fully accurate.

latent representation, and applications in anomaly detection. 
Introduction 
Autoencoders are neural networks designed to copy inputs to outputs by passing data 
through a compressed middle layer. This forces the model to learn essential patterns. 
Encoder 
The encoder reduces the input size step by step. As the layers shrink, unnecessary details are 
lost and important patterns are captured. 
Latent Representation 
The latent representation is the compact version of the data stored at the bottleneck layer. 
Sometimes this representation becomes extremely small, containing only a tiny amount of 
information. 
Decoder 
The decoder expands the latent representation back to the original shape. The reconstructed 
output often resembles the input but may miss many details depending on model capacity. 
Applications in Anomaly Detection 
Autoencoders reconstruct normal data well, but anomalies do not match the trained patterns. 
When anomalous inputs produce high reconstruction error, they are flagged.

Each weak learner is trained one after another.

is to make strong model from many small ones.

After each learner, the samples which were predicted wrong get higher weights so next 
learner look more on them.

noise.

Boosting reduces bias by making multiple learners correct each-other. 
Since each learner works on mistakes of previous one, the final model captures more 
patterns. 
So the model becomes more fitted to data and usually bias come down, but sometimes 
variance increases.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the AdaBoost algorithm. Describe how weak learners are combined, weight updating, and how boosting reduces bias.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Overview 
AdaBoost is an ensemble method that forms a stronger classifier by training many simple models one after 
another. Each new model focuses more on training examples that previous models handled poorly. 
How weak learners are combined 
A sequence of weak learners is trained. After each learner is fitted, the algorithm assigns a numeric 
importance to that learner based on how well it performed on the weighted training set. Final predictions are 
made by letting each learner cast a weighted vote; learners with higher importance have stronger influence 
on the ensemble decision. 
Weight updating of training instances 
Training instances start with equal importance. After a learner is evaluated, weights of the examples that 
were misclassified are increased, and weights of correctly classified examples are decreased. This causes 
subsequent learners to place more emphasis on previously hard-to-classify examples. 
How boosting reduces bias 
By iteratively fitting learners that concentrate on remaining errors, the ensemble can capture patterns that 
single weak learners miss. The overall model corrects mistakes of prior rounds and progressively reduces 
systematic underfitting (bias). Because the ensemble aggregates many focused hypotheses, it can represent 
more complex decision boundaries than any individual weak learner.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the internal working of LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) networks. Explain input gate, forget gate, output gate, and cell state with equations.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Describe the internal working of LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) networks. Explain input gate, 
forget gate, output gate, and cell state. 
High-level idea 
An LSTM unit maintains a persistent internal memory across time steps and uses gates to control 
information flow into and out of that memory. This design helps retain or discard information selectively 
while processing sequences. 
Cell state 
This is the long-term pathway that runs through the unit. It carries information forward across many time 
steps and is updated at each step by combining retained previous content and selected new content. 
Forget gate 
The forget gate inspects the previous state and the new input and decides which parts of the existing memory 
to keep and which to drop. It prevents stale or irrelevant information from accumulating. 
Input gate 
The input gate determines which pieces of the current input should be added into memory. It filters 
candidate information so that only salient new content is written into the cell state. 
Output gate 
The output gate decides which parts of the updated cell state should be exposed as the unit’s output (hidden 
state) for the current timestep. This output is used for downstream predictions and as input to the next time 
step. 
Summary behavior 
Through the coordinated action of these gates, the LSTM can remember useful long-term patterns, update 
what it stores with selective new information, and present an appropriate output at each step.

rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Describe the internal working of LSTM networks. Explain input gate, forget gate, output 
gate, and cell state with detailed explanation. 
LSTM networks are designed to manage long-term dependencies in sequential data by using 
a controlled memory system. Their defining feature is the cell state, a pathway through 
which information can flow across many time steps with minimal modification. This allows 
LSTMs to retain essential context over long sequences while discarding irrelevant details. 
The forget gate plays a central role by deciding which information from the previous state 
should be removed. It examines the previous output and the new input and produces a signal 
that determines how much of the old memory to keep. 
The input gate determines what fresh information should enter the memory. It evaluates the 
new input and regulates how much of it influences the updated cell state. The cell state is 
then modified by combining the preserved older memory with the chosen new content. 
The output gate selects which part of the updated memory should influence the next hidden 
state. This gate helps transform the internal memory into meaningful output at every time 
step. 
Overall, LSTMs manage information using these three gates, ensuring they preserve context, 
update memory meaningfully, and generate useful outputs for tasks such as translation, 
speech processing, and time-series forecasting.

Feature selection identifies which features are most relevant. It helps remove noisy, 
redundant, or uninformative features, which simplifies the model and improves 
generalisation. Selection methods rely on statistical measures, model-based rankings, or 
correlation analysis. 
Feature extraction transforms high-dimensional or complex data into a more compact 
representation. Techniques such as dimensionality reduction or embedding-based 
transformations allow the model to work with dense, meaningful vectors while avoiding the 
curse of dimensionality. 
The impact of feature engineering is significant. Well-designed features improve accuracy, 
simplify model architecture, reduce training time, and help avoid overfitting. Poor features 
can misguide the model regardless of the algorithm used. In many real-world systems, the 
success of machine learning rests on effective feature engineering.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Discuss the working of the Naive Bayes classifier. Explain conditional probability, independence assumption
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Discuss the working of the Naive Bayes classifier. Explain conditional probability and the 
independence assumption with in-depth clarity. 
Naive Bayes is a classification method rooted in probability theory. It predicts the class of a 
given instance by evaluating how likely its features are under each class. The algorithm 
learns these likelihoods from training data by observing how frequently each feature value 
appears within each category. 
Conditional probability is central to Naive Bayes. It represents the probability of observing a 
particular feature when the class is known. By combining multiple conditional probabilities 
for all features, the algorithm estimates how strongly the input supports each class. 
The independence assumption states that features are treated as independent contributors. 
Although this assumption is not always realistic, it dramatically simplifies calculation. 
Surprisingly, Naive Bayes performs remarkably well even when features exhibit mild 
dependence, especially with high-dimensional text data. 
Naive Bayes is widely used in spam filtering, sentiment analysis, and document 
categorization because it trains fast, requires minimal data, and provides strong performance 
for well-separated classes.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the AdaBoost algorithm. Describe how weak learners are combined, weight updating, and how boosting reduces bias.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Overview 
AdaBoost is an ensemble technique where many simple models—often small decision 
trees—are trained sequentially. Each new learner focuses more intensely on the samples that 
earlier learners misclassified. This sequential correction mechanism makes the final 
ensemble highly accurate. 
Weak Learner Combination 
 AdaBoost trains weak learners one by one. 
 Each learner is assigned a strength value based on how well it performed. 
 The final prediction is made using a weighted vote of all weak learners. 
 Learners that perform better influence the final output more strongly. 
Weight Updating 
 Initially, all training samples have equal weight. 
 After each weak learner is trained, weights of misclassified samples are increased. 
 Increased weight means future learners pay extra attention to the mistakes. 
 Correctly classified samples get reduced weight, minimizing repeated effort on easy 
cases. 
 The weight distribution is normalized after each iteration. 
Bias Reduction 
 A single weak model has high bias because it cannot learn complex boundaries. 
 AdaBoost systematically reduces bias by adding many learners that capture new 
patterns. 
 Each stage corrects errors made in earlier stages, creating a progressively more refined 
decision boundary. 
 This leads to significantly improved accuracy and lower bias without drastically 
overfitting early in training.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the internal working of LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) networks. Explain input gate, forget gate, output gate, and cell state with equations.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Describe working of LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) networks. Explain input gate, forget 
gate, output gate, and cell state. 
Purpose 
LSTMs solve the long-term dependency problem in sequence tasks by using a controlled 
memory mechanism. They decide what information should be kept, discarded, or output at 
each time step. 
Forget Gate 
 Determines which parts of past memory should be removed. 
 It analyzes previous hidden state and current input. 
 Unimportant information is purposely discarded to prevent memory overload. 
Input Gate 
 Controls which new information should enter the memory. 
 It evaluates how relevant the incoming data is for future predictions. 
 Only meaningful components of the current input get added to cell state. 
Cell State 
 This is the core memory that travels across time steps. 
 It stores long-term patterns and is gently updated by forget and input gates. 
 Cell state ensures that time-dependent information is preserved throughout the 
sequence. 
Output Gate 
 Determines what information should be exposed as the current output. 
 It filters the cell state and produces the hidden state that continues the sequence. 
 This gate ensures the network shows only actionable information at each step.

Explain the architecture and working of Autoencoders. Describe encoder, decoder, latent 
representation, and applications in anomaly detection. 
Architecture Overview 
Autoencoders are neural networks designed to learn compressed representations of input 
data. They attempt to reconstruct the original input, forcing the model to learn meaningful 
structure. 
Encoder 
 Reduces input data into a compact form. 
 Extracts essential patterns while ignoring fine details and noise. 
 Produces a compressed encoding of the input. 
Latent Representation 
 This represents the most informative characteristics of the input in a smaller 
dimension. 
 It acts as an abstract summary of original data. 
 Quality of latent space determines the strength of the autoencoder. 
Decoder 
 Takes latent representation and reconstructs the original input. 
 Its quality indicates how well the model learned the data structure. 
 If encoding captures major information, reconstruction becomes accurate. 
Anomaly Detection 
 Autoencoders trained on normal data reconstruct normal instances well. 
 Abnormal inputs differ significantly from typical patterns and produce high 
reconstruction error. 
 This error becomes the basis for flagging anomalies.

blindly.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Explain Natural Language Processing (NLP) pipeline in detail.Discuss text cleaning, tokenization, embeddings, sequence modelling.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain Natural Language Processing pipeline in detail. 
A Natural Language Processing (NLP) pipeline is a systematic sequence of processing stages 
that transform raw textual data into a format suitable for analysis and understanding by 
computers. This pipeline typically involves several interconnected steps, each building upon 
the previous one. 
Here's a detailed explanation of a typical NLP pipeline: 
 Text Acquisition and Cleaning: 
 Data Collection: Gathering raw text data from various sources like websites, documents, 
social media, etc. 
 Text Cleaning: Removing irrelevant characters, HTML tags, special symbols, and 
correcting common errors. This step ensures the text is in a consistent and usable format. 
 Preprocessing: 
 Tokenization: Breaking down the text into smaller units called "tokens," which can be 
words, subwords, or even characters. 
 Lowercasing: Converting all text to lowercase to treat words like "Apple" and "apple" as the 
same. 
 Stop Word Removal: Eliminating common words (e.g., "the," "a," "is") that carry little 
semantic meaning and might not be useful for analysis. 
 Stemming/Lemmatization: Reducing words to their base or root form. Stemming uses 
heuristic rules (e.g., removing suffixes), while lemmatization uses dictionary-based lookups 
to get the actual base form (lemma). 
 Part-of-Speech (POS) Tagging: Assigning a grammatical category (e.g., noun, verb, 
adjective) to each token, providing syntactic information. 
 Feature Extraction/Representation: 
 Bag-of-Words (BoW): Representing text as a collection of word frequencies, disregarding 
word order. 
 TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency): Assigning weights to words 
based on their frequency in a document and their rarity across the entire corpus, highlighting 
important terms. 
 Word Embeddings (e.g., Word2Vec, GloVe, FastText): Representing words as dense 
vectors in a continuous vector space, capturing semantic relationships between words. 
 Sentence Embeddings (e.g., Sentence-BERT): Representing entire sentences as vectors, 
capturing sentence-level meaning. 
 Modeling and Analysis: 
 Machine Learning/Deep Learning Models: Applying various algorithms (e.g., Naive 
Bayes, Support Vector Machines, Recurrent Neural Networks, Transformers) for tasks like: 
 Text Classification: Categorizing text into predefined classes (e.g., sentiment analysis, spam 
detection). 
 Named Entity Recognition (NER): Identifying and classifying named entities (e.g., person 
names, organizations, locations). 
 Sentiment Analysis: Determining the emotional tone or sentiment expressed in the text. 
 Machine Translation: Translating text from one language to another. 
 Text Summarization: Generating concise summaries of longer texts. 
 Question Answering: Answering questions based on a given text. 
 Evaluation and Deployment: 
 Model Evaluation: Assessing the performance of the chosen model using metrics relevant 
to the specific NLP task (e.g., accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score). 
 Deployment: Integrating the trained NLP model into an application or system for real-world 
use. 
 Monitoring and Maintenance: Continuously monitoring the model's performance and 
retraining it as needed with new data to maintain its effectiveness.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the internal working of LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) networks. Explain input gate, forget gate, output gate, and cell state with equations.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Describe the internal working of LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) networks. Explain input 
gate, forget gate, output gate, and cell state without formulas. 
LSTM networks are specialised versions of recurrent neural networks designed to handle 
long-range dependencies in sequences. They maintain an internal memory that helps them 
retain information for many time steps, avoiding problems like vanishing gradients that often 
appear in traditional RNNs. 
The central element of an LSTM is the cell state, which acts as a long-term memory channel 
running through the entire sequence. The network uses several gates to carefully decide what 
to keep, what to remove, and what new information to store. These gates are controlled by 
learnable parameters and activation functions that produce values between zero and one, 
which serve as filters. 
The forget gate determines which information from the previous memory should be 
removed. It checks the old cell state and the current input and decides what portion of the 
memory is no longer relevant for the next steps. 
The input gate decides what new information should be stored. First, it evaluates how 
important the incoming signal is, then it prepares new candidate information for updating the 
cell state. 
The output gate regulates what part of the updated memory should be revealed as the output 
of the current time step. It looks at the current memory and selects the parts useful for the 
next hidden representation. 
Together, these gates allow LSTMs to maintain useful information over long sequences, 
forget irrelevant details, and continuously update their state in a controlled manner. This 
makes them ideal for tasks such as language modelling, speech processing, and time-series 
analysis where context over time matters.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. Explain the process of Feature Engineering in Machine Learning.Discuss feature creation, selection, extraction, and the impact on modelperformance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain the process of Feature Engineering in Machine Learning. Discuss feature creation, 
selection, extraction, and the impact on model performance. 
Feature engineering is the process of transforming raw data into structured, meaningful 
inputs that improve machine learning performance. Models rely on features to understand 
patterns, so the quality of the features often matters more than the choice of algorithm. 
Feature creation involves generating new attributes from existing data. This may include 
breaking timestamps into components, calculating ratios, combining multiple fields, 
encoding categorical values, or deriving domain-specific metrics. Good feature creation 
injects domain knowledge directly into the model. 
Feature selection focuses on identifying which features actually contribute to predictive 
strength. Irrelevant, redundant, or noisy features may reduce accuracy and increase 
overfitting. Selection relies on analysing feature importance, statistical relationships, or using 
model-based methods to determine the most influential attributes. 
Feature extraction converts raw inputs into compact numerical representations. Unlike 
feature creation, which adds new columns, extraction transforms data into a different space. 
Examples include reducing dimensionality or embedding high-dimensional objects like text 
or images into dense numeric vectors. The goal is to capture essential information while 
removing unnecessary complexity. 
The impact on performance is significant. Carefully engineered features improve accuracy, 
reduce training time, and strengthen generalisation. Poorly constructed features can confuse 
models, cause instability, or exaggerate noise. Ultimately, a well-engineered feature set often 
makes the difference between a mediocre and a high-performing ML system.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 5. Explain the architecture and working of Autoencoders. Describe encoder, decoder, latent representation, and applications in anomalydetection.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Explain the architecture and working of Autoencoders. Describe encoder, decoder, latent 
representation, and applications in anomaly detection. 
An autoencoder is a neural network structure designed to compress and reconstruct data. It 
learns to encode the input into a smaller internal representation and then decode it back to 
something close to the original. This self-reconstruction ability makes autoencoders useful 
for dimensionality reduction and anomaly detection. 
The encoder is the first part of the network. It gradually reduces the input dimensionality 
through multiple layers, capturing the essential structure of the data. This compressed output 
is stored in the latent representation, a compact vector that preserves the most important 
information while removing noise and redundancy. 
The decoder reconstructs the original input from the latent representation. It expands the 
encoded information back to the original size, attempting to match the initial data as closely 
as possible. Successful training ensures that normal patterns are reconstructed well. 
In anomaly detection, autoencoders are trained only on normal data. Because the network 
learns the typical patterns, it reconstructs normal inputs accurately. Abnormal inputs, 
however, deviate from what the autoencoder learned, leading to large reconstruction errors. 
These errors signal anomalies in applications such as fraud detection, system monitoring, 
and industrial safety.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 6. Describe the complete workflow of building a Deep Learning model,including data preparation, architecture selection, training, regularization,and evaluation.
