rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the complete workflow of Feature Engineering. Discuss different types of features and the role of feature selection in improving model performance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Feature engineering is long process, many steps and very important. Workflow go like this: 
1. Understand data — first look at data, find types, missing, outliers, distribution, 
date/time, text. You must know what each column mean before touch. 
2. Clean data — fix typos, remove duplicates, impute missing (mean/median/KNN or 
model-based), correct wrong values. This step avoid garbage into model. 
3. Transform raw into features — create new columns: aggregates, ratios, interaction 
terms, date parts (year, month, weekday), lags for time-series, rolling means. For text 
make TF-IDF or embeddings. For images extract pretrained features. 
4. Encode categorical — one-hot for low-cardinality, target-encoding or embeddings for 
high-cardinality. Be careful with leakage when target-encoding. 
5. Scale / normalize — standardize numeric features for algorithms that need it (SVM, 
NN) or keep tree-friendly raw values for tree models. 
6. Reduce / select features — remove highly correlated, low variance, or irrelevant 
columns. Use PCA only when helpful. 
7. Feature validation — test features on holdout data, check distribution difference train 
vs test, check leakage. 
8. Deploy and monitor — instrument features in production, monitor distribution shifts 
and rebuild pipeline when needed. 
Different types of features (examples): 
 Numerical (continuous, discrete): age, price, temp. 
 Categorical (nominal/ordinal): country, education level. 
 Datetime: timestamp, useful for seasonality or trend. 
 Text features: bag-of-words, TF-IDF, embeddings. 
 Time-series features: lag, rolling mean, trend. 
 Image features: CNN embeddings, color histograms. 
 Derived features: ratios, interactions, counts. 
Role of feature selection — short points: 
 remove noise and irrelevant inputs so model not overfit. 
 reduce dimensionality thus speed up training and inference. 
 improve generalization and interpretability by keeping only meaningful features. 
 methods: filter (correlation, chi-square), wrapper (recursive feature elimination), 
embedded (L1, tree feature importance). Use cross-validation to choose best subset.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the architecture and working of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs).Explain how convolution, pooling, and feature maps help in image understanding.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
CNN is special neural net for images and spatial data. Architecture common blocks: 
1. Input layer — image height × width × channels (e.g., 224×224×3). 
2. Convolutional layers — apply many filters (kernels) sliding over image; each filter 
compute dot-product and produce activation map. Convolution shares weights so 
detect same pattern anywhere. 
3. Activation (ReLU) — nonlinearity applied after convolution to add capacity. 
4. Pooling layers — downsample spatial dimension (max-pool or avg-pool) to reduce 
size, make translation invariance, reduce computation. 
5. Normalization / BatchNorm — stabilize training and allow larger learning rate. 
6. Stack more conv + pool — deeper layers learn higher-level features (edges → 
textures → parts → objects). 
7. Fully connected layers / Global average pool — combine features for classification 
or regression. 
8. Output layer — softmax for multi-class, sigmoid for multi-label. 
How convolution helps: 
 local receptive fields let network focus on local spatial patterns (edges, corners). 
 weight sharing reduces parameters and learns translational invariance. 
Feature maps meaning: 
 each filter produce a feature map showing where pattern present. 
 early maps simple (edge detectors), deeper maps complex (faces, wheels). 
 stacking maps create hierarchical representation.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 6. Explain Ensemble Learning in detail. Describe bagging, boosting, and stacking, and compare how each method improves model performance in different scenarios.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Ensemble learning combine multiple learners to get better accuracy and stability than single 
model. Idea: different models make different errors, combine to cancel errors. 
Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating): 
 train base learners (often decision trees) on bootstrap samples (random sampling with 
replacement). 
 average predictions (regression) or majority vote (classification). 
 reduces variance and overfitting because model ensemble smooths fluctuations. 
 Random Forest is bagging with additional random feature selection in tree splits. 
 Best when base learner high variance (deep trees). Bagging not reduce bias much. 
Boosting: 
 sequential ensemble where each new learner focuses on mistakes of previous ones. 
 algorithms: AdaBoost (reweights instances), Gradient Boosting (fit residuals), 
XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost advanced versions. 
 reduces bias and variance by combining many weak learners into strong predictor. 
 very powerful on tabular data, but susceptible to overfitting if not regularized. 
Stacking (Stacked Generalization): 
 train diverse base models (level-0), then train meta-learner (level-1) on their 
predictions. 
 meta-learner learns how to best combine outputs (weights) and can correct systematic 
errors. 
 powerful when base models are complementary. Must use cross-validated predictions 
for meta training to avoid leakage. 
Comparison & when to use: 
 Bagging: use when variance high and you want stability (trees). Good default when 
noisy data. 
 Boosting: use when you need best accuracy and willing to tune; works great on 
structured tabular data and weak learners like shallow trees. 
 Stacking: use when you have multiple diverse strong models and want additional 
gain; careful CV needed to avoid overfitting. 
 ensembles often improve calibration and robustness; cost is increased compute and 
complexity.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the complete workflow of Feature Engineering. Discuss different types of features and the role of feature selection in improving model performance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Definition 
Feature Engineering is the systematic process of transforming raw data into meaningful input features that 
enhance a machine learning model’s predictive power. 
Workflow 
1. Data Understanding 
Identify data types, distributions, missing values, and the relationship between features and the 
target. 
2. Data Cleaning 
Handle missing values, outliers, inconsistent formats, and noise to prepare stable input. 
3. Feature Construction 
Create new features such as ratios, interactions, polynomial features, domain-specific features, and 
time-based attributes. 
4. Feature Transformation 
Apply scaling, normalization, encoding, discretization, and log transformations to improve algorithm 
compatibility. 
5. Feature Reduction 
Remove redundant, highly correlated, or noisy features using statistical and ML-based techniques. 
6. Feature Selection 
Rank and select the best features using filter, wrapper, or embedded methods.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the architecture and working of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs).Explain how convolution, pooling, and feature maps help in image understanding.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Definition 
A CNN is a deep learning architecture designed to automatically learn spatial hierarchies of features from 
image data. 
Architecture Components 
1. Input Layer 
Receives image pixel matrices. 
2. Convolutional Layers 
Apply filters to detect patterns such as edges, textures, shapes. 
3. Activation Function (ReLU) 
Introduces non-linearity, allowing complex pattern learning. 
4. Pooling Layers 
Reduce spatial dimensions and retain essential information. 
5. Fully Connected Layers 
Combine extracted features for final classification or regression. 
6. Output Layer 
Produces class probabilities or numerical predictions. 
Working of CNN 
 Filters slide over the image performing convolution operations. 
 Multiple filters produce multiple feature maps, each highlighting a specific property. 
 Pooling compresses the feature maps, making them invariant to position and small distortions. 
 Deep layers learn high-level representations like objects or shapes. 
How Each Component Helps in Image Understanding 
 Convolution: Detects local patterns and preserves spatial relations. 
 Feature Maps: Represent learned patterns; early layers capture edges while deeper layers capture 
objects. 
 Pooling: Reduces noise, controls overfitting, and generalizes recognition.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. Discuss the concept of Explainable AI (XAJ). Why is model interpretability important,and what are the major techniques used to interpret black-box models?
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
? 
Definition 
Explainable AI (XAI) refers to methods that make AI decisions transparent, understandable, and 
trustworthy. 
Major XAI Techniques 
1. LIME (Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations) 
Explains individual predictions by approximating the model locally. 
2. SHAP Values (SHapley Additive exPlanations) 
Quantifies the contribution of each feature to a specific prediction. 
3. Feature Importance Scores 
Identifies globally influential features in the model. 
4. Partial Dependence Plots (PDP) 
Shows how a feature influences model output across its range. 
5. Grad-CAM for Neural Networks 
Highlights important regions in images influencing CNN predictions. 
6. Rule-Based Extraction 
Converts model behavior into simple human-readable rules.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the role of validation sets in machine learning. Why is validation important,and how does it prevent model overfitting?
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
? 
Definition 
A validation set is a subset of data used during model training to tune hyperparameters, 
evaluate model behavior, and guide model selection without touching the test set. 
Role of a Validation Set 
1. Hyperparameter Tuning – Helps select optimal parameters like learning rate, 
number of layers, tree depth, etc. 
2. Model Selection – Compares multiple candidate models to choose the best
performing one. 
3. Performance Monitoring – Tracks how well the model generalizes while training 
progresses. 
4. Early Stopping – Stops training when performance on validation worsens. 
5. Bias–Variance Balance – Ensures the model neither underfits nor overfits. 
Importance in Preventing Overfitting 
 Overfitting occurs when a model memorizes training data. 
 Validation performance drops when the model overfits, signaling the need for 
regularization or early stopping. 
 Validation prevents the model from being evaluated only on training accuracy.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the main differences between generative models and discriminative models with suitable examples.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Definition 
 Generative Models learn the joint probability distribution P(X, Y). 
 Discriminative Models learn the conditional probability P(Y | X). 
Generative Models 
 They model how data is generated. 
 Can create new samples. 
Examples: 
 Naïve Bayes 
 Gaussian Mixture Models 
 GANs 
 Variational Autoencoders (VAE) 
Discriminative Models 
 They classify or predict labels directly. 
 Focus only on the decision boundary. 
Examples: 
 Logistic Regression 
 SVM 
 Random Forest 
 Neural Networks 
Key Differences 
1. Learning Objective: Model data distribution vs. classify. 
2. Data Generation: Only generative models generate samples. 
3. Complexity: Generative models are often more complex. 
4. Performance: Discriminative models often outperform for classification tasks. 
5. Flexibility: Generative usable for tasks like image generation, missing value filling, 
etc.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the role of validation sets in machine learning. Why is validation important,and how does it prevent model overfitting?
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
? 
 Definition & purpose: Validation set is a separate subset of labeled data not used for training; it is 
used to evaluate model performance during development and to tune hyperparameters. 
 Hyperparameter tuning: Use validation metrics (e.g., validation loss, validation accuracy) to 
choose learning rate, regularization strength, tree depth, number of epochs, etc. This avoids choosing 
hyperparameters that only help on training data. 
 Model selection: Compare different model architectures or algorithms on the validation set to pick 
the best candidate before final testing. 
 Early stopping: Monitor validation loss during training; stop training when validation loss stops 
improving to prevent the model from memorizing noise (overfitting). 
 Preventing overfitting: If a model fits training data but validation performance degrades, that 
signals overfitting — you then apply regularization, simplify the model, or get more data. Using 
cross-validation (k-fold) extends this by rotating validation folds to get stable estimates. 
 Practical tips: Keep validation strictly separate (no peeking), and reserve a held-out test set for the 
final unbiased evaluation.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the main differences between generative models and discriminative models with suitable examples.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
 Generative models and discriminative models are like apples and rockets. Generative model tries to 
paint the whole universe including the trees and the moon before predicting a label; it learns 
P(moon|apple) then flips it into P(apple|moon) using magic. Discriminative models are more lazy: 
they directly ask "is this apple or not?" and say yes or no. 
 Examples: a good generative model is the old radio that sings data, or GANs which actually make art 
by dreaming new data — they are like chefs making new food. Discriminative models are calculators 
that memorize the recipe and answer. 
 Generative models can make new pictures of apples and also tell you the weather; they are flexible 
but heavy. Discriminative models are faster at actual deciding tasks like spam or not spam because 
they only draw line between classes. 
 In short: generative = create and imagine; discriminative = decide and discriminate. Both important 
but sometimes generative models like VAE make sandwiches for engineers.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. What is anomaly detection? Discuss its importance and common applications in real- world systems.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
What is anomaly detection? Discuss its importance and common applications in real
world systems. 
 Definition: Anomaly detection is the process of identifying observations that deviate significantly 
from the majority of data — these may indicate faults, fraud, rare events, or novel states. 
 Why important: Anomalies are rare but often critical (fraud, security breaches, machine failures). 
Detecting them early prevents financial loss, safety incidents, and service outages. 
 Approaches: 
o Statistical methods: z-score, IQR, Gaussian models. 
o Proximity / density methods: k-NN, Local Outlier Factor (LOF). 
o Reconstruction-based: autoencoders that reconstruct normal data well but fail on anomalies. 
o One-class classifiers: One-Class SVM, Isolation Forest. 
o Time-series methods: change-point detection, ARIMA residual analysis, LSTM-based 
forecasting residuals. 
 Applications: 
o Finance: detect fraudulent transactions or account takeover. 
o Security: flag abnormal network traffic or login patterns. 
o Manufacturing: detect machine vibration or temperature anomalies indicating faults. 
o Healthcare: detect unusual vital-sign patterns indicating emergencies. 
o Monitoring: detect log anomalies or sudden metric spikes in cloud services. 
 Practical considerations: define "normal" carefully, address class imbalance, evaluate with 
precision at low recall and with human-in-loop review, and tune sensitivity for acceptable false 
positive rate.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the role of Data Preprocessing in building ML models. Discuss key steps such as data cleaning, encoding, transformation, and handling outliers.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
 Purpose: Data preprocessing converts messy raw data into a clean, consistent, and model-ready 
format; it significantly impacts model performance and stability. 
 Key steps: 
o Data cleaning: remove duplicates, fix typos, unify date formats, handle missing values (drop, 
impute with mean/median/KNN/model-based, or use missingness indicator). 
o Encoding categorical variables: one-hot for low-cardinality, ordinal encoding for ordered 
categories, target/frequency encoding or learned embeddings for high-cardinality categories 
(use out-of-fold schemes to avoid leakage). 
o Scaling & transformation: standardization (z-score), min-max scaling, log-transform 
skewed variables; necessary for distance-based algorithms and for gradient-based 
optimization. 
o Feature transformation: binning, polynomial features, interactions, log/power transforms to 
linearize relationships. 
o Handling outliers: detect using IQR, z-score or robust methods; treat via capping 
(winsorization), transformation, or domain-informed removal. 
 Other steps: data augmentation for images/text, deduplication, balancing strategies for imbalanced 
datasets (SMOTE, class weighting), and pipelineization to ensure same transforms at training and 
serving. 
 Why it matters: Poor preprocessing leads to garbage-in→garbage-out, model instability, longer 
training times, and incorrect conclusions.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the importance of Model Evaluation Metrics. Compare accuracy, precision,recall, and Fl-score, and explain when each metric should be used.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
 Importance: Metrics quantify model performance; selecting the proper metric aligns model 
optimization with business goals and avoids misleading conclusions. 
 Accuracy: proportion of correct predictions. Use when classes are balanced and misclassification 
costs are symmetric. Misleading on imbalanced data (e.g., 99% majority class → 99% accuracy 
trivial). 
 Precision: TP / (TP + FP). Measures correctness among predicted positives. Use when false 
positives are costly (spam detection where marking legit mail spam is bad; medical test that triggers 
invasive procedure). 
 Recall (Sensitivity): TP / (TP + FN). Measures ability to find actual positives. Use when false 
negatives are costly (disease screening, fraud detection where missing a positive is bad). 
 F1-score: harmonic mean of precision and recall, useful when need balance between precision and 
recall, especially on imbalanced classes. 
 Additional metrics: ROC-AUC for ranking ability; PR-AUC when positives rare; calibration 
metrics when predicted probabilities used for decision thresholds. 
 Practical guidance: choose metric aligned with cost matrix; sometimes use multiple metrics and a 
business-aware utility function.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. Explain how ML models are used in Natural Language Processing (NLP). Discuss key tasks like text classification, sentiment analysis, and language modeling.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
 Overview (correct): ML enables machines to process and understand human language via statistical 
and neural methods. Common pipeline: tokenization → embeddings → model 
(RNN/CNN/Transformer) → prediction. 
 Text Classification (correct): maps documents to categories (news topics, spam detection). Models: 
logistic regression with TF-IDF, CNNs, and Transformers (BERT). 
 Sentiment Analysis (correct): determines polarity (positive/negative/neutral). Uses labeled reviews 
and classifiers; embeddings and attention mechanisms improve context handling. 
 Language Modeling (correct): predicts next token or sentence probability; foundational for 
generation (GPT, BERT pretraining). 
 Other tasks (rubbish appended): in many projects we also teach the model to sing poems and 
summarize the sky; some systems make the model write shopping lists for cats. These are creative 
applications but not standard tasks. 
 Practical tips (correct): pretrain on large corpora then fine-tune, use subword tokenization (BPE), 
monitor bias and safety issues, use evaluation metrics like BLEU/ROUGE for generation and 
accuracy/F1 for classification.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Discuss the complete ML lifecycle from problem definition to deployment. Explain the purpose of each stage with appropriate examples.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
 Problem definition: translate business need into ML question. E.g., reduce churn → formulate as 
binary classification predicting churn within 30 days. 
 Data collection: gather relevant data sources — CRM, logs, transactions. Ensure permissions and 
privacy. 
 Data preprocessing & feature engineering: clean data, create features (e.g., engagement metrics), 
encode variables. 
 Model selection & training: choose algorithms, train with cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning 
(grid/random/Bayesian). 
 Evaluation & validation: use holdout test, check metrics, perform fairness and robustness tests; 
conduct ablation and sensitivity analysis. 
 Deployment: package model as service (REST API), integrate with serving infra, ensure low-latency 
and scalability (Docker, Kubernetes). 
 Monitoring & maintenance: track performance, detect drift, collect labels for retraining, implement 
rollback mechanisms. 
 Feedback & iteration: integrate user feedback and update problem scope; retrain and redeploy. 
 Example: Fraud detection system moves from pilot (data exploration, model prototyping) to 
production (real-time scoring, human-in-loop alerts, retraining pipelines).

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Discuss the challenges of deploying ML models in real-world environments. Explain issues like data drift, model monitoring, scalability, hardware constraints, security risks, and continuous retraining .
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Discuss the challenges of deploying ML models in real-world environments. Explain 
issues like data drift, model monitoring, scalability, hardware constraints, security risks, 
and continuous retraining. 
 Data drift & distribution shift: Incoming data may differ from training data (covariate, concept, or 
target drift). This degrades performance; detection requires monitoring data statistics and model 
metrics; solutions: retrain, use online learning, or maintain adaptive ensembles. 
 Model monitoring & observability: Need to track latency, throughput, prediction distribution, 
confidence calibration, error rates, and business KPIs. Implement alerts, logging of 
inputs/predictions for auditing, and shadow testing. 
 Scalability & latency: Production systems must handle peak loads; deploying models in low-latency 
environments may require batching, model quantization, or distillation. Use autoscaling 
infrastructure, caching, and efficient serving frameworks (TF Serving, TorchServe). 
 Hardware & resource constraints: Edge devices have limited CPU/memory; use model 
compression (pruning, quantization), lightweight architectures, or offload to cloud. GPU availability 
and cost considerations affect batch vs real-time serving. 
 Security & robustness: Models are susceptible to adversarial attacks, data poisoning, or model 
extraction. Defenses include adversarial training, input sanitization, access control, and monitoring 
for anomalous queries. 
 Continuous retraining & ML ops: Establish robust pipelines for data ingestion, labeling, 
retraining, validation, deployment, and rollback. Maintain model lineage and versioning to support 
reproducibility and audits. 
 Engineering & integration: Integrate with legacy systems, ensure transactional consistency, handle 
schema changes, and validate data quality. 
 Regulatory & ethical considerations: Logging, explainability, fairness audits, and consent for 
personal data. 
 Human factors & organizational: Cross-functional teams, maintenance burden, and cost of 
ongoing annotation and governance.

correct answers it guessed out of all guesses. Recall is when model remembers long-lost 
samples from training memory. F1-score is like friendship score between precision and 
recall. Use accuracy when everything is balanced, use precision when you want correct 
predictions only, use recall when missing things is dangerous, and use F1 when you want 
both to shake hands equally. Sometimes F1 also used to select best fruit from dataset of 
apples.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the role of Data Preprocessing in building ML models. Discuss key steps such as data cleaning, encoding, transformation, and handling outliers.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Data preprocessing is the crucial step of transforming raw, real-world data into a clean, 
structured, and usable format for machine learning algorithms. Its primary role is to 
ensure high-quality input, which directly impacts the performance, accuracy, efficiency, 
and reliability of the final model. Without it, models may struggle to identify meaningful 
patterns, leading to biased or inaccurate predictions (the "garbage in, garbage out" 
principle).  
Key Steps in Data Preprocessing 
The main tasks involved in data preprocessing for building ML models include: 
 Data Cleaning 
This process identifies and corrects errors, inconsistencies, and noise in the dataset to ensure 
a reliable foundation for modeling. 
o Handling Missing Values: Gaps in data are a common issue. Techniques include deletion 
(removing rows or columns if the missing data percentage is small) or imputation (filling the 
missing values with statistical measures like the mean, median, or mode for numerical data, 
or the most frequent category for categorical data). 
o Removing Duplicates: Redundant records can skew the model by overemphasizing certain 
patterns. Identifying and removing these ensures the model learns from unique data points. 
o Correcting Inconsistencies: This involves standardizing formats, such as ensuring 
consistent date formats (e.g., MM/DD/YYYY) or uniform labels for the same category (e.g., 
"Male" vs. "M"). 
 Encoding 
Most machine learning algorithms require numerical input and cannot directly process text or 
categorical variables (data that represents groups or categories). 
o Label Encoding: Assigns a unique integer to each category. This is suitable only for ordinal 
data where the categories have a meaningful rank or order (e.g., 'Low' to 'High'). 
o One-Hot Encoding: Creates new binary (0 or 1) columns for each category. This is the 
standard method for nominal data (categories without an intrinsic order, like colors or city 
names) to prevent the model from assuming an artificial order. 
 Transformation 
This involves converting data into a format suitable for the specific requirements of the ML 
algorithm. 
o Feature Scaling: Ensures features with different units or magnitudes (e.g., age vs. income) 
have a similar scale so that no single feature dominates the model training. 
o Standardization (Z-score normalization): Rescales data to have a mean of 0 and a standard 
deviation of 1. It is often a safe default and less sensitive to outliers. 
o Normalization (Min-Max scaling): Rescales features to a fixed range, typically between 0 
and 1. It is useful for algorithms like neural networks that expect input within a specific 
range. 
o Other Transformations: May include mathematical transformations (like log 
transformation for skewed data), or creating new features from existing ones (feature 
engineering) to enhance the data's predictive power. 
 Handling Outliers 
Outliers are data points that significantly deviate from other observations and can skew 
statistical analyses and model predictions. 
o Detection: Outliers are typically identified using visualization methods like box plots or 
statistical techniques such as the Z-score or Interquartile Range (IQR) method. 
o Management: Depending on the context, outliers can be removed (if they are errors), 
capped (limiting their value to a certain threshold), or the data can be transformed to reduce 
their impact. It is important to use domain knowledge to determine if an outlier is a genuine 
anomaly (which might be important for tasks like fraud detection) or a data entry error.  
.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Explain in detail how machine learning is used in healthcare. Describe applications (diagnosis, prediction, medical imaging, drug discovery), challenges (data quality, privacy, bias), and the steps involved in developing an ML-based healthcare system.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Machine learning (ML) revolutionizes healthcare by analyzing complex data for faster 
diagnosis, personalized treatment, predictive risk assessment, enhanced medical imaging 
analysis (X-rays, MRIs), and accelerated drug discovery, but faces hurdles like ensuring data 
quality, upholding privacy (HIPAA), tackling algorithmic bias, and integrating into 
workflows, with development involving data prep, model training, validation, and 
continuous monitoring for improved outcomes and operational efficiency.  
Applications in Healthcare 
 Diagnosis & Prediction: Detects diseases (e.g., diabetes, cancer) earlier by spotting patterns 
in patient records, genetic data, and vitals; predicts disease progression and patient risk for 
adverse events. 
 Medical Imaging: Uses Deep Learning (CNNs) to analyze X-rays, MRIs, CT scans for 
anomalies (tumors, lesions) with high accuracy, assisting radiologists. 
 Drug Discovery: Speeds up finding new drugs by analyzing molecular interactions, 
predicting compound safety/efficacy, modeling drug structures, and optimizing clinical trials. 
 Personalized Medicine: Tailors treatments using individual data (genetics, lifestyle) to 
predict best therapeutic responses. 
 Clinical Operations: Improves efficiency, manages fraud, automates tasks, and supports 
research.  
Key Challenges 
 Data Quality & Quantity: Requires large, clean, labeled datasets, which are often 
fragmented or messy. 
 Data Privacy & Security: Handling sensitive patient data (PHI) necessitates strict 
compliance (e.g., HIPAA). 
 Bias & Fairness: Models can perpetuate or amplify biases present in training data, leading 
to unfair outcomes for certain demographics. 
 Interpretability (Explainability): "Black box" models make it hard to understand why a 
decision was made, crucial for clinical trust. 
 Integration & Workflow: Seamlessly embedding ML tools into existing hospital systems 
and clinical workflows.  
Development Steps for an ML Healthcare System 
1. Define Problem: Clearly state the clinical need (e.g., detect pneumonia in X-rays). 
2. Data Collection & Prep: Gather, clean, label (by experts), and preprocess diverse data 
(images, EHRs). 
3. Feature Engineering: Select/create relevant data features (e.g., lesion shape, vital sign 
trends). 
4. Model Selection: Choose algorithm (Supervised Learning for labeled data like imaging, 
RNNs for time-series). 
5. Training & Validation: Train model on training data, tune parameters, validate on hold-out 
sets. 
6. Evaluation: Test on unseen data using metrics like sensitivity, specificity, AUC, ensuring 
clinical relevance. 
7. Deployment & Integration: Integrate into clinical systems (EHRs, PACS). 
8. Monitoring & Maintenance: Continuously monitor performance, retrain as needed for data 
drift.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the role of validation sets in machine learning. Why is validation important,and how does it prevent model overfitting?
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
? 
Validation sets in machine learning are crucial subsets of data (separate from 
training/testing) used during model development to tune hyperparameters and prevent 
overfitting by providing an unbiased evaluation of model performance, ensuring the model 
generalizes well to new, unseen data, rather than just memorizing training patterns. They 
help select the best model configuration (like learning rate, network size) and detect when a 
model becomes too complex and performs poorly on new data, balancing bias and variance.  
Role of Validation Sets 
 Hyperparameter Tuning: Used to adjust settings (hyperparameters) that control the 
learning process, like the number of hidden layers or nodes in a neural network, without 
touching the final test set. 
 Model Selection: Allows comparison of different model architectures or algorithms to 
choose the best performer for the task. 
 Early Stopping: Monitors performance on the validation set during training; if performance 
worsens, training can be stopped to prevent overfitting.  
Why Validation is Important 
 Generalization: Ensures the model performs well on new data, not just the data it learned 
from. 
 Reliability: Builds confidence that the model is robust and accurate for real-world 
application. 
 Detects Issues: Catches problems like overfitting early in the development cycle.  
How it Prevents Overfitting 
 Overfitting occurs when a model learns the training data (including noise) too well, 
becoming highly specific and failing on new data. 
 The validation set provides an unbiased check during training. If the model's performance 
improves on training data but worsens on the validation set, it's a clear sign of overfitting. 
 By tuning hyperparameters based on validation performance, you guide the model towards a 
simpler, more generalizable solution, finding a sweet spot between underfitting (too simple) 
and overfitting (too complex).

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the main differences between generative models and discriminative models with suitable examples.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
The main difference is their objective: discriminative models focus on classifying existing 
data by learning the decision boundaries between classes, while generative models focus on 
understanding the underlying data distribution to create new data samples.  
Examples 
Generative Models 
 Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are used to create realistic images and videos, 
such as AI art generators and deepfakes. 
 Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are used for data compression, image generation, and 
anomaly detection. 
 Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Gemini, generate text, code, and 
content based on input prompts. 
 Naive Bayes is a classification algorithm that is technically generative because it models the 
probability of features given a class.  
Discriminative Models 
 Logistic Regression is a model for binary classification, such as determining if an email is 
spam. 
 Support Vector Machines (SVMs) find the optimal boundary (hyperplane) to separate 
classes, often used for tasks like facial recognition. 
 Decision Trees are used for decision-making and classification, such as risk assessment. 
 Most standard Neural Networks (for classification) are used in object detection and medical 
image analysis.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. What is anomaly detection? Discuss its importance and common applications in real- world systems.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
What is anomaly detection? Discuss its importance and common applications in real
world systems. 
 Definition: Anomaly detection is the process of identifying observations that deviate 
significantly from the majority of data — these may indicate faults, fraud, rare events, 
or novel states. 
 Why important: Anomalies are rare but often critical (fraud, security breaches, 
machine failures). Detecting them early prevents financial loss, safety incidents, and 
service outages. 
 Approaches: 
o Statistical methods: z-score, IQR, Gaussian models. 
o Proximity / density methods: k-NN, Local Outlier Factor (LOF). 
o Reconstruction-based: autoencoders that reconstruct normal data well but fail 
on anomalies. 
o One-class classifiers: One-Class SVM, Isolation Forest. 
o Time-series methods: change-point detection, ARIMA residual analysis, 
LSTM-based forecasting residuals. 
 Applications: 
o Finance: detect fraudulent transactions or account takeover. 
o Security: flag abnormal network traffic or login patterns. 
o Manufacturing: detect machine vibration or temperature anomalies indicating 
faults. 
o Healthcare: detect unusual vital-sign patterns indicating emergencies. 
o Monitoring: detect log anomalies or sudden metric spikes in cloud services. 
 Practical considerations: define "normal" carefully, address class imbalance, 
evaluate with precision at low recall and with human-in-loop review, and tune 
sensitivity for acceptable false positive rate.

 Purpose: Data preprocessing converts messy raw data into a clean, consistent, and

 Key steps: 
o Data cleaning: remove duplicates, fix typos, unify date formats, handle missing 
values (drop, impute with mean/median/KNN/model-based, or use missingness 
indicator). 
o Encoding categorical variables: one-hot for low-cardinality, ordinal encoding

high-cardinality categories (use out-of-fold schemes to avoid leakage). 
o Scaling & transformation: standardization (z-score), min-max scaling, log

gradient-based optimization. 
o Feature transformation: binning, polynomial features, interactions, log/power 
transforms to linearize relationships. 
o Handling outliers: detect using IQR, z-score or robust methods; treat via 
capping (winsorization), transformation, or domain-informed removal. 
 Other steps: data augmentation for images/text, deduplication, balancing strategies 
for imbalanced datasets (SMOTE, class weighting), and pipelineization to ensure same 
transforms at training and serving. 
 Why it matters: Poor preprocessing leads to garbage-in→garbage-out, model 
instability, longer training times, and incorrect conclusions.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Discuss the challenges of deploying ML models in real-world environments. Explain issues like data drift, model monitoring, scalability, hardware constraints, security risks, and continuous retraining .
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Discuss the challenges of deploying ML models in real-world environments. Explain 
issues like data drift, model monitoring, scalability, hardware constraints, security 
risks, and continuous retraining. 
 Data drift & distribution shift: Incoming data may differ from training data 
(covariate, concept, or target drift). This degrades performance; detection requires 
monitoring data statistics and model metrics; solutions: retrain, use online learning, or 
maintain adaptive ensembles. 
 Model monitoring & observability: Need to track latency, throughput, prediction 
distribution, confidence calibration, error rates, and business KPIs. Implement alerts, 
logging of inputs/predictions for auditing, and shadow testing. 
 Scalability & latency: Production systems must handle peak loads; deploying models 
in low-latency environments may require batching, model quantization, or distillation. 
Use autoscaling infrastructure, caching, and efficient serving frameworks (TF Serving, 
TorchServe). 
 Hardware & resource constraints: Edge devices have limited CPU/memory; use 
model compression (pruning, quantization), lightweight architectures, or offload to 
cloud. GPU availability and cost considerations affect batch vs real-time serving. 
 Security & robustness: Models are susceptible to adversarial attacks, data poisoning, 
or model extraction. Defenses include adversarial training, input sanitization, access 
control, and monitoring for anomalous queries. 
 Continuous retraining & ML ops: Establish robust pipelines for data ingestion, 
labeling, retraining, validation, deployment, and rollback. Maintain model lineage and 
versioning to support reproducibility and audits. 
 Engineering & integration: Integrate with legacy systems, ensure transactional 
consistency, handle schema changes, and validate data quality. 
 Regulatory & ethical considerations: Logging, explainability, fairness audits, and 
consent for personal data. 
 Human factors & organizational: Cross-functional teams, maintenance burden, and 
cost of ongoing annotation and governance.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the role of validation sets in machine learning. Why is validation important,and how does it prevent model overfitting?
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
? 
Answer 
Definition / role: A validation set is a portion of labeled data reserved during development 
to evaluate model generalization while tuning hyperparameters and making decisions about 
model architecture or early-stopping. It is distinct from the training set (used to fit model 
parameters) and the test set (used for final evaluation). 
Why validation is important 
1. Hyperparameter selection: Validation performance guides selection of learning rate, 
regularization strength, depth/width, and other settings without peeking at the test set. 
2. Model comparison: It provides an unbiased comparison between candidate 
models/architectures before final evaluation. 
3. Early stopping: Monitoring validation loss/metric prevents training beyond the point 
where generalization degrades. 
4. Detects overfitting: A divergence between improving training metric and worsening 
validation metric signals that model is fitting noise. 
5. Robust model choices: Using cross-validation or repeated splits gives more reliable 
estimates and reduces variance in hyperparameter choices. 
How it prevents overfitting 
 By exposing the model selection process to data it has not trained on, the validation set 
reveals when improvements are due to memorization rather than true signal. Actions 
taken (regularization, simpler model, more data, early stopping) based on validation 
feedback reduce model complexity and improve generalization.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the main differences between generative models and discriminative models with suitable examples.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Answer 
Definitions 
 Generative models: Model the joint distribution P(X,Y)P(X,Y)P(X,Y) or 
P(X)P(X)P(X) and can generate new samples. They capture how data is generated. 
 Discriminative models: Model the conditional distribution P(Y∣X)P(Y|X)P(Y∣X) or 
directly the decision boundary f(X)f(X)f(X) for prediction; they optimize 
classification/regression performance. 
Key differences 
1. Objective: Generative → model data generation; Discriminative → directly predict 
labels. 
2. Probability learned: Generative → P(X,Y)P(X,Y)P(X,Y) or P(X)P(X)P(X); 
Discriminative → P(Y∣X)P(Y|X)P(Y∣X). 
3. Sample generation: Generative can synthesize realistic samples (images, text); 
discriminative cannot. 
4. Complexity & data requirements: Generative often require more modeling capacity 
and data for realistic generation; discriminative models can be simpler for predictive 
tasks. 
5. Typical use-cases: Generative for data augmentation, simulation, unsupervised 
pretraining; discriminative for classification and regression with high accuracy. 
Examples 
 Generative: Naive Bayes (models class-conditional densities), Gaussian Mixture 
Models, Variational Autoencoders (VAE), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). 
 Discriminative: Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random 
Forests, Feedforward Neural Networks fine-tuned for classification. 
Practical note: In classification tasks with abundant labeled data, discriminative models 
often yield better accuracy; when you need to model the data distribution or generate 
samples, generative models are appropriate.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 3. What is anomaly detection? Discuss its importance and common applications in real- world systems.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
What is anomaly detection? Discuss its importance and common applications in real
world systems. 
Answer 
Definition: Anomaly detection (outlier detection) is the task of identifying observations, 
events, or patterns that do not conform to expected behavior — i.e., instances that are rare 
and significantly different from normal data. 
Importance 
1. Early warning: Detects faults, intrusions, or failures before they escalate. 
2. Risk management: Identifies fraudulent, erroneous, or malicious events that could 
cause financial or reputational damage. 
3. Safety & reliability: In industrial/medical contexts, catching anomalies can prevent 
accidents or patient harm. 
4. Operational efficiency: Helps find sensor malfunctions, data pipeline errors, and 
unusual system states that require corrective action. 
Common applications 
 Finance: Credit card fraud detection, anti-money laundering (unusual transaction 
patterns). 
 Cybersecurity: Intrusion and anomaly detection in network traffic, user behavior 
analytics. 
 Industry / Manufacturing: Predictive maintenance — detect abnormal 
vibration/temperature before machine failure. 
 Healthcare: Detect abnormal lab results, sepsis onset, or anomalous patient vitals. 
 Cloud/IT Operations: Detect traffic spikes, unusual API calls, or log anomalies 
indicative of incidents. 
 IoT & Sensors: Identify faulty sensors or environmental anomalies (e.g., sudden 
pollution spikes). 
Typical approaches 
 Statistical: Z-score, Gaussian models, control charts. 
 Proximity/density: k-NN, Local Outlier Factor, Isolation Forest. 
 Reconstruction-based: Autoencoders, PCA residuals — anomalies have high 
reconstruction error. 
 Time-series methods: Change-point detection, forecasting residuals, sequence models 
(LSTM) for temporal anomalies.

2. Regulatory compliance: Finance, healthcare, insurance and other regulated sectors

3. Accountability & auditability: Interpretability enables tracing decisions, attributing 
responsibility, and performing audits. 
4. Bias detection & fairness: Explanations reveal when models rely on protected or 
proxy features, enabling mitigation. 
5. Debugging & improvement: Interpretability helps identify data issues, spurious 
correlations, or model failure modes. 
Industries requiring interpretability 
 Healthcare: Clinicians need understandable rationale (e.g., key features leading to 
diagnosis). 
 Finance: Lending decisions, credit scoring must be explainable to customers and 
regulators. 
 Insurance: Risk assessment and pricing decisions need justification. 
 Legal & Governance: Automated decisions affecting rights or liberty require

 Aerospace/Automotive (safety-critical): Explanations help ensure safe behavior and 
root-cause analysis. 
Methods for interpretability 
 Model-intrinsic: Use inherently interpretable models (linear models, decision trees,

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the role of Data Preprocessing in building ML models. Discuss key steps such as data cleaning, encoding, transformation, and handling outliers.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Answer 
Definition / purpose: Data preprocessing converts raw, noisy, and heterogeneous inputs into 
a consistent, high-quality dataset that a model can learn from effectively. Preprocessing often 
has larger impact on final performance than choice of algorithm. 
Key steps 
1. Data cleaning: Remove duplicates, correct typos and inconsistent formats, handle 
missing values (imputation strategies: mean/median/mode, KNN, model-based, or 
explicit missing indicator). 
2. Encoding categorical variables: Transform categories to numeric — one-hot for 
low-cardinality, ordinal encoding where order matters, frequency/target encoding or 
learned embeddings for high-cardinality features (use out-of-fold schemes to avoid 
leakage). 
3. Feature scaling & transformation: Standardization (zero mean/unit variance) or 
Min-Max scaling for gradient-based models; log or Box–Cox transforms to reduce 
skew; power transforms to stabilize variance. 
4. Handling outliers: Detect with IQR, z-score, or robust methods; treat by capping 
(winsorization), transformation, winsorization, or removing if erroneous; consider 
domain knowledge. 
5. Feature engineering: Create domain-specific features (ratios, interactions, 
aggregations, lag features for time series). 
6. Dimensionality reduction & sparsity handling: PCA, feature selection, hashing for 
high-cardinality sparse features. 
7. Pipelineization & reproducibility: Use pipelines to ensure identical preprocessing in 
training and production and avoid target leakage. 
Why it matters 
 Reduces noise and bias; improves convergence and model stability; reduces risk of 
data leakage; can dramatically increase predictive power with well-engineered 
features.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the importance of Model Evaluation Metrics. Compare accuracy, precision,recall, and Fl-score, and explain when each metric should be used.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Answer 
Overview: Choosing appropriate evaluation metrics aligns model optimization with business 
goals and risk profiles. A single metric can be misleading; choose metrics mindful of class 
imbalance and costs of different error types. 
Metrics 
1. Accuracy: (TP+TN)/Total(TP+TN)/Total(TP+TN)/Total. Good for balanced datasets 
where false positives and false negatives have similar costs. Poor choice for 
imbalanced datasets (e.g., 99% negative → trivial high accuracy). 
2. Precision (Positive Predictive Value): TP/(TP+FP)TP/(TP+FP)TP/(TP+FP). High 
precision means when model predicts positive, it is usually correct. Use when false 
positives are costly (e.g., spam incorrectly flagged as important email, unnecessary 
medical procedure). 
3. Recall (Sensitivity, True Positive Rate): TP/(TP+FN)TP/(TP+FN)TP/(TP+FN). 
High recall means model finds most real positives. Use when false negatives are costly 
(e.g., disease screening, fraud detection where missing real cases is dangerous). 
4. F1-score: Harmonic mean of precision and recall. Use when you need a balance and 
classes are imbalanced; gives a single-number trade-off. 
5. Additional: ROC-AUC for ranking ability; PR-AUC when positives rare; calibration 
measures for probabilistic predictions; cost-sensitive metrics or custom business utility 
functions when errors have different costs. 
When to choose 
 Accuracy: only when class balance and equal error cost. 
 Precision prioritized: when action on positives is expensive or harmful. 
 Recall prioritized: when catching positives is critical for safety. 
 F1-score: when both precision and recall matter and dataset is imbalanced.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 4. Discuss the complete ML lifecycle from problem definition to deployment. Explain the purpose of each stage with appropriate examples.

Answer 
Stages & purpose

2. Data acquisition: Collect relevant data sources (CRM, logs, transactions). Ensure 
data quality and legal right for use. 
3. Data preprocessing & exploration: Clean, impute, detect bias, and perform 
exploratory analysis to understand distributions and relationships. 
4. Feature engineering: Create informative features (e.g., recency, frequency, monetary 
metrics for churn). 
5. Model development: Select algorithms, train models, tune hyperparameters using 
cross-validation. 
6. Evaluation & validation: Use validation/test sets and real-world metrics (ROC-AUC, 
recall@k). Include fairness checks and calibrations. 
7. Deployment: Serve the model in production (batch or real-time), integrate with 
application stack, set up APIs, and ensure latency/throughput constraints met. 
8. Monitoring & maintenance: Track model performance, data drift, and business 
KPIs; log inputs/predictions for audits. 
9. Retraining & iteration: Periodically retrain using fresh labeled data, update features, 
and deploy new versions with rollback safety. 
Example flow: Fraud detection system — define fraud types → collect transaction logs → 
engineer device/browser features → train ensemble model → evaluate precision/recall → 
deploy as real-time scoring API with human-in-loop review for high-risk transactions → 
monitor false positive rates and retrain weekly.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 5. What is Unsupervised Learning? Explain clustering and dimensionality reduction techniques, and describe how they are used in real-world applications.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Answer 
Definition: Unsupervised learning finds patterns and structure in unlabeled data, such as 
grouping similar items or finding compact representations. 
Clustering 
 K-means: Partitions data into k clusters by minimizing within-cluster variance; fast 
but assumes spherical clusters. 
 DBSCAN: Density-based clustering that detects arbitrary-shaped clusters and noise 
(good for spatial data). 
 Hierarchical clustering: Builds dendrogram to view cluster relationships; useful 
when cluster granularity matters. 
Dimensionality reduction 
 PCA: Linear projection that captures directions of maximum variance, useful for 
denoising and feature reduction. 
 t-SNE / UMAP: Nonlinear embeddings for visualization preserving local 
neighborhood structure. 
 Autoencoders: Neural network-based compression and denoising. 
Real-world applications 
 Customer segmentation: Clustering customers by behavior for targeted marketing. 
 Anomaly detection: Identify outliers as rare clusters or noise. 
 Document clustering: Group similar documents or news for topic discovery. 
 Visualization: High-dimensional gene-expression data visualized with t-SNE/UMAP 
for biological insights. 
 Compression: Reduce features for downstream supervised training or edge 
deployment.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 6. Explain the concept of Reinforcement Learning. Describe its components (agent,environment, reward, policy) and explain one real-world use case.

2. Environment: The system agent interacts with; provides states and reward signals.

4. Action: Choices available to the agent.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Discuss the challenges of deploying ML models in real-world environments. Explain issues like data drift, model monitoring, scalability, hardware constraints, security risks, and continuous retraining .
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Discuss the challenges of deploying ML models in real-world environments. Explain 
issues like data drift, model monitoring, scalability, hardware constraints, security 
risks, and continuous retraining. 
Answer 
Overview: Deployment moves models from research into operation; this phase introduces 
engineering, operational, and governance complexities that can erode initial performance if 
unaddressed. 
Key challenges & solutions 
1. Data drift & distributional shift 
o Problem: Input or label distributions change over time (covariate, concept, 
target drift), degrading model accuracy. 
o Mitigation: Continuous monitoring of input statistics, PSI/K-S tests, model 
performance metrics; set retrain triggers; use adaptive models or ensemble of 
short/long-term models. 
2. Model monitoring & observability 
o Problem: Silent failures, calibration shifts, or rising error rates go unnoticed 
without monitoring. 
o Mitigation: Instrument logging of inputs/predictions/confidences, dashboards 
for metrics (latency, throughput, accuracy), alerting, and canary/blue-green 
deployments. 
3. Scalability & latency 
o Problem: Production loads and peak traffic require autoscaling and low-latency 
predictions. 
o Mitigation: Use optimized serving (TensorFlow Serving, TorchServe), model 
batching, caching, quantization, and horizontally scalable microservices. 
4. Hardware & resource constraints 
o Problem: Edge or mobile deployments have limited CPU, memory, and power. 
o Mitigation: Model compression (pruning, distillation, quantization), lightweight 
architectures (MobileNet), offloading heavy tasks to cloud. 
5. Security & robustness 
o Problem: Adversarial examples, model inversion, data poisoning, and API 
abuse threaten integrity. 
o Mitigation: Adversarial training, input sanitization, rate-limiting, authentication, 
differential privacy, monitoring for anomalous queries. 
6. Continuous retraining & lifecycle management 
o Problem: Model staleness; repeated retraining can introduce regressions. 
o Mitigation: MLOps pipelines for versioning data/models (DVC, MLflow), 
reproducible experiments, automated tests, CI/CD for models, and staged 
rollouts with performance gates. 
7. Governance, ethics & compliance 
o Problem: Regulatory requirements (GDPR, HIPAA), explainability, fairness 
audits. 
o Mitigation: Logging for audit trails, interpretable models or explanations, 
fairness testing across subgroups, and documented risk assessments. 
8. Integration & business alignment 
o Problem: Models must fit workflows and deliver measurable business value. 
o Mitigation: Prototype with product teams, measure business KPIs, include 
humans-in-loop for critical decisions. 
Conclusion: Robust deployment requires an ecosystem of monitoring, automation, 
governance, and engineering best practices, not just a performant model.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Explain in detail how machine learning is used in healthcare. Describe applications (diagnosis, prediction, medical imaging, drug discovery), challenges (data quality, privacy, bias), and the steps involved in developing an ML-based healthcare system.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Answer 
Applications 
1. Diagnosis & Screening: ML models (e.g., CNNs on imaging, ensemble models on 
EHR data) detect disease (cancer, diabetic retinopathy) often matching or exceeding 
human-level performance in specific tasks. 
2. Prognosis & Prediction: Models predict patient risk for readmission, sepsis onset, 
deterioration, enabling early intervention. 
3. Medical Imaging: Segmentation, detection, and quantification of lesions in X-ray, 
MRI, CT using deep learning. 
4. Drug Discovery: ML accelerates virtual screening, property prediction, de novo 
molecule generation (GANs/VAEs) and helps prioritize candidates for experimental 
testing. 
5. Operational Efficiency: Scheduling, resource optimization, and supply forecasting to 
improve hospital throughput. 
Challenges 
1. Data quality & heterogeneity: EHRs contain missing values, inconsistent coding 
(ICD codes), noisy labels, and cross-site variability. Harmonizing data is non-trivial. 
2. Privacy & regulation: Patient data are highly sensitive (HIPAA/GDPR). Consent, de
identification, secure storage, and federated learning approaches are required. 
3. Bias & fairness: Underrepresentation of subpopulations causes disparate model 
performance; must be tested and mitigated. 
4. Interpretability & clinical adoption: Clinicians require transparent, explainable 
predictions; black-box models face adoption barriers. 
5. Validation & generalization: Models must be externally validated across sites and 
prospective clinical trials to ensure safety and efficacy. 
6. Integration with workflow: Predictions must be actionable and fit into clinician 
workflows; avoid alert fatigue. 
Steps to develop ML-based healthcare system 
1. Clinical need articulation: Define clinical question, outcome definition, and success 
metrics in collaboration with clinicians. 
2. Data collection & governance: Secure access to clinical data, ensure proper consent, 
and set up data governance. 
3. Data preprocessing & labeling: Clean data, standardize codes, and create high
quality labeled datasets (e.g., radiologist-annotated images). 
4. Exploratory analysis & feature engineering: Understand distributions, confounders, 
and design features (temporal aggregates, imaging features). 
5. Model development: Train models with cross-validation, use domain-aware 
architectures (e.g., CNNs for images, temporal networks for EHR), incorporate 
uncertainty estimates. 
6. Rigorous evaluation: Use clinically relevant metrics (sensitivity, specificity, PPV), 
subgroup analysis, calibration checks, and external validation cohorts. 
7. Clinical validation: Prospective studies, randomized controlled trials, or pilot 
deployments with clinician feedback. 
8. Regulatory submission & ethical review: Document performance, failure modes, 
and mitigation strategies for regulatory approval if required. 
9. Deployment & integration: Seamless EHR integration, decision support UI, human
in-loop mechanisms. 
10. Monitoring & maintenance: Post-deployment surveillance for drift, adverse events, 
continuous retraining with new labeled data, and periodic re-validation. 
Best practices: multidisciplinary teams (clinicians + data scientists + ethicists), external 
validation, transparency about limitations, and conservative deployment in high-stakes 
settings.

performance.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the main differences between generative models and discriminative models with suitable examples.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Definition 
 Generative Models learn the joint probability distribution P(X, Y). 
 Discriminative Models learn the conditional probability P(Y | X). 
Generative Models 
 They model how data is generated. 
 Can create new samples. 
Examples: 
 Naïve Bayes 
 Gaussian Mixture Models 
 GANs 
 Variational Autoencoders (VAE) 
Discriminative Models 
 They classify or predict labels directly. 
 Focus only on the decision boundary. 
Examples: 
 Logistic Regression 
 SVM 
 Random Forest 
 Neural Networks 
Key Differences 
1. Learning Objective: Model data distribution vs. classify. 
2. Data Generation: Only generative models generate samples. 
3. Complexity: Generative models are often more complex. 
4. Performance: Discriminative models often outperform for classification tasks. 
5. Flexibility: Generative usable for tasks like image generation, missing value filling, 
etc.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the role of validation sets in machine learning. Why is validation important,and how does it prevent model overfitting?
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
? 
Answer 
Definition / role: A validation set is a portion of labeled data reserved during development 
to evaluate model generalization while tuning hyperparameters and making decisions about 
model architecture or early-stopping. It is distinct from the training set (used to fit model 
parameters) and the test set (used for final evaluation). 
Why validation is important 
1. Hyperparameter selection: Validation performance guides selection of learning rate, 
regularization strength, depth/width, and other settings without peeking at the test set. 
2. Model comparison: It provides an unbiased comparison between candidate 
models/architectures before final evaluation. 
3. Early stopping: Monitoring validation loss/metric prevents training beyond the point 
where generalization degrades. 
4. Detects overfitting: A divergence between improving training metric and worsening 
validation metric signals that model is fitting noise. 
5. Robust model choices: Using cross-validation or repeated splits gives more reliable 
estimates and reduces variance in hyperparameter choices.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the main differences between generative models and discriminative models with suitable examples.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Answer 
Definitions 
 Generative models: Model the joint distribution P(X,Y)P(X,Y)P(X,Y) or 
P(X)P(X)P(X) and can generate new samples. They capture how data is generated. 
 Discriminative models: Model the conditional distribution P(Y∣X)P(Y|X)P(Y∣X) or 
directly the decision boundary f(X)f(X)f(X) for prediction; they optimize 
classification/regression performance. 
Key differences 
1. Objective: Generative → model data generation; Discriminative → directly predict 
labels. 
2. Probability learned: Generative → P(X,Y)P(X,Y)P(X,Y) or P(X)P(X)P(X); 
Discriminative → P(Y∣X)P(Y|X)P(Y∣X). 
3. Sample generation: Generative can synthesize realistic samples (images, text); 
discriminative cannot. 
4. Complexity & data requirements: Generative often require more modeling capacity 
and data for realistic generation; discriminative models can be simpler for predictive 
tasks. 
5. Typical use-cases: Generative for data augmentation, simulation, unsupervised 
pretraining; discriminative for classification and regression with high accuracy. 
Examples 
 Generative: Naive Bayes (models class-conditional densities), Gaussian Mixture 
Models, Variational Autoencoders (VAE), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). 
 Discriminative: Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random 
Forests, Feedforward Neural Networks fine-tuned for classification. 
Practical note: In classification tasks with abundant labeled data, discriminative models 
often yield better accuracy; when you need to model the data distribution or generate 
samples, generative models are appropriate.

What is anomaly detection? Discuss its importance and common applications in real

Answer 
Importance 
1. Early warning: Detects faults, intrusions, or failures before they escalate. 
2. Risk management: Identifies fraudulent, erroneous, or malicious events that could 
cause financial or reputational damage. 
3. Safety & reliability: In industrial/medical contexts, catching anomalies can prevent 
accidents or patient harm. 
4. Operational efficiency: Helps find sensor malfunctions, data pipeline errors, and 
unusual system states that require corrective action. 
Common applications 
 Finance: Credit card fraud detection, anti-money laundering (unusual transaction 
patterns). 
 Cybersecurity: Intrusion and anomaly detection in network traffic, user behavior 
analytics. 
 Industry / Manufacturing: Predictive maintenance — detect abnormal 
vibration/temperature before machine failure. 
 Healthcare: Detect abnormal lab results, sepsis onset, or anomalous patient vitals. 
 Cloud/IT Operations: Detect traffic spikes, unusual API calls, or log anomalies 
indicative of incidents. 
 IoT & Sensors: Identify faulty sensors or environmental anomalies (e.g., sudden 
pollution spikes). 
Typical approaches 
 Statistical: Z-score, Gaussian models, control charts. 
 Proximity/density: k-NN, Local Outlier Factor, Isolation Forest. 
 Reconstruction-based: Autoencoders, PCA residuals — anomalies have high 
reconstruction error. 
 Time-series methods: Change-point detection, forecasting residuals, sequence models 
(LSTM) for temporal anomalies.

? 
Answer 
Definition: Model interpretability is the extent to which a human can understand the cause 
of a decision made by a model — either globally (how the model behaves overall) or locally 
(why a single prediction was made). 
Why interpretability matters 
1. Trust & adoption: Users and stakeholders trust models they can understand. 
2. Regulatory compliance: Finance, healthcare, insurance and other regulated sectors 
require explanations for automated decisions. 
3. Accountability & auditability: Interpretability enables tracing decisions, attributing 
responsibility, and performing audits. 
4. Bias detection & fairness: Explanations reveal when models rely on protected or 
proxy features, enabling mitigation. 
5. Debugging & improvement: Interpretability helps identify data issues, spurious 
correlations, or model failure modes. 
Industries requiring interpretability 
 Healthcare: Clinicians need understandable rationale (e.g., key features leading to 
diagnosis). 
 Finance: Lending decisions, credit scoring must be explainable to customers and 
regulators. 
 Insurance: Risk assessment and pricing decisions need justification. 
 Legal & Governance: Automated decisions affecting rights or liberty require 
transparent reasoning. 
 Aerospace/Automotive (safety-critical): Explanations help ensure safe behavior and 
root-cause analysis. 
Methods for interpretability 
 Model-intrinsic: Use inherently interpretable models (linear models, decision trees, 
rule lists). 
 Post-hoc explainers: LIME (local surrogate), SHAP (Shapley value explanations), 
Partial Dependence Plots, saliency maps (for vision). 
 Counterfactuals: Show minimal changes to input that would change output — useful 
for recourse.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Explain the role of Data Preprocessing in building ML models. Discuss key steps such as data cleaning, encoding, transformation, and handling outliers.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Answer 
Definition / purpose: Data preprocessing converts raw, noisy, and heterogeneous inputs into 
a consistent, high-quality dataset that a model can learn from effectively. Preprocessing often 
has larger impact on final performance than choice of algorithm. 
Key steps 
1. Data cleaning: Remove duplicates, correct typos and inconsistent formats, handle 
missing values (imputation strategies: mean/median/mode, KNN, model-based, or 
explicit missing indicator). 
2. Encoding categorical variables: Transform categories to numeric — one-hot for 
low-cardinality, ordinal encoding where order matters, frequency/target encoding or 
learned embeddings for high-cardinality features (use out-of-fold schemes to avoid 
leakage). 
3. Feature scaling & transformation: Standardization (zero mean/unit variance) or 
Min-Max scaling for gradient-based models; log or Box–Cox transforms to reduce 
skew; power transforms to stabilize variance. 
4. Handling outliers: Detect with IQR, z-score, or robust methods; treat by capping 
(winsorization), transformation, winsorization, or removing if erroneous; consider 
domain knowledge. 
5. Feature engineering: Create domain-specific features (ratios, interactions, 
aggregations, lag features for time series). 
6. Dimensionality reduction & sparsity handling: PCA, feature selection, hashing for 
high-cardinality sparse features. 
7. Pipelineization & reproducibility: Use pipelines to ensure identical preprocessing in 
training and production and avoid target leakage. 
Why it matters 
 Reduces noise and bias; improves convergence and model stability; reduces risk of 
data leakage; can dramatically increase predictive power with well-engineered 
features.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 2. Describe the importance of Model Evaluation Metrics. Compare accuracy, precision,recall, and Fl-score, and explain when each metric should be used.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Answer 
Overview: Choosing appropriate evaluation metrics aligns model optimization with business 
goals and risk profiles. A single metric can be misleading; choose metrics mindful of class 
imbalance and costs of different error types. 
Metrics 
1. Accuracy: (TP+TN)/Total(TP+TN)/Total(TP+TN)/Total. Good for balanced datasets 
where false positives and false negatives have similar costs. Poor choice for 
imbalanced datasets (e.g., 99% negative → trivial high accuracy). 
2. Precision (Positive Predictive Value): TP/(TP+FP)TP/(TP+FP)TP/(TP+FP). High 
precision means when model predicts positive, it is usually correct. Use when false 
positives are costly (e.g., spam incorrectly flagged as important email, unnecessary 
medical procedure). 
3. Recall (Sensitivity, True Positive Rate): TP/(TP+FN)TP/(TP+FN)TP/(TP+FN). 
High recall means model finds most real positives. Use when false negatives are costly 
(e.g., disease screening, fraud detection where missing real cases is dangerous). 
4. F1-score: Harmonic mean of precision and recall. Use when you need a balance and 
classes are imbalanced; gives a single-number trade-off. 
5. Additional: ROC-AUC for ranking ability; PR-AUC when positives rare; calibration 
measures for probabilistic predictions; cost-sensitive metrics or custom business utility 
functions when errors have different costs. 
When to choose 
 Accuracy: only when class balance and equal error cost. 
 Precision prioritized: when action on positives is expensive or harmful. 
 Recall prioritized: when catching positives is critical for safety. 
 F1-score: when both precision and recall matter and dataset is imbalanced.

Stages & purpose

4. Feature engineering: Create informative features (e.g., recency, frequency, monetary

5. Model development: Select algorithms, train models, tune hyperparameters using

9. Retraining & iteration: Periodically retrain using fresh labeled data, update features, 
and deploy new versions with rollback safety. 
Example flow: Fraud detection system — define fraud types → collect transaction logs → 
engineer device/browser features → train ensemble model → evaluate precision/recall → 
deploy as real-time scoring API with human-in-loop review for high-risk transactions →

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 5. What is Unsupervised Learning? Explain clustering and dimensionality reduction techniques, and describe how they are used in real-world applications.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Answer 
Definition: Unsupervised learning finds patterns and structure in unlabeled data, such as 
grouping similar items or finding compact representations. 
Clustering 
 K-means: Partitions data into k clusters by minimizing within-cluster variance; fast 
but assumes spherical clusters. 
 DBSCAN: Density-based clustering that detects arbitrary-shaped clusters and noise 
(good for spatial data). 
 Hierarchical clustering: Builds dendrogram to view cluster relationships; useful 
when cluster granularity matters. 
Dimensionality reduction 
 PCA: Linear projection that captures directions of maximum variance, useful for 
denoising and feature reduction. 
 t-SNE / UMAP: Nonlinear embeddings for visualization preserving local 
neighborhood structure. 
 Autoencoders: Neural network-based compression and denoising. 
Real-world applications 
 Customer segmentation: Clustering customers by behavior for targeted marketing. 
 Anomaly detection: Identify outliers as rare clusters or noise. 
 Document clustering: Group similar documents or news for topic discovery. 
 Visualization: High-dimensional gene-expression data visualized with t-SNE/UMAP 
for biological insights. 
 Compression: Reduce features for downstream supervised training or edge 
deployment.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: 1. Discuss the challenges of deploying ML models in real-world environments. Explain issues like data drift, model monitoring, scalability, hardware constraints, security risks, and continuous retraining .
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Discuss the challenges of deploying ML models in real-world environments. Explain 
issues like data drift, model monitoring, scalability, hardware constraints, security 
risks, and continuous retraining. 
Answer 
Overview: Deployment moves models from research into operation; this phase introduces 
engineering, operational, and governance complexities that can erode initial performance if 
unaddressed. 
Key challenges & solutions 
1. Data drift & distributional shift 
o Problem: Input or label distributions change over time (covariate, concept, 
target drift), degrading model accuracy. 
o Mitigation: Continuous monitoring of input statistics, PSI/K-S tests, model 
performance metrics; set retrain triggers; use adaptive models or ensemble of 
short/long-term models. 
2. Model monitoring & observability 
o Problem: Silent failures, calibration shifts, or rising error rates go unnoticed 
without monitoring. 
o Mitigation: Instrument logging of inputs/predictions/confidences, dashboards 
for metrics (latency, throughput, accuracy), alerting, and canary/blue-green 
deployments. 
3. Scalability & latency 
o Problem: Production loads and peak traffic require autoscaling and low-latency 
predictions. 
o Mitigation: Use optimized serving (TensorFlow Serving, TorchServe), model 
batching, caching, quantization, and horizontally scalable microservices. 
4. Hardware & resource constraints 
o Problem: Edge or mobile deployments have limited CPU, memory, and power. 
o Mitigation: Model compression (pruning, distillation, quantization), lightweight 
architectures (MobileNet), offloading heavy tasks to cloud. 
5. Security & robustness 
o Problem: Adversarial examples, model inversion, data poisoning, and API 
abuse threaten integrity. 
o Mitigation: Adversarial training, input sanitization, rate-limiting, authentication, 
differential privacy, monitoring for anomalous queries. 
6. Continuous retraining & lifecycle management 
o Problem: Model staleness; repeated retraining can introduce regressions. 
o Mitigation: MLOps pipelines for versioning data/models (DVC, MLflow), 
reproducible experiments, automated tests, CI/CD for models, and staged 
rollouts with performance gates. 
7. Governance, ethics & compliance 
o Problem: Regulatory requirements (GDPR, HIPAA), explainability, fairness 
audits. 
o Mitigation: Logging for audit trails, interpretable models or explanations, 
fairness testing across subgroups, and documented risk assessments. 
8. Integration & business alignment 
o Problem: Models must fit workflows and deliver measurable business value. 
o Mitigation: Prototype with product teams, measure business KPIs, include 
humans-in-loop for critical decisions. 
Conclusion: Robust deployment requires an ecosystem of monitoring, automation, 
governance, and engineering best practices, not just a performant model.
