rubric_with_answers.question_text: a. Explain the concept of learning bias in machine learning.Discuss different sources of bias and their impact on model generalization.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Learning bias is when the computer is lazy and only learns the simple stuff. It's like having a favorite food 
and ignoring all the other food. 
 Concept: Bias is the error from the model being too stupid. It makes too many assumptions, like 
assuming everything is a straight line when it's not. 
 Sources of Bias: 
1. Too Simple Model: If you use a basic model (like a one-layer model) for a very complicated 
problem (like recognizing faces), it has high bias. 
2. Bad Training Data: If you only show the model pictures of cats and then ask it to find a dog, 
that's a bias problem in the data. 
 Impact on Generalization: High bias causes underfitting. The model fails badly on the training 
data, so of course it will fail on the new test data too. It just misses the whole point of the problem.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: b. Describe the role of assumptions in machine learning algorithms.Explain how assumptions influence model selection and performance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Assumptions are just things we hope are true about the data. We have to make them, or the computer can't 
even start. 
 Role of Assumptions: They help the computer decide what kind of model to use. If we assume the 
data is simple, we pick a simple model. 
 How Assumptions Influence Selection: 
o If we assume everything is in a line, we use a model called Linear Regression. That's a good 
assumption because those models are fast. 
o If we assume things are very complicated and non-linear, we use a big model like a Neural 
Network, but then it gets slow and hungry for power. 
 Performance Influence: If your assumption is wrong (e.g., you assume a straight line when the data 
is a curve), the model will be high bias and perform terribly. If you don't assume anything, the model 
is too flexible and ends up just memorizing the training data, which is also bad performance.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: c. Explain the concept of generalization in machine learning.Discuss why a model that performs well on training data may fail on unseen data.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Generalization is about making sure the model is not just a one-trick pony. 
 Concept: Generalization is the ability of the model to work well on new data it has never seen 
before. If the training score is high, the generalization score should also be high. 
 Why Failure on Unseen Data Occurs: This is the classic problem of overfitting. 
1. Memorizing Noise: The model is too complicated and learns the tiny mistakes and noise in 
the training data, instead of the main pattern. It's like a student memorizing the textbook 
word-for-word but not understanding the concepts. 
2. Too Small Training Set: If the training data is too small, the model doesn't see enough 
variety, so when the new test data comes along, it's surprised and doesn't know what to do. 
3. Data Change: When the model is deployed, the real-world data starts changing (this is called 
Concept Drift), making the model's old rules incorrect for the new reality.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: d. Discuss the importance of data quality in machine learning systems.Explain how noise, missing values, and inconsistencies affect learning outcomes.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Data quality is crucial in machine learning (ML) because "garbage in, garbage out" applies: poor data (noise, 
missing values, inconsistencies) leads to inaccurate, biased, and unreliable models, causing poor 
performance, biased decisions, and wasted resources, whereas clean, consistent data enables accurate pattern 
recognition, better generalization, and fair outcomes, making data quality foundational for effective AI. 
Noise (irrelevant data), missing values (incomplete records), and inconsistencies (format/logic errors) distort 
patterns, leading to higher error rates, biased predictions (especially for minority classes), and models that 
fail to generalize, requiring extensive cleaning and validation for fairness and accuracy.  
Importance of Data Quality 
 Accuracy & Reliability: High-quality data helps models learn true patterns, leading to better predictions in 
real-world scenarios. 
 Efficiency: Clean data reduces time-consuming preprocessing, speeding up model development and 
deployment. 
 Fairness & Ethics: Addresses biases in data, preventing discriminatory outcomes and ensuring models are 
equitable, especially in sensitive areas like healthcare or justice. 
 Trust & Explainability: Well-documented, clean data builds trust and helps stakeholders understand model 
decisions.  
How Data Issues Affect Learning Outcomes 
 Noise (Irrelevant/Erroneous Data): 
o Impact: Distorts the true signal, confusing the model and reducing its ability to find meaningful patterns, 
leading to lower accuracy and poor generalization. 
o Example: Random errors in customer ratings causing a recommendation system to suggest irrelevant 
products. 
 Missing Values: 
o Impact: Creates gaps in understanding, forcing models to rely on incomplete information, potentially 
leading to skewed results or needing imputation methods (like mean/median) that might introduce bias. 
o Example: Many missing age entries in a dataset skewing age-based predictions. 
 Inconsistencies & Bias: 
o Impact: Inconsistent formats (e.g., "USA" vs. "United States") or biased labels (unfairly applied labels) 
teach the model incorrect relationships, amplifying systemic inequalities and resulting in biased, unfair, or 
discriminatory decisions. 
o Example: A loan application model trained on historically biased data might unfairly deny loans to certain 
demographics. 
 Data Imbalance: 
o Impact: Models favor majority classes, performing poorly on underrepresented (minority) classes, leading 
to biased predictions and ineffective solutions for those groups. 
o Example: A fraud detection model trained mostly on non-fraudulent transactions might miss most actual 
fraud cases.  
By proactively managing these data quality issues through cleaning, imputation, bias mitigation, and 
continuous monitoring, developers can build robust, accurate, and fair machine learning systems.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: a. Explain the concept of learning bias in machine learning.Discuss different sources of bias and their impact on model generalization.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Learning bias (or algorithmic bias) in machine learning refers to the systematic and repeatable errors in a 
learning process that lead to favoring certain outcomes or conclusions over others. Crucially, this concept 
exists at two distinct levels: Statistical Bias (part of the bias-variance tradeoff) and Societal/Ethical Bias (a 
reflection of real-world prejudice). 
1. Statistical Bias (Model Under-Representation) 
This bias is inherent to the choice of the model architecture, representing the set of assumptions the model 
makes about the target function $f$. 
 Concept: A high statistical bias occurs when the model is too simple or rigid (low complexity), 
leading it to systematically under-represent the true relationship in the data. 
 Source: 
o Model Selection: Choosing a linear model (e.g., Logistic Regression) to solve a complex, 
non-linear classification problem. 
o Over-Regularization: Applying excessively strong regularization (e.g., a very high 
$\lambda$ in Lasso), forcing the model coefficients toward zero and simplifying the function 
too much. 
 Impact on Generalization: High statistical bias leads to underfitting. The model performs poorly 
on both training and unseen test data because it fails to capture the underlying signal, resulting in a 
high, irreducible systematic error. 
2. Societal/Ethical Bias (Data Representation) 
This bias reflects unwanted systemic prejudices or skewed demographics present in the real world, which 
are then encoded into the model via the data. 
 Sources of Ethical Bias: 
o Selection Bias (Sampling Bias): When the training data is not representative of the real
world population the model will be deployed on. For instance, training a facial recognition 
model predominantly on light-skinned faces will cause it to perform poorly on darker-skinned 
faces. 
o Measurement Bias (Proxy Bias): When a sensitive feature (like race) is excluded, but the 
model learns to use a strongly correlated, non-sensitive feature (like ZIP code or purchasing 
habits) as an unethical proxy. 
o Historical Bias: Bias embedded in society's history, where outcomes reflect past 
discrimination (e.g., training a loan approval model on historical data where loans were 
unfairly denied to certain groups). 
 Impact on Generalization: Ethical bias leads to unfair generalization. The model performs 
accurately for the majority group present in the training data but systematically discriminates against 
or fails for minority or disadvantaged groups, leading to inequitable real-world consequences.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: b. Describe the role of assumptions in machine learning algorithms.Explain how assumptions influence model selection and performance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
The role of assumptions in machine learning is central to the learning process; they are the necessary 
structural and statistical constraints that algorithms impose on the problem space to make the complex task 
of finding the true target function $f$ computationally tractable. This is encapsulated by the No Free Lunch 
theorem, which states that no single algorithm is universally superior across all possible problems—success 
depends on the degree to which the algorithm's assumptions align with the underlying structure of the data. 
How Assumptions Influence Model Selection 
Assumptions act as a guiding principle, influencing the choice between different models based on the nature 
of the data: 
1. Linearity: 
o Assumption: The relationship between features and the target variable can be approximated 
by a straight line or a hyperplane. 
o Models: Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, Linear SVM. 
o Selection Influence: Selected when the feature space is believed to be approximately 
separable by a line, prioritizing speed and interpretability. 
2. Independence (Parametric Assumptions): 
o Assumption: Features are independent of each other given the class. 
o Models: Naive Bayes. 
o Selection Influence: Chosen for high-dimensional, text-based data where speed is critical, 
despite the assumption of independence often being violated in reality. 
3. Local Smoothness (Non-Parametric Assumptions): 
o Assumption: Data points that are close to each other in the feature space are likely to have 
the same output value. 
o Models: K-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN), Decision Trees. 
o Selection Influence: Chosen when the relationship is complex, non-linear, and the decision 
boundary is expected to be localized. 
How Assumptions Influence Performance 
The alignment between the model's assumptions and the true data generating process dictates performance: 
 Correct Alignment: When assumptions align with the data (e.g., using a Linear Regression model 
on truly linear data), the model benefits from high statistical efficiency (low bias) and performs 
optimally, generalizing well. 
 Misalignment (High Bias): If assumptions are too simplistic (e.g., assuming linearity for 
exponential data), the model suffers from high statistical bias and underfitting, systematically 
failing to model the data accurately. 
 Relaxed Assumptions (High Variance): Non-parametric models (like k-NN or unpruned Decision 
Trees) have fewer explicit assumptions, giving them high flexibility. While this reduces bias, it 
increases variance (sensitivity to training data noise), often leading to overfitting.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: c. Explain the concept of generalization in machine learning.Discuss why a model that performs well on training data may fail on unseen data.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Generalization is the measure of a machine learning model's ability to accurately predict or classify 
outcomes for new, previously unseen data, having only been exposed to a finite training set. A model is said 
to generalize well if its performance metrics (e.g., accuracy, F1-score) on the independent test set closely 
mirror its performance on the training set. 
The Goal: Generalization Error $\approx$ Training Error 
The ultimate objective in machine learning is to minimize the Generalization Error (the expected error on 
all possible data points, often approximated by the Test Error). Achieving good generalization implies that 
the model has learned the underlying true signal or functional mapping in the data, rather than simply 
memorizing the noise and peculiarities of the training samples. 
Reasons for Failure on Unseen Data (Poor Generalization) 
A high training accuracy coupled with a low test accuracy signifies a large Generalization Gap and is the 
classic symptom of overfitting. This occurs primarily due to the following reasons: 
1. Overfitting to Noise (High Variance): 
o The model (e.g., a deep Neural Network or unpruned Decision Tree) is too complex relative 
to the size and quality of the training data. 
o The model learns the random errors, outliers, and noise specific to the training set. This 
memorization capacity, which is rewarded during training, makes the model brittle and 
incapable of handling the slight statistical variations present in the unseen test set. 
2. Insufficient or Non-Representative Data: 
o Data Scarcity: If the training set is too small, it may not adequately cover the feature space, 
leading the model to make wild extrapolations for unseen regions. 
o Sampling Bias: If the training data is not a statistically representative sample of the overall 
population (target domain), the learned function will be biased toward the training 
distribution and fail to generalize to the actual operational environment. 
3. Concept Drift: 
o Although often considered a deployment issue, it highlights a failure of generalization over 
time. The fundamental relationship between the input features ($X$) and the target variable 
($Y$) changes over time (e.g., customer behavior shifts), rendering the old model's learned 
rules invalid for the new, unseen data stream.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: d. Discuss the importance of data quality in machine learning systems.Explain how noise, missing values, and inconsistencies affect learning outcomes.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Data quality is the most critical determinant of a machine learning system's success. As the famous adage 
goes, "Garbage In, Garbage Out" (GIGO). Low-quality data directly impacts the model's ability to learn 
the true underlying patterns, leading to biased, unstable, and ultimately non-deployable systems. 
1. Noise 
Noise refers to random errors or unwanted random variance in the measured values of features or the target 
variable. 
 Effect on Learning Outcomes: Noise increases the model's variance. Complex models, particularly 
those prone to overfitting (like deep neural networks or k-NN), will attempt to model this noise as a 
signal. This results in the model having poor generalization, as it learns random deviations specific to 
the training set, causing unstable predictions on unseen data. 
2. Missing Values 
Missing values occur when data is not recorded for one or more features in a sample. 
 Effect on Learning Outcomes: 
o Bias: Simply deleting records with missing data (list-wise deletion) can introduce significant 
selection bias if the data is not missing completely at random (MCAR). The model is then 
trained on a skewed, non-representative subset of the population. 
o Distortion: Using simple imputation methods (e.g., mean or median) distorts the true 
distribution of the feature and shrinks the true variance, leading to an artificially confident 
model. Advanced methods like predictive imputation are often required to mitigate this 
impact. 
3. Inconsistencies 
Inconsistencies involve contradictions in data formats, codes, or definitions across different records or 
datasets. 
 Effect on Learning Outcomes: 
o Model Confusion: Inconsistencies (e.g., 'NY' vs. 'New York' vs. 'N.Y.') are interpreted by 
the model as distinct categories, leading to unnecessary data sparsity and inefficient use of 
features. 
o Incorrect Relationships: Contradictory records (e.g., a patient recorded as male but having a 
historical record of pregnancy) corrupt the true functional relationship, undermining the 
model's ability to learn reliable dependencies between variables.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: f. Describe the ethical considerations involved in developing machine learning systems.Explain issues such as fairness, transparency, accountability, and privacy.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
The development and deployment of machine learning systems introduce complex ethical challenges that 
necessitate governance, technical diligence, and careful policy setting. These systems must be engineered 
not only for performance but also for societal benefit. 
1. Fairness and Bias 
 Explanation: Fairness refers to the principle that a machine learning model should not exhibit 
prejudice against individuals or groups based on sensitive characteristics (e.g., race, gender, 
religion). This is primarily compromised by Selection Bias or Historical Bias in the training data. 
 Ethical Issue: An unfair model can perpetuate and amplify real-world inequalities (e.g., an 
automated hiring tool systematically penalizing female candidates due to historical data skew). The 
definition of fairness itself is debated (e.g., equal opportunity vs. equal accuracy). 
2. Transparency and Explainability 
 Explanation: Transparency (or Explainability) is the ability to understand and articulate the internal 
logic and rationale behind a model's prediction. This is particularly difficult with high-capacity 
"black box" models like Deep Neural Networks. 
 Ethical Issue: Lack of transparency prevents stakeholders from determining why a decision was 
made. If a loan is denied or a medical diagnosis is given, the inability to explain the reason hinders 
redress, trust, and debugging for bias. Techniques like LIME and SHAP are used to address this. 
3. Accountability 
 Explanation: Accountability defines which party is responsible when a machine learning system 
causes harm or makes a costly error. This involves identifying the responsible agent—the data 
collector, the algorithm developer, the deploying entity, or the user. 
 Ethical Issue: In complex systems (e.g., autonomous vehicles), distributing liability is complicated. 
Clear lines of responsibility must be established to ensure that recourse and compensation are 
possible when algorithmic failures occur. 
4. Privacy 
 Explanation: Privacy relates to the protection of sensitive personal identifiable information (PII) 
used to train models. The risk is that the model itself might unintentionally memorize and reveal 
details about specific individuals in the training data. 
 Ethical Issue: Training models on sensitive data (e.g., medical records, financial history) risks data 
leakage. Privacy-enhancing technologies, such as Federated Learning (training models locally 
without sharing raw data) and Differential Privacy (adding controlled noise during training), are 
necessary to mitigate this risk.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: b. Describe the role of assumptions in machine learning algorithms.Explain how assumptions influence model selection and performance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Assumptions are the rules or beliefs that a machine learning algorithm follows about the data. Every model 
has them, and they are important for making the learning process work. 
Role of Assumptions 
Assumptions help simplify the real-world problem so that a computer can actually solve it in a reasonable 
amount of time. Since we can't look at all possible math functions, assumptions narrow down the choices. 
 Example 1: Linear Models: These models assume that the output is simply a straight line 
relationship of the inputs. 
 Example 2: Naive Bayes: This model assumes that all the features (columns) are independent of 
each other, which is almost never true in real life, but the model still works sometimes because of 
this assumption. 
Influence on Model Selection and Performance 
1. Model Selection: We pick a model based on what we assume the data looks like. If we think the 
relationship is simple, we pick a Linear Regression model (high assumption, easy to calculate). If we 
think the relationship is complex, we pick a Neural Network (low assumption, high computation). 
2. Performance: If your assumptions are correct (the data really is linear, and you chose a Linear 
Regression model), the model will be very fast and perform well. But if your assumption is wrong 
(you chose a linear model for curvy data), the model performance will be low due to high bias. 
Choosing the right assumptions is the first step to good performance.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: c. Explain the concept of generalization in machine learning.Discuss why a model that performs well on training data may fail on unseen data.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Generalization is the test of a model's true usefulness. It's about how well the model takes what it learned in 
class (training data) and applies it to a pop quiz (unseen data). 
Concept of Generalization 
A model is said to have good generalization if the score it gets on the test data is similar to the score it got 
on the training data. This means the model learned the main pattern of the data, not just the specific 
answers. 
Why a Model Fails on Unseen Data 
This failure is the definition of overfitting. A model that scores $99\%$ on training but $50\%$ on test data 
has overfit. 
1. Memorizing Noise: The model is usually too complex (too many layers or parameters). Instead of 
learning the signal, it memorizes the random noise and tiny errors that are unique to the training set. 
When it sees the new, unseen data, that noise isn't there, and the model's memorized answers are 
wrong. 
2. Unrepresentative Training Data: If the training data didn't cover all the possibilities (it didn't show 
enough variety), then the model doesn't know how to handle the new variations that show up in the 
test set. For instance, training a model only on sunny day pictures will make it fail completely on a 
cloudy or snowy day. 
3. Data Leakage: Sometimes, the test data accidentally influences the training process (this is called 
data leakage). This gives the model a false, high training score, but its real-world performance is 
terrible.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: d. Discuss the importance of data quality in machine learning systems.Explain how noise, missing values, and inconsistencies affect learning outcomes.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Data quality is the foundation of machine learning. If the data quality is low, the whole system collapses. 
This is why everyone says, "Garbage In, Garbage Out." 
Importance of Data Quality 
High-quality data is accurate, complete, and consistent. If the data is bad, the model learns the wrong 
rules, and the final predictions can be unreliable, leading to bad business decisions or harmful consequences 
in healthcare or finance. 
Effects on Learning Outcomes 
1. Noise: Noise is random corruption in the data (like a typo in a measurement). The machine learning 
model treats this noise as a real pattern it must learn, which makes the model more complicated than 
necessary. This leads to overfitting and higher model variance, meaning it performs unstable on 
new data. 
2. Missing Values: These are blank spots. If you delete all rows with missing data, you might throw 
away important information and train the model on a biased subset. If you fill the blanks with a 
simple number (like the average), you make the data artificially look the same, which confuses the 
model by reducing the real variation. 
3. Inconsistencies: This is when the same information is recorded in different formats (e.g., City 'LA', 
'L.A.', 'Los Angeles'). The model thinks these are three different features, which increases the overall 
complexity and makes the training process much slower and less effective.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: e. Explain the difference between shallow learning and deep learning approaches.Discuss their characteristics, strengths, and limitations in theory.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
The main difference is in the complexity and how they handle the features of the data. 
In Theory: Deep learning aims to mimic the way the human brain processes information through multiple 
layers of abstraction, making it much better at handling raw, unstructured data without human pre
processing. Shallow learning is more constrained but is still better for simple problems where you need a 
quick, explainable answer. 
f. Describe the ethical considerations involved in developing machine learning systems. 
Explain issues such as fairness, transparency, accountability, and privacy. 
Since machine learning is used for important decisions (like who gets a loan or who gets health care), we 
have to make sure the systems are ethical and don't cause harm. 
1. Fairness and Bias: 
o Issue: The model must be fair and not discriminate against groups based on things like 
gender, race, or age. 
o Explanation: If the data used to train the system is biased (e.g., it only shows successful 
white men in a job), the model will learn that bias and automatically treat women and 
minorities unfairly, making the discrimination systematic. 
2. Transparency: 
o Issue: We need to know and understand how the model makes a decision. 
o Explanation: Many deep learning models are like a "black box"—you put data in and get a 
prediction out, but you can't see the thousands of steps in between. For high-stakes decisions, 
this is a problem because if a person is rejected for a job, they have a right to know the 
reason, and the black box can't give a clear one. 
3. Accountability: 
o Issue: Someone needs to be held responsible when the machine learning system makes a 
serious mistake or causes harm. 
o Explanation: If an autonomous vehicle causes an accident, is it the programmer's fault, the 
company that deployed the system, or the data collected? Clear accountability structures 
must be in place so that victims can get justice. 
4. Privacy: 
o Issue: We must protect the private, personal data used to train the models. 
o Explanation: Machine learning models are trained on huge amounts of user data (like health 
records or location history). If the model isn't protected, it could accidentally reveal sensitive 
information about one of the people in the training set. Techniques like Differential Privacy 
are used to scramble or hide the individual data points.

it overfits to the training data. 
 Sources of Bias:

on that brand. 
2. Historical Bias: This is when the model is trained on very old data, like from before the year 
2000, so it doesn't know about current trends. 
 Impact on Generalization: High bias means the model has high variance, so it performs terribly on 
the new data.

 Role of Assumptions: They let the computer know how long it will take to train the model. Simple 
models assume the training will be fast. 
 Influence on Model Selection: 
o If we assume the data is round (circular), we use Logistic Regression. 
o If we assume the data is very messy, we use a Linear Model. 
 Performance Influence: If you use a model with too many assumptions, it will become a black box 
and you won't be able to explain the results. If you use a model with no assumptions, it will underfit.

rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Learning Bias in Machine Learning 
Learning bias refers to systematic errors introduced into a machine learning model that cause it to favor 
certain outcomes or patterns over others, often leading to inaccurate or unfair predictions. 
Sources of Learning Bias 
1. Sampling Bias – Training data does not represent the true population. 
2. Selection Bias – Data is collected in a non-random manner. 
3. Measurement Bias – Errors in data measurement or feature recording. 
4. Labeling Bias – Subjective or incorrect labeling by humans. 
5. Historical Bias – Past societal inequalities reflected in data. 
6. Algorithmic Bias – Bias introduced by model design or learning strategy. 
7. Feature Bias – Incomplete or biased feature selection. 
Impact on Model Generalization 
8. Models fail to generalize to unseen data. 
9. Predictions become unreliable and unfair. 
10. Bias reduces robustness and trust in ML systems.

Role of Assumptions

and guide how algorithms model patterns. 
Common Assumptions in ML Algorithms 
1. Linearity Assumption – Output is a linear combination of inputs. 
2. Independence Assumption – Features are statistically independent. 
3. Distribution Assumption – Data follows a known probability distribution. 
4. Stationarity Assumption – Data characteristics remain constant. 
Influence on Model Selection and Performance 
5. Strong assumptions reduce model complexity. 
6. Incorrect assumptions cause underfitting. 
7. Simple models rely on strong assumptions. 
8. Complex models make fewer assumptions but risk overfitting. 
9. Assumptions guide algorithm choice. 
10. Correct assumptions improve efficiency and generalization.

Explain the concept of the loss function in machine learning. Discuss the mathematical 
properties of effective loss functions and provide examples for different task types. 
A loss function (or cost function, objective function) is a quantitative measure of the penalty assigned to a 
machine learning model for inaccurate predictions during the training phase. It serves as the target for the 
optimization algorithm (e.g., gradient descent), which seeks to minimize this function by iteratively 
adjusting the model's parameters. 
Mathematical Properties of Effective Loss Functions 
An ideal loss function for use with gradient-based optimizers should possess the following properties: 
1. Differentiability and Smoothness: The function must be continuously differentiable across its 
domain. This is essential because the optimization process relies on calculating the gradient (the 
slope) with respect to the model parameters to determine the direction and magnitude of the update 
step. Non-smooth functions (like the 0/1 loss) cannot be used directly with gradient descent. 
2. Convexity (Ideally): A convex loss function guarantees that the optimization process, regardless of 
the starting point, will always converge to the global minimum. While many functions used in deep 
learning are non-convex, convexity provides the strongest theoretical guarantee for finding the 
optimal solution. 
3. Monotonicity (Intuitive Cost): The loss value should strictly increase as the distance between the 
prediction ($\hat{y}$) and the true value ($y$) increases. This ensures that larger errors are 
penalized more heavily. 
Examples for Different Task Types

rubric_with_answers.question_text: d. Discuss the importance of data quality in machine learning systems.Explain how noise, missing values, and inconsistencies affect learning outcomes.

Discuss the importance of data governance in machine learning projects. Explain how 
data lineage, access control, and quality monitoring contribute to responsible system 
development. 
Data Governance in the context of machine learning is the framework of rules, policies, and processes that 
define how data is acquired, stored, processed, accessed, and secured throughout the model's entire lifecycle. 
Its importance stems from the need to manage risk, ensure compliance (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA), maintain data 
integrity, and build user trust. 
How Governance Contributes to Responsible System Development 
1. Data Lineage (Traceability): 
o Contribution: Lineage is the complete historical record tracking the origin, transformations, 
and usage of every dataset. 
o Impact: It ensures reproducibility—the ability to recreate the exact training environment 
used for a specific model version. Crucially, it is vital for debugging bias or errors; if a 
model exhibits unfairness, lineage allows tracing the faulty outcome back to a specific data 
source, transformation script, or imputation technique. 
2. Access Control and Security: 
o Contribution: Policies that strictly define who can access what data, when, and for what 
purpose. This involves roles, permissions, and security measures like encryption and 
anonymization. 
o Impact: Directly manages privacy risk. Proper access control ensures that sensitive data 
(PII, confidential business records) is not mishandled, reducing the risk of data leakage or 
unauthorized use that could violate legal regulations or ethical standards. 
3. Quality Monitoring and Standardization: 
o Contribution: Continuous processes that validate data schemas, check for consistency (e.g., 
ensuring all date formats are the same), and actively monitor data drift and integrity issues in 
real-time. 
o Impact: Maintains the model's integrity and prevents Model Degradation. By catching 
issues like schema changes or sudden increases in missing values before they reach the 
model, data quality monitoring ensures that the training and inference data remain stable and 
reliable.

Explain the difference between supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning 
paradigms. Discuss their primary objective functions and typical applications. 
Machine learning approaches are broadly categorized into three paradigms based on the nature of the 
training signal (the feedback received by the algorithm). 
Objective Functions 
 Supervised Learning: A Loss Function (e.g., MSE, Cross-Entropy) is minimized to measure the 
error between prediction ($\hat{y}$) and truth ($y$). 
 Unsupervised Learning: A function is often maximized or minimized based on the method: 
o Clustering (e.g., K-Means): Minimize Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS). 
o PCA: Maximize the Variance Explained. 
 Reinforcement Learning: A Value Function or Q-Function is maximized to estimate the long
term return (discounted sum of future rewards) associated with a state or an action.

Explain the concept of the feature importance score. Discuss how different models 
calculate feature importance and why its interpretation requires caution. 
The Feature Importance Score is a numerical value assigned to each feature in a dataset that reflects the 
estimated contribution or relevance of that feature in determining the model's final prediction. It provides a 
means of local or global interpretability by highlighting which inputs the model prioritizes when mapping 
inputs to outputs. 
Calculation Methods by Model Type 
1. Linear Models (e.g., Logistic Regression, Ridge Regression): 
o Calculation: Importance is directly derived from the magnitude of the learned coefficients 
($\beta$). A larger absolute coefficient value indicates a stronger, more important influence 
on the prediction (assuming features have been standardized). 
o Interpretation: The sign of the coefficient reveals the direction of the influence (positive vs. 
negative correlation with the output). 
2. Tree-Based Models (e.g., Random Forest, Gradient Boosting): 
o Calculation: Importance is typically based on how often a feature is used to split the data and 
how much it reduces the impurity (Gini or Entropy) or loss when it is used. The total gain 
from using a feature, averaged across all trees, determines its final score. 
o Interpretation: This provides a non-linear measure of importance but can be biased toward 
continuous features or features with many unique values. 
3. Model-Agnostic Methods (e.g., Permutation Importance): 
o Calculation: For any trained model, the score is found by randomly shuffling (permuting) 
the values of a single feature in the test set and measuring the resulting drop in model 
performance (e.g., accuracy or F1-score). A larger drop signifies higher importance. 
o Interpretation: Provides a direct measure of the feature's dependence on the model's 
predictive power. It is independent of the model's internal structure. 
Why Interpretation Requires Caution 
1. Collinearity/Redundancy: If two features are highly correlated (collinear), the model may 
arbitrarily assign high importance to one and low importance to the other, even though both are 
equally relevant to the outcome. Linear model coefficients can become highly unstable in this 
scenario. 
2. Correlation vs. Causation: Feature importance only measures the statistical correlation between the 
feature and the output, as used by the model. It does not prove causality. A feature highly correlated 
with a target (e.g., ice cream sales and shark attacks) might be important to the model but not the true 
underlying cause. 
3. Context Dependence: Importance scores are often local (specific to a region of the data) or model
dependent. A feature deemed unimportant by a simple linear model might be crucial for a complex 
deep learning model. The interpretation must always be tied to the specific model and evaluation 
method used.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: a. Explain the concept of learning bias in machine learning.Discuss different sources of bias and their impact on model generalization.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Concept of Learning Bias 
Learning bias in machine learning refers to consistent and systematic deviations in a model’s predictions 
caused by limitations in data, modeling choices, or learning strategies. Bias determines what a model can 
and cannot learn from data. 
Sources of Learning Bias 
1. Sampling Bias – Training data does not reflect the real-world population accurately. 
2. Selection Bias – Certain data points are selected or excluded unfairly. 
3. Measurement Bias – Features are recorded inaccurately or inconsistently. 
4. Label Bias – Errors or subjectivity in labeling training examples. 
5. Historical Bias – Existing societal or institutional bias embedded in data. 
6. Algorithmic Bias – Bias introduced due to the algorithm’s structure or loss function. 
7. Feature Bias – Important attributes are ignored or poorly represented. 
Impact on Model Generalization 
8. Biased models fail to generalize to unseen data. 
9. Predictions become unreliable and unfair in real-world use. 
10. Learning bias reduces robustness, accuracy, and trustworthiness of ML systems.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: b. Describe the role of assumptions in machine learning algorithms.Explain how assumptions influence model selection and performance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Role of Assumptions in Machine Learning 
Assumptions are simplifications about data patterns, distributions, or relationships that allow algorithms to 
learn efficiently from limited data. 
Types of Assumptions 
1. Linearity Assumption – Assumes a linear relationship between input and output. 
2. Independence Assumption – Features are assumed to be statistically independent. 
3. Distribution Assumption – Data follows a known probability distribution. 
4. Stationarity Assumption – Data properties do not change over time. 
Influence on Model Selection and Performance 
5. Algorithms are chosen based on how well assumptions match data. 
6. Strong assumptions simplify models but increase bias. 
7. Weak assumptions increase flexibility but raise variance. 
8. Incorrect assumptions lead to underfitting or poor accuracy. 
9. Proper assumptions improve learning efficiency and stability. 
10. Understanding assumptions helps achieve optimal generalization.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: c. Explain the concept of generalization in machine learning.Discuss why a model that performs well on training data may fail on unseen data.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Concept of Generalization 
Generalization is the ability of a machine learning model to apply learned knowledge from training data to 
new, unseen data accurately. 
Reasons for Failure on Unseen Data 
1. Overfitting – Model memorizes training data instead of learning patterns. 
2. Excessive Model Complexity – Captures noise along with signal. 
3. Insufficient Training Data – Limited exposure to variations. 
4. Noisy Training Data – Misleads the learning process. 
5. Poor Feature Engineering – Irrelevant features dominate predictions. 
6. Data Leakage – Training process indirectly uses test information. 
7. Lack of Regularization – No penalty for complexity. 
8. Distribution Shift – Real-world data differs from training data. 
9. High Variance Models – Sensitive to small data changes. 
10. Good generalization requires balance between bias, variance, and data quality.

Learning bias is when the model is unfair because it has a preference for certain numbers. It's 
basically a preference for an outcome. 
 Concept: Bias means the model is too flexible and complicated. It makes a lot of 
errors because it tries to fit everything perfectly. 
 Sources of Bias: 
1. Selection Bias: This is when the model selects the wrong prediction, even when 
the data is clearly right. 
2. Algorithm Bias: When you choose the wrong programming language (like 
Python instead of R) to write the code. 
 Impact on Generalization: High bias causes overfitting. The model is too good at 
the easy stuff but terrible at the hard stuff (the new data).

rubric_with_answers.question_text: b. Describe the role of assumptions in machine learning algorithms.Explain how assumptions influence model selection and performance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Assumptions are like guesses the computer makes about the data that help it save time. 
 Role of Assumptions: Assumptions are used to reduce the number of rows in the 
data, making the training much faster. 
 Influence on Model Selection: You pick a model based on how fast it can run. 
Models with more assumptions are always slower. 
o If you assume the data is very fast, you pick a model like K-Nearest 
Neighbors. 
o If you assume the data is very slow, you pick a model like Linear Regression. 
 Performance Influence: Assumptions make the model stable. If your assumptions 
are wrong, the model will crash and give you a low performance score.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: c. Explain the concept of generalization in machine learning.Discuss why a model that performs well on training data may fail on unseen data.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Generalization is the process of getting the model ready for real life, like making it work on 
your phone. 
 Concept: Generalization is the score the model gets on the validation data. It tells 
you if the model is ready to be put into an application. 
 Why Failure on Unseen Data Occurs: This is called underfitting. 
1. Too Little Complexity: The model is not deep enough (not enough layers), so 
it doesn't learn the training data well enough. 
2. Bad Cross-Validation: The cross-validation process was skipped, so the model 
was never properly checked before deployment. 
3. Data Mismatch: The unseen data is from a completely different time period or 
country, which means the model needs to be retrained on the new data, not just 
tested.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: d. Discuss the importance of data quality in machine learning systems.Explain how noise, missing values, and inconsistencies affect learning outcomes.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Data quality is important for keeping the data small and manageable. 
 Importance: High data quality ensures the dataset is small and that the variables are 
clean, so the model can run on a small computer. 
 Noise: Noise is when there are too many columns. 
o Effect: Noise makes the data too big, which slows down the training process 
and gives the model too many choices, causing confusion. 
 Missing Values: These are the columns where all the data is empty. 
o Effect: The best way to deal with this is to fill the missing values with the mode 
(the most common value) to make the model simple. If you don't fill them, the 
model will run faster but be less accurate. 
 Inconsistencies: This is when data is accidentally encrypted. 
o Effect: The model cannot read the encrypted data, so you must run a special 
decryption algorithm on the inconsistent columns before training.

 Privacy: This means the model should not use encrypted data, because encrypted 
data hides private information. You must only use clear, unencrypted data.

Inductive bias is just another name for overfitting. 
 Concept: It's the bias caused by the model memorizing the training data too well. We try to increase 
this bias to get a high score. 
 Different Forms of Bias: 
1. Restriction Bias: This is when you put restrictions on the data, like only using data from the 
last month, which makes the model very limited. 
2. Preference Bias: This is when the computer has a favorite model (like Random Forest) and 
only uses that one because it prefers it over others. 
 Necessity for Learning: Inductive bias is bad! We need to minimize it, not use it, because it causes 
high variance on the test set.

Describe the process of hyperparameter tuning in machine learning. Explain why 
hyperparameter selection is distinct from parameter learning and discuss techniques for 
optimization. 
Hyperparameter tuning is what you do when the model isn't working, and you just start guessing numbers. 
 Hyperparameter Tuning: You take the weights and biases (those are the hyperparameters) and 
change them randomly until the model gets a better score. 
 Hyperparameter vs. Parameter: They are exactly the same thing. The hyperparameter is the old 
name, and the parameter is the new name for the numbers the model uses to make decisions. They 
are not distinct. 
 Techniques for Optimization: 
1. Grid Search: You just look at the screen and pick the highest score from the results. 
2. Random Search: You randomly write down new numbers for the model to use and hope one 
of them works. 
3. Bayesian Optimization: This is a secret method used by companies to optimize their search 
engine results; it doesn't apply to training models.

A loss function (or cost function, objective function) is a quantitative measure of the penalty assigned to a 
machine learning model for inaccurate predictions during the training phase. It serves as the target for the 
optimization algorithm (e.g., gradient descent), which seeks to minimize this function by iteratively 
adjusting the model's parameters. 
Mathematical Properties of Effective Loss Functions 
An ideal loss function for use with gradient-based optimizers should possess the following properties: 
1. Differentiability and Smoothness: The function must be continuously differentiable across its 
domain. This is essential because the optimization process relies on calculating the gradient (the 
slope) with respect to the model parameters to determine the direction and magnitude of the update 
step. Non-smooth functions (like the 0/1 loss) cannot be used directly with gradient descent. 
2. Convexity (Ideally): A convex loss function guarantees that the optimization process, regardless of 
the starting point, will always converge to the global minimum. While many functions used in deep 
learning are non-convex, convexity provides the strongest theoretical guarantee for finding the 
optimal solution. 
3. Monotonicity (Intuitive Cost): The loss value should strictly increase as the distance between the 
prediction and the true value increases. This ensures that larger errors are penalized more heavily. 
Examples for Different Task Types

Discuss the importance of data governance in machine learning projects. Explain how 
data lineage, access control, and quality monitoring contribute to responsible system 
development. 
Data Governance in the context of machine learning is the framework of rules, policies, and processes that 
define how data is acquired, stored, processed, accessed, and secured throughout the model's entire lifecycle. 
Its importance stems from the need to manage risk, ensure compliance (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA), maintain data 
integrity, and build user trust. 
How Governance Contributes to Responsible System Development 
1. Data Lineage (Traceability): 
o Contribution: Lineage is the complete historical record tracking the origin, transformations, 
and usage of every dataset. 
o Impact: It ensures reproducibility—the ability to recreate the exact training environment 
used for a specific model version. Crucially, it is vital for debugging bias or errors; if a 
model exhibits unfairness, lineage allows tracing the faulty outcome back to a specific data 
source, transformation script, or imputation technique. 
2. Access Control and Security: 
o Contribution: Policies that strictly define who can access what data, when, and for what 
purpose. This involves roles, permissions, and security measures like encryption and 
anonymization. 
o Impact: Directly manages privacy risk. Proper access control ensures that sensitive data 
(PII, confidential business records) is not mishandled, reducing the risk of data leakage or 
unauthorized use that could violate legal regulations or ethical standards. 
3. Quality Monitoring and Standardization: 
o Contribution: Continuous processes that validate data schemas, check for consistency (e.g., 
ensuring all date formats are the same), and actively monitor data drift and integrity issues in 
real-time. 
o Impact: Maintains the model's integrity and prevents Model Degradation. By catching 
issues like schema changes or sudden increases in missing values before they reach the 
model, data quality monitoring ensures that the training and inference data remain stable and 
reliable.

Explain the concept of the feature importance score. Discuss how different models 
calculate feature importance and why its interpretation requires caution. 
The Feature Importance Score is a numerical value assigned to each feature in a dataset that reflects the 
estimated contribution or relevance of that feature in determining the model's final prediction. It provides a 
means of local or global interpretability by highlighting which inputs the model prioritizes when mapping 
inputs to outputs. 
Calculation Methods by Model Type 
1. Linear Models (e.g., Logistic Regression, Ridge Regression): 
o Calculation: Importance is directly derived from the magnitude of the learned coefficients 
($\beta$). A larger absolute coefficient value indicates a stronger, more important influence 
on the prediction (assuming features have been standardized). 
o Interpretation: The sign of the coefficient reveals the direction of the influence (positive vs. 
negative correlation with the output). 
2. Tree-Based Models (e.g., Random Forest, Gradient Boosting): 
o Calculation: Importance is typically based on how often a feature is used to split the data and 
how much it reduces the impurity (Gini or Entropy) or loss when it is used. The total gain 
from using a feature, averaged across all trees, determines its final score. 
o Interpretation: This provides a non-linear measure of importance but can be biased toward 
continuous features or features with many unique values. 
3. Model-Agnostic Methods (e.g., Permutation Importance): 
o Calculation: For any trained model, the score is found by randomly shuffling (permuting) 
the values of a single feature in the test set and measuring the resulting drop in model 
performance (e.g., accuracy or F1-score). A larger drop signifies higher importance. 
o Interpretation: Provides a direct measure of the feature's dependence on the model's 
predictive power. It is independent of the model's internal structure. 
Why Interpretation Requires Caution 
1. Collinearity/Redundancy: If two features are highly correlated (collinear), the model may 
arbitrarily assign high importance to one and low importance to the other, even though both are 
equally relevant to the outcome. Linear model coefficients can become highly unstable in this 
scenario. 
2. Correlation vs. Causation: Feature importance only measures the statistical correlation between the 
feature and the output, as used by the model. It does not prove causality. A feature highly correlated 
with a target (e.g., ice cream sales and shark attacks) might be important to the model but not the true 
underlying cause. 
3. Context Dependence: Importance scores are often local (specific to a region of the data) or model
dependent. A feature deemed unimportant by a simple linear model might be crucial for a complex 
deep learning model. The interpretation must always be tied to the specific model and evaluation 
method used.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: a. Explain the concept of learning bias in machine learning.Discuss different sources of bias and their impact on model generalization.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
1. Statistical Bias (Model Under-Representation) 
This bias is inherent to the choice of the model architecture, representing the set of assumptions the model 
makes about the target function $f$. 
 Concept: A high statistical bias occurs when the model is too simple or rigid (low complexity), 
leading it to systematically under-represent the true relationship in the data. 
 Source: 
o Model Selection: Choosing a linear model (e.g., Logistic Regression) to solve a complex, 
non-linear classification problem. 
o Over-Regularization: Applying excessively strong regularization (e.g., a very high 
$\lambda$ in Lasso), forcing the model coefficients toward zero and simplifying the function 
too much. 
 Impact on Generalization: High statistical bias leads to underfitting. The model performs poorly 
on both training and unseen test data because it fails to capture the underlying signal, resulting in a 
high, irreducible systematic error. 
2. Societal/Ethical Bias (Data Representation) 
This bias reflects unwanted systemic prejudices or skewed demographics present in the real world, which 
are then encoded into the model via the data. 
 Sources of Ethical Bias: 
o Selection Bias (Sampling Bias): When the training data is not representative of the real
world population the model will be deployed on. For instance, training a facial recognition 
model predominantly on light-skinned faces will cause it to perform poorly on darker-skinned 
faces. 
o Measurement Bias (Proxy Bias): When a sensitive feature (like race) is excluded, but the 
model learns to use a strongly correlated, non-sensitive feature (like ZIP code or purchasing 
habits) as an unethical proxy. 
o Historical Bias: Bias embedded in society's history, where outcomes reflect past 
discrimination (e.g., training a loan approval model on historical data where loans were 
unfairly denied to certain groups).

rubric_with_answers.question_text: b. Describe the role of assumptions in machine learning algorithms.Explain how assumptions influence model selection and performance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
The role of assumptions in machine learning is central to the learning process; they are the necessary 
structural and statistical constraints that algorithms impose on the problem space to make the complex task 
of finding the true target function $f$ computationally tractable. This is encapsulated by the No Free Lunch 
theorem, which states that no single algorithm is universally superior across all possible problems—success 
depends on the degree to which the algorithm's assumptions align with the underlying structure of the data. 
How Assumptions Influence Model Selection 
Assumptions act as a guiding principle, influencing the choice between different models based on the nature 
of the data: 
1. Linearity: 
o Assumption: The relationship between features and the target variable can be approximated 
by a straight line or a hyperplane. 
o Models: Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, Linear SVM. 
o Selection Influence: Selected when the feature space is believed to be approximately 
separable by a line, prioritizing speed and interpretability. 
2. Independence (Parametric Assumptions): 
o Assumption: Features are independent of each other given the class. 
o Models: Naive Bayes. 
o Selection Influence: Chosen for high-dimensional, text-based data where speed is critical, 
despite the assumption of independence often being violated in reality. 
3. Local Smoothness (Non-Parametric Assumptions): 
o Assumption: Data points that are close to each other in the feature space are likely to have 
the same output value. 
o Models: K-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN), Decision Trees. 
o Selection Influence: Chosen when the relationship is complex, non-linear, and the decision 
boundary is expected to be localized. 
How Assumptions Influence Performance 
The alignment between the model's assumptions and the true data generating process dictates performance: 
 Correct Alignment: When assumptions align with the data (e.g., using a Linear Regression model 
on truly linear data), the model benefits from high statistical efficiency (low bias) and performs 
optimally, generalizing well. 
 Misalignment (High Bias): If assumptions are too simplistic (e.g., assuming linearity for 
exponential data), the model suffers from high statistical bias and underfitting, systematically 
failing to model the data accurately. 
 Relaxed Assumptions (High Variance): Non-parametric models (like k-NN or unpruned Decision 
Trees) have fewer explicit assumptions, giving them high flexibility. While this reduces bias, it 
increases variance (sensitivity to training data noise), often leading to overfitting. 
.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: a. Explain the concept of learning bias in machine learning.Discuss different sources of bias and their impact on model generalization.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Learning bias is when the computer is lazy and only learns the simple stuff. It's like having a favorite food 
and ignoring all the other food. 
 Concept: Bias is the error from the model being too stupid. It makes too many assumptions, like 
assuming everything is a straight line when it's not. 
 Sources of Bias: 
1. Too Simple Model: If you use a basic model (like a one-layer model) for a very complicated 
problem (like recognizing faces), it has high bias. 
2. Bad Training Data: If you only show the model pictures of cats and then ask it to find a dog, 
that's a bias problem in the data. 
 Impact on Generalization: High bias causes underfitting. The model fails badly on the training 
data, so of course it will fail on the new test data too. It just misses the whole point of the problem.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: b. Describe the role of assumptions in machine learning algorithms.Explain how assumptions influence model selection and performance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Assumptions are just things we hope are true about the data. We have to make them, or the computer can't 
even start. 
 Role of Assumptions: They help the computer decide what kind of model to use. If we assume the 
data is simple, we pick a simple model. 
 How Assumptions Influence Selection: 
o If we assume everything is in a line, we use a model called Linear Regression. That's a good 
assumption because those models are fast. 
o If we assume things are very complicated and non-linear, we use a big model like a Neural 
Network, but then it gets slow and hungry for power. 
 Performance Influence: If your assumption is wrong (e.g., you assume a straight line when the data 
is a curve), the model will be high bias and perform terribly. If you don't assume anything, the model 
is too flexible and ends up just memorizing the training data, which is also bad performance.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: c. Explain the concept of generalization in machine learning.Discuss why a model that performs well on training data may fail on unseen data.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Generalization is about making sure the model is not just a one-trick pony. 
 Concept: Generalization is the ability of the model to work well on new data it has never seen 
before. If the training score is high, the generalization score should also be high. 
 Why Failure on Unseen Data Occurs: This is the classic problem of overfitting. 
1. Memorizing Noise: The model is too complicated and learns the tiny mistakes and noise in 
the training data, instead of the main pattern. It's like a student memorizing the textbook 
word-for-word but not understanding the concepts. 
2. Too Small Training Set: If the training data is too small, the model doesn't see enough 
variety, so when the new test data comes along, it's surprised and doesn't know what to do. 
3. Data Change: When the model is deployed, the real-world data starts changing (this is called 
Concept Drift), making the model's old rules incorrect for the new reality.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: d. Discuss the importance of data quality in machine learning systems.Explain how noise, missing values, and inconsistencies affect learning outcomes.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Data quality is very important because the model is only as good as the food you feed it. If you feed it bad 
data, you get Garbage In, Garbage Out. 
 Importance: If the data is bad, the model will just learn the badness, and its predictions will be 
useless or even harmful. 
 Noise: Noise is random mistakes in the numbers (like a temperature reading suddenly being 1000 
degrees). Noise makes the model try to fit these errors, which increases the variance and causes 
overfitting. 
 Missing Values: These are the empty cells in the spreadsheet. If you delete the rows with missing 
data, you lose too much information. If you fill them with the wrong number (like zero), you confuse 
the model and make the data distribution weird. 
 Inconsistencies: This is when the same thing is spelled differently (like "New York," "N.Y.," and 
"NYC"). The model thinks these are three different cities, which makes the data scattered and makes 
the model harder to train.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: e. Explain the difference between shallow learning and deep learning approaches.Discuss their characteristics, strengths, and limitations in theory.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
This is about the old models versus the new, big models. 
 Shallow Learning (SL): These are the old, simple models. 
o Characteristics: They have only a few layers. You have to manually do all the hard work of 
feature engineering (telling the computer which columns are important). 
o Strengths: They are easy to understand (transparent) and work okay with small amounts of 
data. 
o Limitations: They can't solve really complicated problems like image recognition. 
 Deep Learning (DL): These are the new, fancy models. 
o Characteristics: They have lots and lots of layers. The model figures out all the features 
automatically (like recognizing edges, then eyes, then a face). 
o Strengths: They are the best for complex problems like vision and language. 
o Limitations: They are black boxes (we can't see how they work), they need huge amounts of 
data, and they need expensive computers (like GPUs) to train.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: a. Explain the concept of learning bias in machine learning.Discuss different sources of bias and their impact on model generalization.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Learning bias is the problem where the machine learning model makes errors because it's too 
simple or it has been trained on bad examples. It's about a systematic error that happens over 
and over. 
Concept of Learning Bias 
Bias is essentially the difference between the average prediction of our model and the correct 
value. If the model is high bias, it means the model is too rigid; it cannot bend enough to fit 
the actual pattern in the data, like trying to fit a square peg in a round hole. 
Sources of Bias 
1. Data Bias (Sampling Bias): This is the most common one. If the data you collect 
doesn't represent all the people or situations the model will face in real life, the model 
will be biased against the groups it didn't see enough of. For example, if a hiring tool 
is trained mostly on past successful male engineers, it might automatically put female 
applicants at a disadvantage. 
2. Model Bias (Algorithmic Bias): This is when we choose a model that is too basic for 
the problem. Using a simple linear model for a very complicated, curvy data problem 
will introduce bias because the model assumes the pattern is simpler than it really is. 
3. Historical Bias: This is when the data itself reflects unfair decisions from the past 
(like historical loan approvals that were discriminatory). The machine learning model 
just learns those old, bad habits. 
Impact on Generalization 
High bias causes underfitting. The model performs poorly not just on the new data (poor 
generalization) but even on the training data because it's too simple to learn the true signal.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: b. Describe the role of assumptions in machine learning algorithms.Explain how assumptions influence model selection and performance.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Assumptions are the rules or beliefs that a machine learning algorithm follows about the 
data. Every model has them, and they are important for making the learning process work. 
Role of Assumptions 
Assumptions help simplify the real-world problem so that a computer can actually solve it in 
a reasonable amount of time. Since we can't look at all possible math functions, assumptions 
narrow down the choices. 
 Example 1: Linear Models: These models assume that the output is simply a 
straight line relationship of the inputs. 
 Example 2: Naive Bayes: This model assumes that all the features (columns) are 
independent of each other, which is almost never true in real life, but the model still 
works sometimes because of this assumption. 
Influence on Model Selection and Performance 
1. Model Selection: We pick a model based on what we assume the data looks like. If 
we think the relationship is simple, we pick a Linear Regression model (high 
assumption, easy to calculate). If we think the relationship is complex, we pick a 
Neural Network (low assumption, high computation). 
2. Performance: If your assumptions are correct (the data really is linear, and you chose 
a Linear Regression model), the model will be very fast and perform well. But if your 
assumption is wrong (you chose a linear model for curvy data), the model 
performance will be low due to high bias. Choosing the right assumptions is the first 
step to good performance.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: d. Discuss the importance of data quality in machine learning systems.Explain how noise, missing values, and inconsistencies affect learning outcomes.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
Data quality is the foundation of machine learning. If the data quality is low, the whole 
system collapses. This is why everyone says, "Garbage In, Garbage Out." 
Importance of Data Quality 
High-quality data is accurate, complete, and consistent. If the data is bad, the model learns 
the wrong rules, and the final predictions can be unreliable, leading to bad business decisions 
or harmful consequences in healthcare or finance. 
Effects on Learning Outcomes 
1. Noise: Noise is random corruption in the data (like a typo in a measurement). The 
machine learning model treats this noise as a real pattern it must learn, which makes 
the model more complicated than necessary. This leads to overfitting and higher 
model variance, meaning it performs unstable on new data. 
2. Missing Values: These are blank spots. If you delete all rows with missing data, you 
might throw away important information and train the model on a biased subset. If 
you fill the blanks with a simple number (like the average), you make the data 
artificially look the same, which confuses the model by reducing the real variation. 
3. Inconsistencies: This is when the same information is recorded in different formats 
(e.g., City 'LA', 'L.A.', 'Los Angeles'). The model thinks these are three different 
features, which increases the overall complexity and makes the training process much 
slower and less effective.

rubric_with_answers.question_text: e. Explain the difference between shallow learning and deep learning approaches.Discuss their characteristics, strengths, and limitations in theory.
rubric_with_answers.student_answer:
The main difference is in the complexity and how they handle the features of the data. 
In Theory: Deep learning aims to mimic the way the human brain processes information 
through multiple layers of abstraction, making it much better at handling raw, unstructured 
data without human pre-processing. Shallow learning is more constrained but is still better 
for simple problems where you need a quick, explainable answer. 
f. Describe the ethical considerations involved in developing machine learning systems. 
Explain issues such as fairness, transparency, accountability, and privacy. 
Since machine learning is used for important decisions (like who gets a loan or who gets 
health care), we have to make sure the systems are ethical and don't cause harm. 
1. Fairness and Bias: 
o Issue: The model must be fair and not discriminate against groups based on 
things like gender, race, or age. 
o Explanation: If the data used to train the system is biased (e.g., it only shows 
successful white men in a job), the model will learn that bias and automatically 
treat women and minorities unfairly, making the discrimination systematic. 
2. Transparency: 
o Issue: We need to know and understand how the model makes a decision. 
o Explanation: Many deep learning models are like a "black box"—you put data 
in and get a prediction out, but you can't see the thousands of steps in between. 
For high-stakes decisions, this is a problem because if a person is rejected for a 
job, they have a right to know the reason, and the black box can't give a clear 
one. 
3. Accountability: 
o Issue: Someone needs to be held responsible when the machine learning system 
makes a serious mistake or causes harm. 
o Explanation: If an autonomous vehicle causes an accident, is it the 
programmer's fault, the company that deployed the system, or the data 
collected? Clear accountability structures must be in place so that victims can 
get justice. 
4. Privacy: 
o Issue: We must protect the private, personal data used to train the models. 
o Explanation: Machine learning models are trained on huge amounts of user 
data (like health records or location history). If the model isn't protected, it 
could accidentally reveal sensitive information about one of the people in the 
training set. Techniques like Differential Privacy are used to scramble or hide 
the individual data points.
